datatype/AdReward.d: The AdReward data type represents a reward that can be used to trigger a rewarded video ad to play on the client via AdService:ShowRewardedVideoAdAsync().
datatype/AdReward.s: A reward that can be granted to users upon watching rewarded video ads.

datatype/Axes.d:
The Axes data type contains a set of enabled 3D axes, represented as a bitmask. It is used by the ArcHandles class through its Axes property to control which rotation arc handles are visible.

Axes exposes three axis properties (X, Y, Z) and six face properties (Top, Bottom, Left, Right, Front, Back). Because faces map to their corresponding axis, face pairs always share the same value: Top and Bottom both reflect the Y axis, Left and Right both reflect the X axis, and Front and Back both reflect the Z axis.

-- Enable arc handles for the X and Y axes only
local arcHandles = Instance.new("ArcHandles")
arcHandles.Axes = Axes.new(Enum.Axis.X, Enum.Axis.Y)

Like most data types on Roblox, the Axes data type is immutable: you cannot assign to its properties once created.
datatype/Axes.s: The `Axes` data type is for the `Class.ArcHandles` class to control which rotation axes are currently enabled.

m.d: Whether the X axis is enabled. Defaults to false when constructed via Axes.new() with no arguments. This property is equivalent to both Left and Right, which also reflect the X axis state.
m.s: Whether the X axis is enabled.

m.d: Whether the Y axis is enabled. Defaults to false when constructed via Axes.new() with no arguments. This property is equivalent to both Top and Bottom, which also reflect the Y axis state.
m.s: Whether the Y axis is enabled.

m.d: Whether the Z axis is enabled. Defaults to false when constructed via Axes.new() with no arguments. This property is equivalent to both Front and Back, which also reflect the Z axis state.
m.s: Whether the Z axis is enabled.

m.d: Whether the top face is included. This corresponds to the positive Y direction (NormalId.Top) and is always equal to the Y property. Defaults to false.
m.s: Whether the top face is included.

m.d: Whether the bottom face is included. This corresponds to the negative Y direction (NormalId.Bottom) and is always equal to the Y property. Defaults to false.
m.s: Whether the bottom face is included.

m.d: Whether the left face is included. This corresponds to the negative X direction (NormalId.Left) and is always equal to the X property. Defaults to false.
m.s: Whether the left face is included.

m.d: Whether the right face is included. This corresponds to the positive X direction (NormalId.Right) and is always equal to the X property. Defaults to false.
m.s: Whether the right face is included.

m.d: Whether the back face is included. This corresponds to the positive Z direction (NormalId.Back) and is always equal to the Z property. Defaults to false.
m.s: Whether the back face is included.

m.d: Whether the front face is included. This corresponds to the negative Z direction (NormalId.Front) and is always equal to the Z property. Defaults to false.
m.s: Whether the front face is included.

m.d:
Creates a new Axes from up to 6 Axis or NormalId values. Each NormalId is converted to its corresponding axis (for example, NormalId.Top and NormalId.Bottom both enable the Y axis). Calling Axes.new() with no arguments returns an Axes with all properties set to false.

-- Using Enum.Axis values
local axes = Axes.new(Enum.Axis.X, Enum.Axis.Z)
print(axes.X) -- true
print(axes.Y) -- false

-- Using Enum.NormalId values (converted to axes)
local axes2 = Axes.new(Enum.NormalId.Top, Enum.NormalId.Right)
print(axes2.Y) -- true (Top -> Y axis)
print(axes2.X) -- true (Right -> X axis)
m.s: Creates a new Axes using list of axes and/or faces. NormalIds (faces) are converted to the corresponding axes.

p.s: Any combination of Axis and/or NormalId values (up to 6) specifying which axes to enable.

datatype/BrickColor.d:
The BrickColor data type provides a predefined list of named colors, not to be confused with Color3, a more general data type that describes RGB colors. The following code shows how to use BrickColor.new() to declare the BrickColor property of a Part.

local part = Instance.new("Part")

-- By color name
part.BrickColor = BrickColor.new("Pastel Blue")
print(part.BrickColor) --> Pastel Blue

-- By numerical index
part.BrickColor = BrickColor.new(11)
print(part.BrickColor) --> Pastel Blue

-- By RGB decimal values in range of 0-1
part.BrickColor = BrickColor.new(0.502, 0.734, 0.859)
print(part.BrickColor) --> Pastel Blue

-- By palette index
part.BrickColor = BrickColor.palette(70)
print(part.BrickColor) --> Gold

datatype/BrickColor.s: A data type that provides a predefined list of named colors.

m.d: The unique number that identifies the BrickColor. This is the same integer used by BrickColor.new() to construct the color and corresponds to the Number column in the color table above. Read-only.
m.s: The unique number that identifies the `Datatype.BrickColor`.

kid.simple: The ID number of this BrickColor, the same number you can pass to BrickColor.new. Read-only.
kid.example: print(BrickColor.new("Pastel Blue").Number) --> 11

m.d: The red component of the BrickColor (between 0 and 1). This is equivalent to BrickColor.Color.R. Read-only.
m.s: The red component of the `Datatype.BrickColor` (between 0 and 1).

kid.simple: How much red is in this BrickColor, from 0 to 1. Same as .Color.R. Read-only.
kid.example: print(BrickColor.new("Really red").r) --> 1

m.d: The green component of the BrickColor (between 0 and 1). This is equivalent to BrickColor.Color.G. Read-only.
m.s: The green component of the `Datatype.BrickColor` (between 0 and 1).

kid.simple: How much green is in this BrickColor, from 0 to 1. Same as .Color.G. Read-only.
kid.example: print(BrickColor.new("Lime green").g) --> 1

m.d: The blue component of the BrickColor (between 0 and 1). This is equivalent to BrickColor.Color.B. Read-only.
m.s: The blue component of the `Datatype.BrickColor` (between 0 and 1).

kid.simple: How much blue is in this BrickColor, from 0 to 1. Same as .Color.B. Read-only.
kid.example: print(BrickColor.new("Really blue").b) --> 1

m.d: The name associated with the BrickColor, for example "Pastel Blue". This is the same string accepted by BrickColor.new(). Read-only.
m.s: The name associated with the `Datatype.BrickColor`.

kid.simple: The name of this BrickColor, like "Pastel Blue". It is the same text you can give to BrickColor.new. Read-only.
kid.example:
local c = BrickColor.random()
print("You got: " .. c.Name)

m.d: The Color3 associated with the BrickColor. The individual components of this value are the same as BrickColor.r, BrickColor.g, and BrickColor.b. Read-only.
m.s: The `Datatype.Color3` associated with the `Datatype.BrickColor`.

kid.simple: The same color as a Color3. Use it when something needs a Color3, like a GUI background, but you started with a BrickColor. Read-only.
kid.example:
local label = Instance.new("TextLabel")
label.BackgroundColor3 = BrickColor.new("Bright orange").Color

m.d: Constructs a BrickColor from its numerical index (Number in color reference table). If the provided number does not correspond to a valid BrickColor, the constructor returns the default "Medium stone grey".
m.s: Constructs a `Datatype.BrickColor` from its numerical index.

p.s: The unique numerical index that identifies a brick color.

kid.simple: Makes a BrickColor. You can give it a name ("Bright red"), an ID number (11), three numbers from 0 to 1 for red, green, blue, or a Color3. With colors, it finds the closest named color in the list. If the name or number does not exist, you get "Medium stone grey".
kid.example:
local byName = BrickColor.new("Pastel Blue")
local byNumber = BrickColor.new(11)               -- also Pastel Blue
local byRGB = BrickColor.new(0.502, 0.734, 0.859) -- closest match: Pastel Blue
local byColor3 = BrickColor.new(Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0)) -- closest to pure red
print(byName, byNumber, byRGB)
kid.gotcha: A typo in the name gives gray, not an error. Print the result if a color looks wrong.

m.d: Constructs a BrickColor from its zero-based 128-color palette index (Palette Index in color reference table). This is the same palette shown in the Studio color picker. An error is thrown if the index is out of bounds.
m.s: Constructs a `Datatype.BrickColor` from its palette index.

p.s: A zero-based index into the 128-color palette (0 through 127).

kid.simple: Makes a BrickColor from its spot in the 128-color palette (the grid in Studio's color picker). Spots go from 0 to 127.
kid.example:
local gold = BrickColor.palette(70)
print(gold) --> Gold
kid.gotcha: Numbers outside 0 to 127 throw an error.

m.d: Returns a random BrickColor selected from the 128-color palette. Each call may return a different color.
m.s: Returns a random `Datatype.BrickColor`.

kid.simple: Gives a random BrickColor from the 128-color palette. Each call can give a different one.
kid.example:
local part = workspace:FindFirstChild("Part")
if part then
	part.BrickColor = BrickColor.random()
end

m.d: Returns the "White" BrickColor.
m.s: Returns the "White" `Datatype.BrickColor`.

kid.simple: A shortcut that gives the "White" BrickColor.
kid.example:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.BrickColor = BrickColor.White()
part.Parent = workspace

m.d: Returns the "Medium stone grey" BrickColor. This is the same color used as the default when a BrickColor cannot be resolved.
m.s: Returns the "Medium stone grey" `Datatype.BrickColor`.

kid.simple: A shortcut that gives "Medium stone grey", the default gray. It is also what you get when a name or number is not found.
kid.example: print(BrickColor.Gray()) --> Medium stone grey

m.d: Returns the "Dark stone grey" BrickColor.
m.s: Returns the "Dark stone grey" `Datatype.BrickColor`.

kid.simple: A shortcut that gives the "Dark stone grey" BrickColor.
kid.example: print(BrickColor.DarkGray()) --> Dark stone grey

m.d: Returns the "Black" BrickColor.
m.s: Returns the "Black" `Datatype.BrickColor`.

kid.simple: A shortcut that gives the "Black" BrickColor.
kid.example: print(BrickColor.Black()) --> Black

m.d: Returns the "Bright red" BrickColor.
m.s: Returns the "Bright red" `Datatype.BrickColor`.

kid.simple: A shortcut that gives the "Bright red" BrickColor.
kid.example: print(BrickColor.Red()) --> Bright red

m.d: Returns the "Bright yellow" BrickColor.
m.s: Returns the "Bright yellow" `Datatype.BrickColor`.

kid.simple: A shortcut that gives the "Bright yellow" BrickColor.
kid.example: print(BrickColor.Yellow()) --> Bright yellow

m.d: Returns the "Dark green" BrickColor.
m.s: Returns the "Dark green" `Datatype.BrickColor`.

kid.simple: A shortcut that gives the "Dark green" BrickColor. Note it is dark green, not bright green.
kid.example: print(BrickColor.Green()) --> Dark green

m.d: Returns the "Bright blue" BrickColor.
m.s: Returns the "Bright blue" `Datatype.BrickColor`.

kid.simple: A shortcut that gives the "Bright blue" BrickColor.
kid.example: print(BrickColor.Blue()) --> Bright blue

kid.simple: A BrickColor is a color picked from Roblox's fixed list of named colors, like "Bright red", "Lime green", or "Pastel Blue". Each one has a name and a number. It is the older, simpler way to color parts. For any exact color you want, use Color3 instead.
kid.analogy: BrickColor is like a box of crayons with a set number of colors, each with a name printed on it. Color3 is like a paint mixer where you can make any shade.
whenToUse: Coloring a part by a friendly name, like BrickColor.new("Really red")
Picking a random color from the list with BrickColor.random()
Checking a team's color, since Team.TeamColor is a BrickColor
Matching a part to the palette shown in Studio's color picker
kid.where: Works in any script on the server or client. Make one with BrickColor.new, BrickColor.palette, BrickColor.random, or shortcuts like BrickColor.Red().

terms.named color: One of the colors in Roblox's built-in list, each with an exact name like "Bright blue".
terms.Number: Every BrickColor has an ID number. For example "Pastel Blue" is number 11.
terms.palette: A grid of 128 BrickColors, the same ones shown in Studio's BrickColor picker. Palette spots are numbered 0 to 127.
terms.Color3: The more flexible color type that can be any mix of red, green, and blue.
terms.read-only: You can look at the value but not change it.

examples.title: Color a part three different ways
examples.code:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Anchored = true
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)
part.Parent = workspace

part.BrickColor = BrickColor.new("Really red") -- by name
task.wait(1)
part.BrickColor = BrickColor.new(11)           -- by number (Pastel Blue)
task.wait(1)
part.BrickColor = BrickColor.random()          -- a surprise color
print(part.BrickColor.Name)
explain: We make an anchored part so it floats in place.
BrickColor.new("Really red") picks a color by its exact name.
BrickColor.new(11) picks by number. 11 is Pastel Blue.
BrickColor.random() picks a random color from the 128-color palette, and we print its name.

examples.title: Turn a part a random color when touched
examples.place: Script inside a Part in Workspace
examples.code:
local part = script.Parent

part.Touched:Connect(function(otherPart)
	-- Only react to players, not other parts
	local humanoid = otherPart.Parent:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
	if humanoid then
		part.BrickColor = BrickColor.random()
	end
end)
explain: script.Parent is the part this Script is inside.
Touched fires whenever something bumps the part.
We check for a Humanoid so only characters change the color.
BrickColor.random() gives a new random named color.

gotchas: Names must match exactly, including spaces and capitals. If the name is wrong, you silently get "Medium stone grey" instead of an error.
BrickColor only has a fixed list of colors. If you need an exact shade, use part.Color with a Color3.
BrickColor.palette(n) errors if n is not between 0 and 127.

datatype/CFrame.d:
The CFrame data type, short for coordinate frame, describes a 3D position and orientation. It is made up of a positional component and a rotational component and includes essential arithmetic operations for working with 3D data on Roblox.

-- Create a CFrame at a certain position and Euler rotation
local cf = CFrame.new(0, 5, 0) * CFrame.fromEulerAngles(math.rad(45), 0, 0)

For an introduction to the CFrame data type, see CFrames.

Positional Component

The positional component is available as a Vector3. In addition, the components of a CFrame object's position are also available in the X, Y and Z properties like a Vector3.

Rotational Component

CFrame stores 3D rotation data in a 3×3 rotation matrix. These values are returned by the CFrame:GetComponents() function after the x, y and z positional values. This matrix is used internally when doing calculations involving rotations, using radians as their unit (for conversion from one to the other, use math.rad() or math.deg()). For more information on how the Roblox Engine performs rotations, see RotationOrder.

The table below represents the components of a CFrame object's rotation matrix and their relationship with the available vector properties such as LookVector and RightVector. Although the individual components of the rotation matrix are rarely useful by themselves, the vector properties which derive from them are much more useful.

XVector, RightVector YVector, UpVector ZVector, -LookVector†
R00 R01 R02
R10 R11 R12
R20 R21 R22
datatype/CFrame.s: A data type that represents both a 3D position and orientation.

m.d: An identity CFrame with no translation or rotation. This property is a constant and must be accessed globally as opposed to through an individual CFrame object.
m.s: An identity `Datatype.CFrame` with no translation or rotation.

kid.simple: The "do nothing" CFrame: position (0, 0, 0) and no rotation. Same as `CFrame.new()`. Multiplying any CFrame by it leaves it unchanged.
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.new(1, 2, 3)
print(cf * CFrame.identity == cf) --> true
kid.gotcha: Use it as `CFrame.identity`, not on a CFrame you made (`myCFrame.identity` is not how it is meant to be used).

m.d: The positional component of the CFrame as a Vector3. Equivalent to Vector3.new(cf.X, cf.Y, cf.Z).
m.s: The 3D position of the `Datatype.CFrame`.

kid.simple: The position part of the CFrame as a Vector3: where it is in the world.
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.new(3, 7, -2) * CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(45), 0)
print(cf.Position) --> 3, 7, -2  (turning does not change the position)
kid.gotcha: You cannot set it: `cf.Position = ...` errors. Make a new CFrame instead, for example `CFrame.new(newPos) * cf.Rotation`.

m.d: A copy of the CFrame with the positional component set to (0, 0, 0), retaining only the rotational component. Useful for isolating a CFrame object's orientation independent of its position.
m.s: A copy of the `Datatype.CFrame` with no translation.

kid.simple: A copy of the CFrame with the same turning but the position moved to (0, 0, 0). Use it when you only care which way something faces, or to keep a part's rotation while moving it somewhere new.
kid.example:
local part = workspace.Part
local newSpot = Vector3.new(0, 20, 0)
-- Move the part to newSpot but keep the way it is facing
part.CFrame = CFrame.new(newSpot) * part.CFrame.Rotation

m.d: The X component of the CFrame object's world-space position. Equivalent to CFrame.Position.X.
m.s: The **X** coordinate of the position.

kid.simple: The X number of the position (left/right in the world). Same as `cf.Position.X`.
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.new(3, 7, -2)
print(cf.X) --> 3

m.d: The Y component of the CFrame object's world-space position. Equivalent to CFrame.Position.Y.
m.s: The **Y** coordinate of the position.

kid.simple: The Y number of the position (how high up). Same as `cf.Position.Y`.
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.new(3, 7, -2)
print(cf.Y) --> 7

m.d: The Z component of the CFrame object's world-space position. Equivalent to CFrame.Position.Z.
m.s: The **Z** coordinate of the position.

kid.simple: The Z number of the position (forward/back in the world). Same as `cf.Position.Z`.
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.new(3, 7, -2)
print(cf.Z) --> -2

m.d:
The forward-direction component of the CFrame object's orientation, equivalent to the negated ZVector or the negated third column of the rotation matrix.

local cf = CFrame.new(0, 0, 0)
local x, y, z, R00, R01, R02, R10, R11, R12, R20, R21, R22 = cf:GetComponents()

print(cf.LookVector)     --> (-0, -0, -1)
print(-cf.ZVector)       --> (-0, -0, -1)
print(-R02, -R12, -R22)  --> (-0 -0 -1)

Adding a CFrame object's LookVector to itself produces a CFrame moved forward in whichever direction it's facing by 1 unit.
m.s: The forward-direction component of the `Datatype.CFrame` object's orientation, equivalent to the negated form of `Datatype.CFrame.ZVector|ZVector`.

kid.simple: The direction the CFrame is FACING, as an arrow 1 stud long (a unit vector). This is the part's front. For a CFrame with no rotation it is (0, 0, -1). Multiply it by a number to get "that many studs forward".
kid.example:
local part = workspace.Part
-- A spot 10 studs in front of the part, whichever way it is turned
local ahead = part.Position + part.CFrame.LookVector * 10

-- Unturned CFrame faces -Z
print(CFrame.new().LookVector) --> 0, 0, -1
-- After a 90 degree turn around Y it faces -X
print((CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0)).LookVector) --> about -1, 0, 0
kid.gotcha: Front is -Z, so LookVector is the opposite of ZVector.

m.d:
The right-direction component of the CFrame object's orientation. Equivalent to XVector or the first column of the rotation matrix.

local cf = CFrame.new(0, 0, 0)
local x, y, z, R00, R01, R02, R10, R11, R12, R20, R21, R22 = cf:GetComponents()

print(cf.RightVector)  --> (1, 0, 0)
print(cf.XVector)      --> (1, 0, 0)
print(R00, R10, R20)   --> (1 0 0)
m.s: The right-direction component of the `Datatype.CFrame` object's orientation.

kid.simple: The direction to the CFrame's own RIGHT side, as a 1-stud arrow. For a CFrame with no rotation it is (1, 0, 0). Great for side-stepping or strafing.
kid.example:
local part = workspace.Part
-- Move the part 4 studs to its own right
part.CFrame = part.CFrame + part.CFrame.RightVector * 4

print(CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0).RightVector) --> about 0, 0, -1

m.d:
The up-direction component of the CFrame object's orientation. Equivalent to YVector or the second column of the rotation matrix.

local cf = CFrame.new(0, 0, 0)
local x, y, z, R00, R01, R02, R10, R11, R12, R20, R21, R22 = cf:GetComponents()

print(cf.UpVector)    --> (0, 1, 0)
print(cf.YVector)     --> (0, 1, 0)
print(R01, R11, R21)  --> (0 1 0)
m.s: The up-direction component of the `Datatype.CFrame` object's orientation.

kid.simple: The direction out of the CFrame's own TOP, as a 1-stud arrow. For an unturned CFrame it is (0, 1, 0). If the part is tipped over, UpVector tips with it.
kid.example:
local part = workspace.Part
-- Is the part lying on its side? (its top no longer points mostly up)
if part.CFrame.UpVector.Y < 0.5 then
	print("The part has fallen over!")
end

m.d:
The X component of the CFrame object's orientation. Equivalent to RightVector or the first column of the rotation matrix.

local cf = CFrame.new(0, 0, 0)
local x, y, z, R00, R01, R02, R10, R11, R12, R20, R21, R22 = cf:GetComponents()

print(cf.XVector)      --> (1, 0, 0)
print(cf.RightVector)  --> (1, 0, 0)
print(R00, R10, R20)   --> (1 0 0)
m.s: Equivalent to `Datatype.CFrame.RightVector|RightVector`.

kid.simple: Another name for RightVector: the CFrame's own X direction (its right side).
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.new()
print(cf.XVector) --> 1, 0, 0

m.d:
The Y component of the CFrame object's orientation. Equivalent to UpVector or the second column of the rotation matrix.

local cf = CFrame.new(0, 0, 0)
local x, y, z, R00, R01, R02, R10, R11, R12, R20, R21, R22 = cf:GetComponents()

print(cf.YVector)     --> (0, 1, 0)
print(cf.UpVector)    --> (0, 1, 0)
print(R01, R11, R21)  --> (0 1 0)
m.s: Equivalent to `Datatype.CFrame.UpVector|UpVector`.

kid.simple: Another name for UpVector: the CFrame's own Y direction (its top).
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.new()
print(cf.YVector) --> 0, 1, 0

m.d:
The Z component of the CFrame object's orientation. Equivalent to the negated LookVector or the third column of the rotation matrix.

local cf = CFrame.new(0, 0, 0)
local x, y, z, R00, R01, R02, R10, R11, R12, R20, R21, R22 = cf:GetComponents()

print(cf.ZVector)      --> (0, 0, 1)
print(-cf.LookVector)  --> (0, 0, 1)
print(R02, R12, R22)   --> (0 0 1)
m.s: The Z component of the `Datatype.CFrame` object's orientation. Equivalent to the third column of the rotation matrix.

kid.simple: The CFrame's own Z direction, which points out of its BACK. It is the exact opposite of LookVector.
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.new()
print(cf.ZVector)      --> 0, 0, 1
print(-cf.LookVector)  --> 0, 0, 1  (same thing)

m.d: Returns the inverse of the CFrame, representing the transformation that undoes the original. For any CFrame cf, the expression cf * cf:Inverse() produces the identity CFrame. The inverse reverses both the rotation (transposing the rotation matrix) and the translation.
m.s: Returns the inverse of the `Datatype.CFrame`.

r.s: The inverse CFrame that reverses this transformation.

kid.simple: Gives the CFrame that UNDOES this one. If `cf` means "move 5 studs right and turn left", `cf:Inverse()` means "turn back right and move 5 studs back". `cf * cf:Inverse()` gives the identity (no movement, no turn).
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.new(5, 0, 0)
print(cf:Inverse().Position) --> -5, 0, 0
print((cf * cf:Inverse()).Position) --> 0, 0, 0
kid.gotcha: `cf:ToObjectSpace(x)` is the same as `cf:Inverse() * x`, so you usually do not need Inverse directly.

m.d: Returns a CFrame interpolated between itself and goal by the fraction alpha. The positional component is interpolated linearly while the rotational component is interpolated using spherical linear interpolation (slerp), producing a constant-speed rotation along the shortest arc. An alpha of 0 returns the original CFrame and an alpha of 1 returns goal.
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.CFrame` interpolated between itself and `goal` by the fraction `alpha`.

p.s: The target CFrame to interpolate toward.
The interpolation fraction, where 0 is the original and 1 is goal.

r.s: The interpolated CFrame between the original and goal.

kid.simple: Finds a CFrame part-way between this one and `goal`. `alpha` is how far along: 0 is the start, 1 is the goal, 0.5 is halfway. Both position AND rotation blend smoothly, so it is great for simple smooth movement.
kid.example:
local startCF = CFrame.new(0, 0, 0)
local goalCF = CFrame.new(10, 0, 0) * CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0)

local quarter = startCF:Lerp(goalCF, 0.25)
print(quarter.Position) --> 2.5, 0, 0  (and turned about 22.5 degrees)

-- Slide a part to the goal over 1 second
local part = workspace.Part
for i = 1, 30 do
	part.CFrame = startCF:Lerp(goalCF, i / 30)
	task.wait(1 / 30)
end
kid.gotcha: For fancy animations with easing (speeding up and slowing down), TweenService is often easier.

m.d: Returns an orthonormalized copy of the CFrame. The BasePart.CFrame property automatically applies orthonormalization, but other APIs which take CFrames do not, so this method is occasionally necessary when incrementally updating a CFrame and using it with them.
m.s: Returns an orthonormalized copy of the `Datatype.CFrame`.

r.s: A copy of this CFrame with its rotation matrix orthonormalized.

kid.simple: Cleans up a CFrame's rotation so its three direction arrows are exactly 1 stud long and exactly at right angles. After many, many small multiplications, tiny rounding errors can make a rotation slightly "bent". `BasePart.CFrame` cleans itself automatically, but other places that take a CFrame do not.
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.new()
for i = 1, 10000 do
	cf = cf * CFrame.Angles(0, 0.001, 0)
end
cf = cf:Orthonormalize() -- fix any tiny errors that built up

m.d:
Receives one or more CFrame objects and returns them transformed from object to world space. Equivalent to:

CFrame * cf

local cf = CFrame.new(5, 10, 0)

local offset = CFrame.new(0, 2, 0)

-- Output world space of offset CFrame relative to calling CFrame
print(cf:ToWorldSpace(offset))  --> 5, 12, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1
m.s: Receives one or more `Datatype.CFrame` objects and returns them transformed from object to world space.

p.s: One or more CFrames specified in object (local) space.

r.s: The CFrames transformed into world space.

kid.simple: Takes a CFrame described from THIS CFrame's point of view and tells you where it is in the world. Same as `cf * other`. Example: "2 studs above me" turns into a real world spot.
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.new(5, 10, 0)
local offset = CFrame.new(0, 2, 0) -- "2 studs above me"
print(cf:ToWorldSpace(offset).Position) --> 5, 12, 0

-- With turning: stand at (0, 5, 0) facing -X, then "10 studs forward"
local turned = CFrame.new(0, 5, 0) * CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0)
print(turned:ToWorldSpace(CFrame.new(0, 0, -10)).Position) --> about -10, 5, 0
kid.gotcha: You can pass several CFrames at once and get several back.

m.d:
Receives one or more CFrame objects and returns them transformed from world to object space. Equivalent to:

CFrame:Inverse() * cf
m.s: Receives one or more `Datatype.CFrame` objects and returns them transformed from world to object space.

p.s: One or more CFrames specified in world space.

r.s: The CFrames transformed into object (local) space.

kid.simple: The opposite of ToWorldSpace. Takes a CFrame in the world and tells you where it is FROM THIS CFrame's point of view (as if this CFrame were the center of the world). Same as `cf:Inverse() * other`. Great for saving how two things are placed relative to each other, like a hat on a head, so you can put it back later.
kid.example:
local hinge = CFrame.new(10, 0, 0)
local door = CFrame.new(12, 3, 0)
local relative = hinge:ToObjectSpace(door)
print(relative.Position) --> 2, 3, 0  (door is 2 right and 3 up from the hinge)

-- Later, after the hinge moves or turns, put the door back in the same spot relative to it:
local newDoor = hinge:ToWorldSpace(relative)

m.d:
Receives one or more Vector3 objects and returns them transformed from object to world space. Equivalent to:

CFrame * v3

local cf = CFrame.new(5, 10, 0)

-- Output core world space of the CFrame
print(cf:PointToWorldSpace())  --> 5, 10, 0
-- Output world space of a Vector3 (0, 4, 0) relative to the CFrame (object space)
print(cf:PointToWorldSpace(Vector3.new(0, 4, 0)))  --> 5, 14, 0
m.s: Receives one or more `Datatype.Vector3` objects and returns them transformed from object to world space.

p.s: One or more points specified in object (local) space.

r.s: The points transformed into world space.

kid.simple: Takes a point (a Vector3) described from this CFrame's point of view and gives its spot in the world. Same as `cf * point`. Uses both the position and the turning.
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.new(5, 10, 0)
print(cf:PointToWorldSpace(Vector3.new(0, 4, 0))) --> 5, 14, 0

-- Turned 90 degrees around Y, standing at (0, 5, 0):
local turned = CFrame.new(0, 5, 0) * CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0)
-- "10 studs in front of me" (front is -Z)
print(turned:PointToWorldSpace(Vector3.new(0, 0, -10))) --> about -10, 5, 0

m.d:
Receives one or more Vector3 objects and returns them transformed from world to object space. Equivalent to:

CFrame:Inverse() * v3
m.s: Receives one or more `Datatype.Vector3` objects and returns them transformed from world to object space.

p.s: One or more points specified in world space.

r.s: The points transformed into object (local) space.

kid.simple: Takes a point in the world and tells you where it is from this CFrame's point of view. In the answer, negative Z means in front, positive Z means behind, positive X means to the right, positive Y means above. Perfect for "is the player in front of me?" or "which side of the door am I on?".
kid.example:
local turned = CFrame.new(0, 5, 0) * CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0)
-- The world point (-10, 5, 0) seen from this CFrame:
print(turned:PointToObjectSpace(Vector3.new(-10, 5, 0))) --> about 0, 0, -10
-- That means: 10 studs straight in front of it.

m.d:
Receives one or more Vector3 objects and returns them rotated from object to world space. Equivalent to:

(CFrame - CFrame.Position) * v3
m.s: Receives one or more `Datatype.Vector3` objects and returns them rotated from object to world space.

p.s: One or more direction vectors specified in object (local) space.

r.s: The vectors rotated into world space (translation ignored).

kid.simple: Like PointToWorldSpace, but for DIRECTIONS instead of spots: it only turns the arrow and ignores the position. Example: "my forward direction" (0, 0, -1) becomes a direction in the world.
kid.example:
local turned = CFrame.new(0, 5, 0) * CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0)
print(turned:VectorToWorldSpace(Vector3.new(0, 0, -1))) --> about -1, 0, 0  (same as turned.LookVector)
-- The position (0, 5, 0) was ignored, because directions do not have a place.

m.d:
Receives one or more Vector3 objects and returns them rotated from world to object space. Equivalent to:

(CFrame:Inverse() - CFrame:Inverse().Position) * v3
m.s: Receives one or more `Datatype.Vector3` objects and returns them rotated from world to object space.

p.s: One or more direction vectors specified in world space.

r.s: The vectors rotated into object (local) space (translation ignored).

kid.simple: Takes a direction in the world and tells you what that direction is from this CFrame's point of view. Only turning is used; position is ignored. Handy for checking if a car is driving forward or backward.
kid.example:
local car = workspace.Car -- a Part
local v = car.CFrame:VectorToObjectSpace(car.AssemblyLinearVelocity)
if v.Z < 0 then
	print("Driving forward")   -- moving toward the car's own front (-Z)
elseif v.Z > 0 then
	print("Driving backward")
end

m.d:
Returns the 12 numeric components of the CFrame as a tuple: x, y, z (position), followed by R00, R01, R02, R10, R11, R12, R20, R21, R22 (the 3×3 rotation matrix in row-major order). This is the reverse of the 12-argument CFrame.new() constructor.

local cf = CFrame.new(1, 2, 3) * CFrame.fromEulerAnglesXYZ(0, math.rad(90), 0)
local x, y, z, R00, R01, R02, R10, R11, R12, R20, R21, R22 = cf:GetComponents()
m.s: Returns the values `x`, `y`, `z`, `R00`, `R01`, `R02`, `R10`, `R11`, `R12`, `R20`, `R21`, and `R22`, where `x` `y` `z` represent the position of the `Datatype.CFrame` and `R00`‑`R22` represent its 3×3 rotation matrix.

r.s: The 12 numeric values: x, y, z, R00, R01, R02, R10, R11, R12, R20, R21, R22.

kid.simple: Gives back all 12 numbers inside the CFrame: x, y, z (the position) and then the 9 numbers of the rotation grid (R00 to R22). Mostly useful for saving a CFrame or advanced math.
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.new(1, 2, 3)
print(cf:GetComponents()) --> 1 2 3 1 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 1
local x, y, z = cf:GetComponents() -- you can keep just the first few

m.d: Returns approximate angles that could be used to generate the CFrame using the optional RotationOrder. If you don't provide order, the method uses RotationOrder.XYZ.
m.s: Returns approximate angles that could be used to generate the `Datatype.CFrame` using the optional `Enum.RotationOrder`.

p.s: The rotation order used for decomposition.

r.s: The X-axis rotation angle in radians.
The Y-axis rotation angle in radians.
The Z-axis rotation angle in radians.

kid.simple: Breaks the rotation back into three angles (in radians) around X, Y and Z. You can choose the order with an `Enum.RotationOrder`; the default is X-Y-Z. Use `math.deg` to read them as degrees.
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(45), 0)
local rx, ry, rz = cf:ToEulerAngles()
print(math.deg(ry)) --> about 45
kid.gotcha: The angles you get back can be a different-looking set that still makes the same final rotation, especially near 90 degree tilts (gimbal lock).

m.d: Returns the approximate angles, in radians, that could be used to generate the CFrame using RotationOrder.XYZ. The three returned values represent rotations around the X, Y, and Z axes respectively. Due to the nature of Euler angle decomposition, the angles are approximate and subject to gimbal lock near pitch angles of ±90 degrees.
m.s: Returns the approximate angles (in radians) that could be used to generate the `Datatype.CFrame` using `Enum.RotationOrder.XYZ`.

r.s: The X-axis rotation angle in radians.
The Y-axis rotation angle in radians.
The Z-axis rotation angle in radians.

kid.simple: Breaks the rotation into three angles in radians using the X-Y-Z order, the same order `CFrame.Angles` uses. So it is the reverse of `CFrame.Angles`.
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.Angles(math.rad(10), math.rad(20), math.rad(30))
local rx, ry, rz = cf:ToEulerAnglesXYZ()
print(math.deg(rx), math.deg(ry), math.deg(rz)) --> about 10 20 30

m.d: Returns the approximate angles, in radians, that could be used to generate the CFrame using RotationOrder.YXZ. The three returned values represent rotations around the X, Y, and Z axes respectively. Due to the nature of Euler angle decomposition, the angles are approximate and subject to gimbal lock near pitch angles of ±90 degrees.
m.s: Returns the approximate angles (in radians) that could be used to generate the `Datatype.CFrame` using `Enum.RotationOrder.YXZ`.

r.s: The X-axis rotation angle in radians.
The Y-axis rotation angle in radians.
The Z-axis rotation angle in radians.

kid.simple: Breaks the rotation into three angles in radians using the Y-X-Z order. It is the reverse of `CFrame.fromEulerAnglesYXZ` and `CFrame.fromOrientation`.
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.fromEulerAnglesYXZ(math.rad(20), math.rad(90), 0)
local rx, ry, rz = cf:ToEulerAnglesYXZ()
print(math.deg(rx), math.deg(ry)) --> about 20 90

m.d: Returns the approximate angles, in radians, that could be used to generate the CFrame using RotationOrder.YXZ. Equivalent to CFrame:ToEulerAnglesYXZ().
m.s: Returns the approximate angles (in radians) that could be used to generate the CFrame using the YXZ rotation order.

r.s: The X-axis rotation angle in radians.
The Y-axis rotation angle in radians.
The Z-axis rotation angle in radians.

kid.simple: Same as ToEulerAnglesYXZ. Gives the three angles (in radians) that match how a part's Orientation property works. Use `math.deg` to compare them with the numbers in the Properties window.
kid.example:
local part = workspace.Part
local rx, ry, rz = part.CFrame:ToOrientation()
print(math.deg(rx), math.deg(ry), math.deg(rz)) -- about the same as part.Orientation

m.d: Returns a unit Vector3 representing the axis of rotation and a number representing the angle of rotation in radians. A positive angle represents counter-clockwise rotation when looking from the tip of the axis vector toward the origin (right-hand rule). This is the inverse of CFrame.fromAxisAngle().
m.s: Returns a tuple containing a unit `Datatype.Vector3` axis and a rotation angle in radians.

r.s: A unit vector representing the axis of rotation.
The rotation angle in radians.

kid.simple: Describes the rotation as ONE turn: an axis (a 1-stud arrow to spin around) and an angle in radians. It is the reverse of `CFrame.fromAxisAngle`.
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0)
local axis, angle = cf:ToAxisAngle()
print(axis)             --> about 0, 1, 0
print(math.deg(angle))  --> about 90

m.d: Equivalent to CFrame:GetComponents().
m.s: Equivalent to `Datatype.CFrame:GetComponents()`.

r.s: The 12 numeric values: x, y, z, R00, R01, R02, R10, R11, R12, R20, R21, R22.

kid.simple: An older lowercase name for GetComponents. Use `cf:GetComponents()` instead.
kid.example: local x, y, z = CFrame.new(1, 2, 3):GetComponents() -- use this name

m.d: Returns true if the other CFrame is sufficiently close to this CFrame in both position and rotation. The epsilon value is used to control the tolerance for this similarity; this value is optional and should be a small positive value if provided. The similarity for position is component-wise while rotation uses a fast approximation of the angle difference.
m.s: Returns `true` if the other `Datatype.CFrame` is sufficiently close to this `Datatype.CFrame` in both position and rotation.

p.s: The CFrame to compare against.
The tolerance for comparing position and rotation components.

r.s: True if the two CFrames are within epsilon of each other.

kid.simple: Checks if two CFrames are ALMOST the same, in both position and rotation. Computers make tiny rounding errors, so `==` can say false for CFrames that are basically equal. The optional `epsilon` is how much difference you allow (a small positive number).
kid.example:
local a = CFrame.new(0, 5, 0)
local b = CFrame.new(0, 5.000001, 0)
print(a == b)         --> false (not exactly equal)
print(a:FuzzyEq(b))   --> true  (close enough)

m.d: Returns the angle, in radians, between the orientation of one CFrame and another. This function does not take the position of either CFrame into account and only looks at the relative orientation.
m.s: Returns the angle, in radians, between the orientation of one `Datatype.CFrame` and another.

p.s: The CFrame whose orientation is compared against this CFrame.

r.s: The angle in radians between the two orientations, in the range [0, pi].

kid.simple: Tells you how far apart two CFrames are turned, as one angle in radians (from 0 to pi, which is 0 to 180 degrees). Position is ignored.
kid.example:
local a = CFrame.new(0, 0, 0)
local b = CFrame.new(50, 0, 0) * CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0)
print(math.deg(a:AngleBetween(b))) --> about 90  (the 50 stud move does not count)

m.d: Creates an identity CFrame with position (0, 0, 0) and no rotation (identity rotation matrix). This is equivalent to CFrame.identity.
m.s: Returns a blank identity `Datatype.CFrame`.

kid.simple: Makes a new CFrame. With no arguments you get the identity (spot (0, 0, 0), no turning). With a Vector3 or three numbers you get that position with no turning. There are also older or advanced versions: `CFrame.new(pos, lookAt)` (use `CFrame.lookAt` instead), 7 numbers (position plus a quaternion rotation), and 12 numbers (position plus all 9 rotation-grid numbers).
kid.example:
local a = CFrame.new()                      -- at (0, 0, 0), no rotation
local b = CFrame.new(0, 10, 0)              -- 10 studs up, no rotation
local c = CFrame.new(Vector3.new(4, 2, 0))  -- same idea using a Vector3
print(b.Position) --> 0, 10, 0
kid.gotcha: `CFrame.new` never turns anything (unless you use the advanced versions). Multiply by `CFrame.Angles(...)` to add rotation.

m.d: Returns a new CFrame with the position of at and facing towards lookAt, optionally specifying the upward direction (up) with a default of (0, 1, 0).
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.CFrame` with the position of the first `Datatype.Vector3` and an orientation pointed toward the second.

p.s: The world-space position of the CFrame.
The world-space point the CFrame should face toward.
The unit vector specifying the upward direction. Defaults to (0, 1, 0).

kid.simple: Makes a CFrame placed at `at` whose front (LookVector) points toward the spot `lookAt`. Perfect for aiming turrets, cameras, or making an NPC face a player. The optional third value says which way is "up" (normally (0, 1, 0)).
kid.example:
-- Stand at (0, 5, 0) and look at (10, 5, 0)
local cf = CFrame.lookAt(Vector3.new(0, 5, 0), Vector3.new(10, 5, 0))
print(cf.Position)    --> 0, 5, 0
print(cf.LookVector)  --> about 1, 0, 0  (facing +X, toward the target)
kid.gotcha: Both arguments are positions (spots), not directions. If you have a direction instead, use `CFrame.lookAlong`. Looking straight up or straight down can give a strange sideways turn.

m.d:
Returns a new CFrame with the position of at and facing along direction, optionally specifying the upward direction (up) with a default of (0, 1, 0).

This constructor is equivalent to CFrame.lookAt(at, at + direction).
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.CFrame` with the position of the first `Datatype.Vector3` and an orientation directed along the second.

p.s: The world-space position of the CFrame.
The direction the CFrame should face along.
The unit vector specifying the upward direction. Defaults to (0, 1, 0).

kid.simple: Like `CFrame.lookAt`, but the second value is a DIRECTION to face along instead of a spot to look at. `CFrame.lookAlong(at, dir)` is the same as `CFrame.lookAt(at, at + dir)`.
kid.example:
-- Stand at (0, 5, 0) and face along +X
local cf = CFrame.lookAlong(Vector3.new(0, 5, 0), Vector3.new(1, 0, 0))
print(cf.LookVector) --> about 1, 0, 0

m.d:
Returns a CFrame whose rotation represents the shortest-arc rotation that aligns vector from with vector to. The input vectors do not need to be unit length; they are normalized internally. The resulting CFrame has its position set to (0, 0, 0).

-- Rotate a direction to face another direction
local from = Vector3.new(0, 1, 0)
local to = Vector3.new(1, 0, 0)
local cf = CFrame.fromRotationBetweenVectors(from, to)
print(cf * from) --> approximately (1, 0, 0)
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.CFrame` representing the orientation needed to rotate from the first `Datatype.Vector3` to the second, with the position set to zero.

p.s: Vector representing the "from" direction.
Vector representing the "to" direction.

kid.simple: Gives a rotation-only CFrame (position (0, 0, 0)) that turns the first direction so it points the same way as the second direction, using the shortest turn. Handy for tilting something so its top lines up with a slope.
kid.example:
local from = Vector3.new(0, 1, 0)  -- pointing up
local to = Vector3.new(1, 0, 0)    -- pointing right
local turn = CFrame.fromRotationBetweenVectors(from, to)
print(turn * from) --> about 1, 0, 0  ("up" got turned into "right")

m.d:
Returns a rotated CFrame from angles rx, ry, and rz in radians. Rotations are applied in the optional RotationOrder with a default of XYZ, equivalent to:

local rx, ry, rz = math.rad(30), math.rad(45), math.rad(60)
local cframe = CFrame.fromEulerAngles(rx, 0, 0) -- X
               * CFrame.fromEulerAngles(0, ry, 0) -- Y
               * CFrame.fromEulerAngles(0, 0, rz) -- Z
local rx_out, ry_out, rz_out = cframe:ToEulerAnglesXYZ()
print(string.format("rx: %.2f, ry: %.2f, rz: %.2f", math.deg(rx_out), math.deg(ry_out), math.deg(rz_out))) --> rx: 30.00, ry: 45.00, rz: 60.00
m.s: Returns a rotated `Datatype.CFrame` from angles `rx`, `ry`, and `rz` in radians. Rotations are applied in the optional `Enum.RotationOrder` with a default of `XYZ`.

p.s: Rotation angle around the X axis in radians.
Rotation angle around the Y axis in radians.
Rotation angle around the Z axis in radians.
The order in which rotations are applied.

kid.simple: Makes a rotation-only CFrame from three angles in radians: turn around X, around Y, and around Z. The optional fourth value (an `Enum.RotationOrder`) picks which turn happens first; the default is X, then Y, then Z, which is the same as `CFrame.Angles`.
kid.example:
-- Tilt 30 degrees around X, using the default X-Y-Z order
local tilt = CFrame.fromEulerAngles(math.rad(30), 0, 0)

-- Same three angles, but do Y first, then X, then Z
local other = CFrame.fromEulerAngles(math.rad(30), math.rad(45), 0, Enum.RotationOrder.YXZ)
kid.gotcha: Remember radians: use `math.rad(degrees)`.

m.d:
Returns a rotated CFrame from angles rx, ry, and rz in radians using RotationOrder.XYZ, equivalent to:

local rx, ry, rz = math.rad(30), math.rad(45), math.rad(60)
local cframe = CFrame.fromEulerAngles(rx, 0, 0) -- X
               * CFrame.fromEulerAngles(0, ry, 0) -- Y
               * CFrame.fromEulerAngles(0, 0, rz) -- Z
local rx_out, ry_out, rz_out = cframe:ToEulerAnglesXYZ()
print(string.format("rx: %.2f, ry: %.2f, rz: %.2f", math.deg(rx_out), math.deg(ry_out), math.deg(rz_out))) --> rx: 30.00, ry: 45.00, rz: 60.00
m.s: Returns a rotated `Datatype.CFrame` from angles `rx`, `ry`, and `rz` in radians using `Enum.RotationOrder.XYZ`.

p.s: Rotation angle around the X axis in radians.
Rotation angle around the Y axis in radians.
Rotation angle around the Z axis in radians.

kid.simple: Rotation-only CFrame from three angles in radians, turning around X first, then Y, then Z. Exactly the same as `CFrame.Angles`.
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.fromEulerAnglesXYZ(0, math.rad(90), 0) -- quarter turn around Y
print(cf.LookVector) --> about -1, 0, 0

m.d:
Returns a rotated CFrame from angles rx, ry, and rz in radians using RotationOrder.YXZ, equivalent to:

local rx, ry, rz = math.rad(30), math.rad(45), math.rad(60)
local cframe = CFrame.fromEulerAngles(0, ry, 0) -- Y
               * CFrame.fromEulerAngles(rx, 0, 0) -- X
               * CFrame.fromEulerAngles(0, 0, rz) -- Z
local rx_out, ry_out, rz_out = cframe:ToEulerAnglesYXZ()
print(string.format("rx: %.2f, ry: %.2f, rz: %.2f", math.deg(rx_out), math.deg(ry_out), math.deg(rz_out))) --> rx: 30.00, ry: 45.00, rz: 60.00
m.s: Returns a rotated `Datatype.CFrame` from angles `rx`, `ry`, and `rz` in radians using `Enum.RotationOrder.YXZ`.

p.s: Rotation angle around the X axis in radians.
Rotation angle around the Y axis in radians.
Rotation angle around the Z axis in radians.

kid.simple: Rotation-only CFrame from three angles in radians, turning around Y first, then X, then Z. Exactly the same as `CFrame.fromOrientation`. This order is nice for cameras and characters: first turn left/right (Y), then look up/down (X).
kid.example:
-- Face 90 degrees to the left, then tip the nose 20 degrees up
local cf = CFrame.fromEulerAnglesYXZ(math.rad(20), math.rad(90), 0)

m.d: Equivalent to fromEulerAnglesXYZ().
m.s: Equivalent to `Datatype.CFrame.fromEulerAnglesXYZ()|fromEulerAnglesXYZ()`.

p.s: Rotation angle around the X axis in radians.
Rotation angle around the Y axis in radians.
Rotation angle around the Z axis in radians.

kid.simple: The most common way to make a rotation. Gives a CFrame with no position change that turns by `rx` around X, `ry` around Y, and `rz` around Z (in radians, X first, then Y, then Z). Multiply it onto another CFrame to turn that thing.
kid.example:
local part = workspace.Part -- an Anchored part
-- Spin the part 90 degrees around its own up axis, like a top
part.CFrame = part.CFrame * CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0)
kid.gotcha: `CFrame.Angles(0, 90, 0)` uses 90 RADIANS (about 5157 degrees). Always wrap degrees in `math.rad`. If you only use one of the three angles, Angles, fromEulerAngles and fromOrientation all give the same result; they only differ when you mix two or more angles.

m.d: Equivalent to fromEulerAnglesYXZ().
m.s: Equivalent to `Datatype.CFrame.fromEulerAnglesYXZ()|fromEulerAnglesYXZ()`.

p.s: Rotation angle around the X axis in radians.
Rotation angle around the Y axis in radians.
Rotation angle around the Z axis in radians.

kid.simple: Rotation-only CFrame from three angles in radians, turning Y first, then X, then Z. This matches how a part's Orientation property (the numbers you see in Studio's Properties window) works, so it is the easiest way to copy those numbers into a CFrame.
kid.example:
local part = workspace.Part
local o = part.Orientation -- in degrees, for example (0, 45, 0)
-- Rebuild the same rotation as a CFrame (degrees -> radians!)
local rotation = CFrame.fromOrientation(math.rad(o.X), math.rad(o.Y), math.rad(o.Z))

m.d:
Returns a CFrame rotated r radians around the axis v. The axis vector is normalized internally, so it does not need to be unit length. The resulting CFrame has no translation (position is (0, 0, 0)). A positive angle represents a counter-clockwise rotation when looking from the tip of the axis vector toward the origin (right-hand rule).

-- Rotate 90 degrees around the Y axis
local cf = CFrame.fromAxisAngle(Vector3.yAxis, math.rad(90))
m.s: Returns a rotated `Datatype.CFrame` from a unit `Datatype.Vector3` and a rotation in radians.

p.s: The axis of rotation (normalized internally).
The rotation angle in radians.

kid.simple: Rotation-only CFrame that turns `r` radians around any direction you choose (the axis), like spinning a wheel on an axle pointing that way. Positive angles turn counter-clockwise when you look down the axis toward its start.
kid.example:
-- Quarter turn around the up axis (same as CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0))
local cf = CFrame.fromAxisAngle(Vector3.yAxis, math.rad(90))

-- Tilt around a slanted axis
local slanted = CFrame.fromAxisAngle(Vector3.new(1, 1, 0), math.rad(45))

m.d: Returns a CFrame from a translation and the columns of a rotation matrix. If vZ is excluded, the third column is calculated as vX:Cross(vY).Unit.
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.CFrame` from a translation and the columns of a rotation matrix.

p.s: The 3D position of the CFrame.
Equivalent to RightVector.
Equivalent to UpVector.
Equivalent to -LookVector.

kid.simple: Builds a CFrame from a position plus the three direction arrows you want it to have: its right direction (`vX`) and up direction (`vY`), and optionally its back direction (`vZ`). Useful when you already know which way "right" and "up" should point, for example lining a part up with the ground's surface.
kid.example:
local pos = Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)
local right = Vector3.new(0, 0, -1)
local up = Vector3.new(0, 1, 0)
local cf = CFrame.fromMatrix(pos, right, up)
print(cf.LookVector) --> about -1, 0, 0  (same as a 90 degree turn around Y)
kid.gotcha: The right and up arrows should be length 1 and at a right angle (90 degrees) to each other, or the result can be squished.

m.d: An identity CFrame with no translation or rotation. This property is a constant and must be accessed globally as opposed to through an individual CFrame object.
m.s: An identity `Datatype.CFrame` with no translation or rotation.

kid.simple: The "do nothing" CFrame: position (0, 0, 0) and no rotation. Same as `CFrame.new()`. Multiplying any CFrame by it leaves it unchanged.
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.new(1, 2, 3)
print(cf * CFrame.identity == cf) --> true
kid.gotcha: Use it as `CFrame.identity`, not on a CFrame you made (`myCFrame.identity` is not how it is meant to be used).

m.d: Composes two CFrame transformations, producing a new CFrame that applies the right operand's transform in the left operand's local space. This is equivalent to CFrame:ToWorldSpace() and is the standard way to combine translations and rotations.
m.s: Produces a new `Datatype.CFrame` representing the composition of the two `Datatype.CFrame|CFrames`.

kid.simple: Combines two CFrames: start at the left one, then do the right one FROM THE LEFT ONE'S POINT OF VIEW (its local space). Same as `left:ToWorldSpace(right)`. Order matters: `a * b` and `b * a` usually give different answers.
kid.example:
local move = CFrame.new(10, 0, 0)
local turn = CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0)
print((move * turn).Position) --> 10, 0, 0       (walk, then spin in place)
print((turn * move).Position) --> about 0, 0, -10 (spin, then walk along your new right side)
kid.gotcha: Want to turn a part in place? Put the rotation on the right: `part.CFrame * CFrame.Angles(...)`.

m.d: Transforms a Vector3 from the CFrame object's local (object) space into world space, applying both rotation and translation. Equivalent to CFrame:PointToWorldSpace().
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.Vector3` transformed from object to world coordinates.

kid.simple: Takes a point described from the CFrame's point of view and returns where it is in the world. Same as `cf:PointToWorldSpace(v)`.
kid.example:
local turned = CFrame.new(0, 5, 0) * CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0)
print(turned * Vector3.new(0, 0, -10)) --> about -10, 5, 0
-- (0, 0, -10) means "10 studs in front"; this CFrame faces -X, so that is (-10, 5, 0)

m.d: Produces a CFrame with its position offset by the Vector3 in world space. The orientation remains unchanged. Only the translational component is affected; rotation is preserved as-is.
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.CFrame` translated in world space by the `Datatype.Vector3`.

kid.simple: Slides the CFrame by a Vector3 using WORLD directions. The rotation stays the same. This ignores which way the CFrame faces.
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.new(1, 2, 3) * CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0)
local moved = cf + Vector3.new(0, 10, 0)
print(moved.Position) --> 1, 12, 3  (still turned the same way)
kid.gotcha: To move in the CFrame's OWN directions (like forward), use `cf * CFrame.new(0, 0, -5)` or `cf + cf.LookVector * 5` instead.

m.d: Produces a CFrame with its position offset by the negated Vector3 in world space. The orientation remains unchanged. Equivalent to CFrame + (-v).
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.CFrame` translated in world space by the negative `Datatype.Vector3`.

kid.simple: Slides the CFrame backward by a Vector3 using world directions; rotation stays the same. `cf - v` is the same as `cf + (-v)`.
kid.example:
local cf = CFrame.new(1, 12, 3)
print((cf - Vector3.new(0, 10, 0)).Position) --> 1, 2, 3

kid.simple: A CFrame (short for "coordinate frame") stores two things at once: WHERE something is (its position) and WHICH WAY it is facing (its rotation). Every part in your game has a CFrame. If you only change Position, you move a part; if you change its CFrame, you can move it AND turn it in one step. CFrames also let you say things like "5 studs in front of this part", no matter which way the part is turned.
kid.analogy: A CFrame is like a person standing on a map holding a compass. The spot they stand on is the position. The way their nose points is the rotation. "Take 3 steps forward" means something different depending on which way that person is facing, and CFrames do exactly that kind of math for you.
whenToUse: Moving AND turning a part at the same time (set `part.CFrame`).
Making something face something else, like a turret aiming at a player (`CFrame.lookAt`).
Placing things relative to another thing, like a sword in front of a character or a door around its hinge.
Spinning or tilting a part by a set number of degrees (`CFrame.Angles` with `math.rad`).
Teleporting a character (`character:PivotTo(someCFrame)`).
Finding out where something is from another object's point of view, like "is the player in front of or behind this NPC?".
kid.where: CFrame is a built-in data type, so it works everywhere: in a Script (server) or a LocalScript (client). You do not need game:GetService. Make one with `CFrame.new(...)`, or read one from a part with `part.CFrame`.

terms.CFrame: Short for coordinate frame. A value that holds a position plus a rotation.
terms.position: Where something is, written as three numbers X, Y, Z (a Vector3). Example: (0, 5, 0) means 5 studs up from the center of the world.
terms.rotation / orientation: Which way something is turned or facing.
terms.stud: Roblox's unit of distance. A default baseplate tile is 4 studs wide.
terms.vector: A group of numbers, like (X, Y, Z), that can mean a spot in the world OR a direction plus a length. See Vector3.
terms.unit vector: A vector whose length is exactly 1. It only tells you a direction, like an arrow that is 1 stud long.
terms.world space: Measuring from the center of the whole game world (0, 0, 0), where +Y is always straight up and the axes never turn. Like using north, south, east, west.
terms.object space / local space: Measuring from a specific object's own point of view: its center is (0, 0, 0), its forward is its own front, its right is its own right. Like saying "to my left" instead of "to the west".
terms.relative: Measured compared to something else. "5 studs in front of the part" is relative to the part.
terms.offset: An extra amount you add to move something away from a starting point. A part at (0, 5, 0) moved by an offset of (2, 0, 0) ends up at (2, 5, 0).
terms.radians: The unit Roblox uses for angles in CFrames. A full circle is about 6.283 radians (2 times pi) instead of 360 degrees. Use `math.rad(degrees)` to convert, for example `math.rad(90)` is about 1.5708.
terms.axis: One of the three directions: X (left/right), Y (up/down), Z (forward/back). Rotating "around the Y axis" means spinning like a top or a merry-go-round.
terms.LookVector: The direction a CFrame is facing (its front), as a unit vector.
terms.identity: The "do nothing" CFrame: position (0, 0, 0) and no rotation at all.
terms.inverse: The CFrame that undoes another one. If one CFrame means "move 5 right", its inverse means "move 5 left".
terms.interpolate / lerp: To find a spot part-way between a start and a goal. Lerp with 0.5 means exactly halfway.
terms.Euler angles: Describing a rotation as three separate turns: one around X, one around Y, one around Z. The order you do them in changes the result.
terms.rotation order: Which of the three turns (X, Y, Z) happens first. `CFrame.Angles` uses X then Y then Z; `CFrame.fromOrientation` uses Y then X then Z.
terms.matrix / rotation matrix: A 3 by 3 grid of 9 numbers that the CFrame uses inside to store rotation. You almost never need to touch it; use RightVector, UpVector and LookVector instead.
terms.quaternion: Another math way to store a rotation using 4 numbers. Advanced, and rarely needed in Roblox scripts.
terms.gimbal lock: A math hiccup where two of the three Euler angles line up (around 90 degrees of tilt up or down), so the numbers you get back can look odd even though the rotation is fine.
terms.anchored: A part with Anchored = true does not fall or get pushed by physics, so setting its CFrame moves it cleanly.
terms.tuple: When a function gives back several values at once, like `local a, b, c = something()`.

examples.title: Move and turn a part in one line
examples.place: Script inside an Anchored Part in Workspace
examples.code:
local part = script.Parent

-- Put the part 10 studs up, then turn it 45 degrees around the Y axis (like a spinning top).
-- math.rad changes degrees into radians, which is what CFrame.Angles wants.
part.CFrame = CFrame.new(0, 10, 0) * CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(45), 0)

print(part.Position) --> 0, 10, 0
explain: `CFrame.new(0, 10, 0)` makes a CFrame at position (0, 10, 0) with no turning.
`CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(45), 0)` is a CFrame that only turns: 45 degrees around the up-and-down (Y) axis.
Multiplying them with `*` means: go to that spot, then turn there.
Setting `part.CFrame` moves and rotates the part at the same time.

examples.title: Spin a part forever
examples.place: Script inside an Anchored Part in Workspace
examples.code:
local part = script.Parent

while true do
	-- Take the part's current CFrame and turn it 2 more degrees around its own Y axis.
	part.CFrame = part.CFrame * CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(2), 0)
	task.wait() -- wait one frame so the game does not freeze
end
explain: Each loop takes the part's current CFrame and adds a small 2 degree turn.
Because the turn is on the RIGHT side of `*`, it happens around the part's own center, so it spins in place.
`task.wait()` pauses for about one frame, so the spin looks smooth.

examples.title: Why the order of * matters (local vs world)
examples.code:
local move = CFrame.new(10, 0, 0)               -- "go 10 studs along X"
local turn = CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0)  -- "turn 90 degrees around Y"

-- Move first, then turn: you walk 10 studs, then spin on the spot.
local a = move * turn
print(a.Position) --> 10, 0, 0

-- Turn first, then move: you spin, THEN walk 10 studs along your NEW X direction.
local b = turn * move
print(b.Position) --> about 0, 0, -10
explain: Read `A * B` as: start at A, then do B using A's own directions (A's local space).
`move * turn`: you are already at (10, 0, 0) when you turn, so you only spin in place.
`turn * move`: after turning 90 degrees, your own "right" (X) direction points toward world (0, 0, -1). Walking 10 studs that way lands you at (0, 0, -10).
Rule of thumb: `part.CFrame * something` means "do something from the part's point of view". The thing on the right uses the left one's directions.
Tiny numbers like -4.37e-07 may show up instead of 0. That is normal rounding, not a bug.

examples.title: Put something 5 studs in front of a part, whichever way it faces
examples.place: Script in ServerScriptService (needs a Part named Base in Workspace)
examples.code:
local base = workspace:WaitForChild("Base")

local marker = Instance.new("Part")
marker.Size = Vector3.new(1, 1, 1)
marker.Anchored = true
marker.BrickColor = BrickColor.new("Bright red")

-- In a CFrame's own space, "forward" is -Z. So (0, 0, -5) means 5 studs in front.
marker.CFrame = base.CFrame * CFrame.new(0, 0, -5)
marker.Parent = workspace

-- Same spot, a different way: start at the base and add 5 times its forward direction.
print(base.Position + base.CFrame.LookVector * 5)
explain: `base.CFrame * CFrame.new(0, 0, -5)` means "from the base's point of view, go 5 studs forward".
If the base is at (0, 5, 0) and turned 90 degrees around Y, its front points toward world (-1, 0, 0), so the marker ends up at (-5, 5, 0).
`LookVector` is the direction the base faces. Multiplying it by 5 makes an arrow 5 studs long, and adding it to the position gives the same spot.

examples.title: Make a part face a target
examples.place: Script in ServerScriptService (needs Parts named Turret and Target in Workspace)
examples.code:
local turret = workspace:WaitForChild("Turret")
local target = workspace:WaitForChild("Target")

while true do
	-- Stay where you are, but point your front at the target.
	turret.CFrame = CFrame.lookAt(turret.Position, target.Position)
	task.wait(0.1)
end
explain: `CFrame.lookAt(from, to)` builds a CFrame placed at `from` whose front (LookVector) points at `to`.
Running it in a loop keeps the turret aimed even if the target moves.

examples.title: Is the player in front of or behind this NPC?
examples.place: Script in ServerScriptService (needs a Part named Guard in Workspace)
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local guard = workspace:WaitForChild("Guard")

while true do
	for _, player in Players:GetPlayers() do
		local character = player.Character
		local root = character and character:FindFirstChild("HumanoidRootPart")
		if root then
			-- Turn the player's world position into the guard's own point of view.
			local seen = guard.CFrame:PointToObjectSpace(root.Position)
			if seen.Z < 0 then
				print(player.Name .. " is in front of the guard")
			else
				print(player.Name .. " is behind the guard")
			end
		end
	end
	task.wait(1)
end
explain: `PointToObjectSpace` answers: where is this point if the guard is the center of the world and the guard's front is forward?
In object space, negative Z is in front, positive Z is behind, positive X is to the guard's right, positive Y is above.
So `seen.Z < 0` means the player is somewhere in front of the guard.

gotchas: Angles are in radians, not degrees. `CFrame.Angles(0, 90, 0)` spins about 14 full turns plus a bit, not 90 degrees. Write `CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0)`.
Order matters: `a * b` is usually NOT the same as `b * a`. Put the thing you want to happen "from the part's point of view" on the right: `part.CFrame * CFrame.new(0, 0, -5)`.
`part.CFrame * CFrame.new(0, 0, -5)` moves forward the way the part faces, but `part.CFrame + Vector3.new(0, 0, -5)` moves toward world -Z no matter how the part is turned.
A CFrame's front is -Z, not +Z. `CFrame.new(0, 0, -5)` is 5 studs in FRONT.
CFrames cannot be changed piece by piece. `part.CFrame.Position = ...` or `cf.X = 5` gives an error. Build a new CFrame and assign the whole thing.
If a part is not Anchored, setting its CFrame works but physics may move it again right away.
To move a whole character or model, use `model:PivotTo(cframe)` instead of setting each part's CFrame.
Printing a CFrame shows 12 numbers (3 for position, 9 for rotation). Print `cf.Position` or `cf.LookVector` instead if you just want to read it.

datatype/CatalogSearchParams.d:
The CatalogSearchParams data type stores the parameters of a catalog search via AvatarEditorService:SearchCatalogAsync().

When accessing the value of the CatalogSearchParams.BundleTypes or CatalogSearchParams.AssetTypes property the returned table will be read-only to avoid confusion when not directly accessing the CatalogSearchParams instance.

local params = CatalogSearchParams.new()
params.SearchKeyword = "Test"
params.MinPrice = 5000
params.MaxPrice = 10000
params.BundleTypes = {Enum.BundleType.Animations, Enum.BundleType.BodyParts}

local types = params.BundleTypes
for _, val in types do
  print(val)
end
