datatype/Collection.d:
A Collection is a live, query-based group of instances created by CollectionService:CreateCollection() using a selector string and an optional root instance. From then on, membership is automatic such that an instance is added the moment it matches the query and removed the moment it stops matching. You never add or remove instances manually.

You can interact with a Collection by assigning callbacks to it. Rather than connecting a signal for each instance and remembering to disconnect it, you declare behavior once on the collection and it is applied to every matching instance for you. The collection owns those connections and tears them down automatically when an instance leaves the set. See the accompanying code sample for a collection that uses each kind of callback together.

A collection's lifetime is tied to the root instance passed to CreateCollection() (defaulting to Workspace). When that root is destroyed or when you call Destroy(), the collection is torn down.

Callback Assignment Syntax

Callbacks are assigned as fields on the collection using function-statement syntax, which reads like the contents of a ModuleScript. Both of the following forms are equivalent and assign through the collection's overloaded __newindex:

local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")

local collection = CollectionService:CreateCollection("Part")

function collection.OnAdded(instance)

end

local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")

local collection = CollectionService:CreateCollection("Part")

collection.OnAdded = function(instance)

end

Each callback can be assigned only once; reassigning the same callback raises an error. This keeps a collection's behavior declarative at its definition so that it cannot be silently replaced elsewhere.

Core Members and Aliases

OnAdded, OnRemoved, and ForEach() are the collection's primitive members:

  • OnAdded(instance: Instance) — Fires when an instance begins matching the query. When you first assign OnAdded, it immediately fires once for every instance already in the collection, so a single callback handles both current and future members.
  • OnRemoved(instance: Instance) — Fires when an instance that was in the collection stops matching, for example its tag is removed, it is reparented out of the collection's root, it is destroyed, or the collection's Enabled property is set to false.
  • ForEach() — Imperatively iterates the instances currently in the collection, operating on a snapshot taken at call time.

A collection can also bind a callback to non-deprecated RunService steps through aliases which exist for performance as well as convenience:

Collection Callback Equivalent
OnHeartbeat Class.RunService.Heartbeat
OnPreRender Class.RunService.PreRender
OnPreAnimation Class.RunService.PreAnimation
OnPreSimulation Class.RunService.PreSimulation
OnPostSimulation Class.RunService.PostSimulation
OnSimulate Class.RunService:BindToSimulation()

The collection subscribes to each RunService event once and dispatches to its members internally, rather than every instance holding its own connection. The callback fires once per step for each instance in the collection and receives the instance followed by the step's deltaTime:

local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")

local collection = CollectionService:CreateCollection("Part")

function collection.OnHeartbeat(instance, deltaTime)

end

Event, Property, and Attribute Wrappers

Beyond the RunService aliases, a collection can wrap any signal on its member instances. In these callbacks, X stands for the name of an event, property, or attribute.

  • function collection.OnX(instance, ...) wraps the X event on each member and the callback receives the instance followed by that event's arguments. For example, OnTouched wraps BasePart.Touched.

```lua local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")

local collection = CollectionService:CreateCollection("Part")

function collection.OnTouched(part, otherPart) print(part, otherPart) end ```

  • function collection.OnPropertyChanged.X(instance) fires when property X changes on a member, equivalent to connecting GetPropertyChangedSignal() on each instance.

```lua local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")

local collection = CollectionService:CreateCollection("Part")

function collection.OnPropertyChanged.Color(instance) print(instance) end ```

  • function collection.OnAttributeChanged.X(instance) fires when attribute X changes on a member, equivalent to GetAttributeChangedSignal().

```lua local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")

local collection = CollectionService:CreateCollection("Humanoid")

function collection.OnAttributeChanged.CharacterHealth(instance) print(instance) end ```

Note that a single collection can match instances of different classes, so a wrapped signal may not apply to every member:

  • If a member does not have the signal or property named by the callback, that member silently ignores the assignment. For example, a collection matching both Part and Folder can safely define OnTouched, but only the Parts respond.
  • If a callback names an event or property that exists nowhere in the API (for example a misspelled OnToched), an error is raised at assignment time.

Typing and Autocomplete

When the query constrains the class of its matches, the collection is typed accordingly and callbacks are typed to match. For example, CreateCollection("Part.TagName") yields a collection whose callbacks receive a Part, and autocomplete only suggests callbacks relevant to that class (so collection.OnTouched(part: Part, other: BasePart) is suggested, but not for a query that cannot match a BasePart). When no type can be inferred from the query, the first argument defaults to Instance.
datatype/Collection.s: A live, query-based group of instances returned by `Class.CollectionService:CreateCollection()`.

m.d: Defaults to true. Setting this to false fires OnRemoved for every instance currently in the collection and stops all of its callbacks. Setting it back to true re-evaluates the query and fires OnAdded again for every matching instance. Assigning a non-boolean value raises an error.
m.s: Controls whether the collection is actively tracking instances and firing callbacks.

m.d: Iterates over the instances currently in the collection, calling callback with each one. ForEach() operates on a snapshot taken at call time, so it is safe to add, remove, or destroy instances from within the callback; instances that begin matching during iteration are not visited. Calling ForEach() after the collection has been destroyed raises an error.
m.s: Invokes a function once for each instance currently in the collection.

p.s: A function called with each instance currently in the collection.

m.d: Stops firing the collection's callbacks, releases the connections it manages on its members, and empties its set of instances. After a collection is destroyed, calling ForEach() raises an error. A collection is also destroyed automatically when the root passed to CreateCollection() is destroyed.
m.s: Destroys the collection, stopping all tracking and callbacks.

datatype/Color3.d: The Color3 data type describes a color using red, green, and blue components in the range of 0 to 1. Unlike the BrickColor data type which describes named colors, Color3 is used for precise coloring of objects on screen through properties like BasePart.Color and GuiObject.BackgroundColor3.
datatype/Color3.s: A color value comprised of red, green, and blue components.

m.d: The red value of the color.
m.s: The red value of the color.

kid.simple: How much red is in the color, from 0 to 1. Read-only.
kid.example:
local c = Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0)
print(c.R) --> 1

m.d: The green value of the color.
m.s: The green value of the color.

kid.simple: How much green is in the color, from 0 to 1. Read-only.
kid.example:
local c = Color3.fromRGB(0, 51, 0)
print(c.G) --> 0.2 (51 out of 255)

m.d: The blue value of the color.
m.s: The blue value of the color.

kid.simple: How much blue is in the color, from 0 to 1. Read-only.
kid.example:
local c = Color3.new(0, 0, 0.75)
print(c.B) --> 0.75

m.d:
Returns a Color3 interpolated between two colors. The alpha value should be within the range of 0 to 1.

local white = Color3.new(1, 1, 1)
local black = Color3.new(0, 0, 0)

local gray10 = white:Lerp(black, 0.1)
print(gray10)  --> 0.9, 0.9, 0.9

local gray50 = white:Lerp(black, 0.5)
print(gray50)  --> 0.5, 0.5, 0.5

local gray85 = white:Lerp(black, 0.85)
print(gray85)  --> 0.15, 0.15, 0.15
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.Color3` interpolated between two colors.

p.s: The color to interpolate toward.
An interpolation value between 0 and 1, where 0 returns this color and 1 returns the target color.

kid.simple: Gives a color part of the way between this color and another one. alpha 0 gives this color, 1 gives the other, 0.5 gives the mix halfway between. Handy for health bars that fade from green to red.
kid.example:
local white = Color3.new(1, 1, 1)
local black = Color3.new(0, 0, 0)
print(white:Lerp(black, 0.5)) --> 0.5, 0.5, 0.5 (gray)

m.d:
Returns the hue, saturation, and value of a Color3. This function is the inverse operation of the Color3.fromHSV() constructor.

local red = Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0)
local green = Color3.fromRGB(0, 255, 0)

local redH, redS, redV = red:ToHSV()
print(redH, redS, redV)  --> 1 1 1

local greenH, greenS, greenV = green:ToHSV()
print(greenH, greenS, greenV)  --> 0.3333333 1 1
m.s: Returns the hue, saturation, and value of a `Datatype.Color3`.

kid.simple: Gives back three numbers for this color: hue, saturation, and value (brightness), each 0 to 1. It is the reverse of Color3.fromHSV.
kid.example:
local green = Color3.fromRGB(0, 255, 0)
local h, s, v = green:ToHSV()
print(h, s, v) --> 0.3333333 1 1

m.d:
Converts the color to a six-character hexadecimal string representing the color in the format RRGGBB. It is not prefixed with an octothorpe (#).

The returned string can be provided to Color3.fromHex() to produce the original color.

local red = Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0)
local magenta = Color3.fromRGB(236, 0, 140)

local redHex = red:ToHex()
print(redHex)  --> ff0000

local magentaHex = magenta:ToHex()
print(magentaHex)  --> ec008c
m.s: Returns the hex code of a `Datatype.Color3`.

kid.simple: Turns the color into a 6-character hex code string like "ff0000", with no # in front. You can give it back to Color3.fromHex to get the same color.
kid.example:
local red = Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0)
print(red:ToHex()) --> ff0000

m.d:
Returns a Color3 with the given red, green, and blue values. The parameters should be within the range of 0 to 1.

local red = Color3.new(1, 0, 0)
local green = Color3.new(0, 1, 0)
local blue = Color3.new(0, 0, 1)
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.Color3` with the given red, green, and blue values.

p.s: The red component of the color, from 0 to 1.
The green component of the color, from 0 to 1.
The blue component of the color, from 0 to 1.

kid.simple: Makes a color from red, green, and blue amounts, each from 0 to 1. Leave them out and they are 0, so Color3.new() is black.
kid.example:
local red = Color3.new(1, 0, 0)
local gray = Color3.new(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) -- half of each
local white = Color3.new(1, 1, 1)
kid.gotcha: Numbers above 1 are not the 0 to 255 style. Use fromRGB for that.

m.d:
Creates a Color3 with the given red, green, and blue components. Unlike most other Color3 functions, the parameters for this function should be within the range of 0 to 255.

local red = Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0)
local green = Color3.fromRGB(0, 255, 0)
local blue = Color3.fromRGB(0, 0, 255)
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.Color3` from given components within the range of 0 to 255.

p.s: The red component of the color, from 0 to 255.
The green component of the color, from 0 to 255.
The blue component of the color, from 0 to 255.

kid.simple: Makes a color from red, green, and blue amounts from 0 to 255. These are the numbers most color pickers (including Studio's) show you, so this is usually the easiest one.
kid.example:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 170, 0) -- orange
part.Parent = workspace

m.d:
Creates a Color3 with the given hue, saturation, and value. The parameters should be within the range of 0 to 1.

local red = Color3.fromHSV(1, 1, 1)
local green = Color3.fromHSV(0.3333333, 1, 1)
local white = Color3.fromHSV(0, 0, 1)
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.Color3` from the given hue, saturation, and value components.

p.s: The hue of the color, from 0 to 1.
The saturation of the color, from 0 to 1.
The value (brightness) of the color, from 0 to 1.

kid.simple: Makes a color from hue (which rainbow color), saturation (how strong), and value (how bright), each from 0 to 1. Great for rainbow effects, because you only change one number to go around the rainbow.
kid.example:
local red = Color3.fromHSV(0, 1, 1)
local green = Color3.fromHSV(0.333, 1, 1)
local white = Color3.fromHSV(0, 0, 1) -- no saturation = no color, full bright = white

m.d:
Returns a new Color3 from a six- or three-character hexadecimal format, case insensitive. A preceding hashtag (#) is ignored, if present. This function interprets the given string as a typical web hex color in the format RRGGBB or RGB (shorthand for RRGGBB). For example, #FFAA00 produces an orange color and is the same as #FA0.

local red = Color3.fromHex("FF0000")
local magenta = Color3.fromHex("ec008c")
local black = Color3.fromHex("000")
local white = Color3.fromHex("#FFF")
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.Color3` from a given hex value.

p.s: A three- or six-character hexadecimal color string, optionally prefixed with #.

kid.simple: Makes a color from a hex code string like "FF0000" or "#FF0000". A 3-letter short form also works: "#FA0" is the same as "#FFAA00". Capital or small letters both work.
kid.example:
local magenta = Color3.fromHex("ec008c")
local white = Color3.fromHex("#FFF")

m.d: Returns the hue, saturation, and value of a Color3. This function is the inverse operation of the Color3.fromHSV() constructor.
m.s: Returns the hue, saturation, and value of a `Datatype.Color3`.

p.s: The Color3 to convert to HSV.

m.dep: This function is functionally equivalent to Color3:ToHSV().

kid.simple: Old — use Color3:ToHSV instead.

A Color3 is a color, made by mixing red, green, and blue light. Each of the three parts goes from 0 (none) to 1 (full). You use it to color parts, UI backgrounds, text, lights, and more, and you can pick any color you want, not just a fixed list.
kid.analogy: Color3 is like three flashlights (red, green, and blue) shining on the same spot, each with a brightness dial. All three dials at full makes white, all off makes black, and red plus green at full makes yellow.
whenToUse: Changing the color of a part with BasePart.Color
Coloring UI with BackgroundColor3 or TextColor3
Picking an exact color from a hex code like #FF8800
Fading smoothly between two colors with Lerp
kid.where: Works in any script on the server or the client. Make one with Color3.new, Color3.fromRGB, Color3.fromHSV, or Color3.fromHex.

terms.RGB: Short for Red, Green, Blue: the three light colors mixed to make every color on a screen.
terms.0 to 1 vs 0 to 255: Two ways to write the same brightness. Color3.new uses 0 to 1 (0.5 is half). Color3.fromRGB uses 0 to 255 (128 is about half). Most color pickers show 0 to 255.
terms.hex code: A color written as 6 letters and numbers, like FF0000 for red. The first two are red, the middle two are green, the last two are blue. Websites and art apps use these a lot.
terms.HSV: Another way to describe a color: Hue (which color on the rainbow), Saturation (how strong vs. grayish), and Value (how bright). In Roblox each goes from 0 to 1.
terms.hue: Where the color sits on the rainbow circle. 0 is red, about 0.33 is green, about 0.67 is blue, and 1 wraps back to red.
terms.interpolate / lerp: Find a value part of the way between two values. Halfway between white and black is gray.
terms.BrickColor: An older way to color parts using a fixed list of named colors, like "Bright red".

examples.title: Paint a part with three different color styles
examples.code:
-- Make three parts in a row
local function makePart(x, color)
	local part = Instance.new("Part")
	part.Anchored = true
	part.Position = Vector3.new(x, 5, 0)
	part.Color = color
	part.Parent = workspace
end

makePart(0, Color3.new(1, 0, 0))        -- red, using 0 to 1
makePart(5, Color3.fromRGB(0, 170, 255)) -- sky blue, using 0 to 255
makePart(10, Color3.fromHex("#FFAA00"))  -- orange, using a hex code
explain: makePart is a helper that builds an anchored part at a spot and colors it.
Color3.new(1, 0, 0) means full red, no green, no blue.
Color3.fromRGB(0, 170, 255) uses the 0 to 255 numbers you see in most color pickers.
Color3.fromHex("#FFAA00") reads a web-style hex code.

examples.title: Rainbow part that cycles through every color
examples.code:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Anchored = true
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)
part.Parent = workspace

local hue = 0
while true do
	-- Full saturation and full brightness, only the hue changes
	part.Color = Color3.fromHSV(hue, 1, 1)
	hue = (hue + 0.01) % 1 -- go up a little, wrap back to 0 after 1
	task.wait(0.05)
end
explain: Color3.fromHSV takes hue, saturation, and value, each from 0 to 1.
Only the hue changes, so the part walks around the rainbow: red, yellow, green, blue, purple, then red again.
% 1 keeps hue between 0 and 1 by wrapping it back to 0.
task.wait(0.05) pauses a tiny bit each time so the loop does not freeze the game.

gotchas: Color3.new(255, 0, 0) is wrong: Color3.new expects 0 to 1. Use Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0) for 0 to 255 numbers.
Color3 values cannot be changed after they are made (part.Color.R = 1 does not work). Make a new Color3 instead.
Setting part.Color also changes part.BrickColor to the closest named color, and the other way around.

datatype/ColorSequence.d:
The ColorSequence data type represents a gradient of color values from 0 to 1. The color values are expressed using the ColorSequenceKeypoint type. This type is used in various properties of ParticleEmitter, Trail, Beam, and other objects that use color gradients.

Equality

Two ColorSequence objects are equivalent only if the values of their ColorSequenceKeypoint are equivalent, even if both would result in similar gradients.

Evaluation

The ColorSequence type does not have a built-in method for getting the value at a certain time/point. However, you can use the following function to evaluate at a specific time.

local function evalColorSequence(sequence: ColorSequence, time: number)
    -- If time is 0 or 1, return the first or last value respectively
    if time == 0 then
        return sequence.Keypoints[1].Value
    elseif time == 1 then
        return sequence.Keypoints[#sequence.Keypoints].Value
    end

    -- Otherwise, step through each sequential pair of keypoints
    for i = 1, #sequence.Keypoints - 1 do
        local thisKeypoint = sequence.Keypoints[i]
        local nextKeypoint = sequence.Keypoints[i + 1]
        if time >= thisKeypoint.Time and time < nextKeypoint.Time then
            -- Calculate how far alpha lies between the points
            local alpha = (time - thisKeypoint.Time) / (nextKeypoint.Time - thisKeypoint.Time)
            -- Evaluate the real value between the points using alpha
            return Color3.new(
                (nextKeypoint.Value.R - thisKeypoint.Value.R) * alpha + thisKeypoint.Value.R,
                (nextKeypoint.Value.G - thisKeypoint.Value.G) * alpha + thisKeypoint.Value.G,
                (nextKeypoint.Value.B - thisKeypoint.Value.B) * alpha + thisKeypoint.Value.B
            )
        end
    end
end

local colorSequence = ColorSequence.new{
    ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0, Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0)),
    ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0.5, Color3.fromRGB(0, 190, 200)),
    ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(1, Color3.fromRGB(190, 0, 255))
}

print(evalColorSequence(colorSequence, 0.75))  --> 0.372549, 0.372549, 0.892157
datatype/ColorSequence.s: A gradient of color values comprised of `Datatype.ColorSequenceKeypoint|ColorSequenceKeypoints`.

m.d: An array containing ColorSequenceKeypoint values for the ColorSequence.
m.s: An array of `Datatype.ColorSequenceKeypoint` values in ascending order.

kid.simple: The list of ColorSequenceKeypoints in this gradient, in time order. Read it to see each color stop.
kid.example:
local seq = ColorSequence.new(Color3.new(1, 0, 0), Color3.new(0, 0, 1))
for _, keypoint in seq.Keypoints do
	print(keypoint.Time, keypoint.Value)
end

m.d:
Returns a sequence of two keypoints with c for both the start and end values.

local colorSequence = ColorSequence.new(c)
-- Equivalent to
local colorSequence = ColorSequence.new{
    ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0, c),
    ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(1, c)
}
m.s: Returns a new `Datatype.ColorSequence` that is entirely the specified color.

p.s: The Color3 value used for both the start and end of the sequence.

kid.simple: Makes a ColorSequence. Give it one Color3 (that color the whole way), two Color3s (start and end), or a list of ColorSequenceKeypoints for more colors.
kid.example:
local allRed = ColorSequence.new(Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0))
local sunset = ColorSequence.new(Color3.fromRGB(255, 150, 0), Color3.fromRGB(150, 0, 200))
local three = ColorSequence.new({
	ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0, Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0)),
	ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0.5, Color3.fromRGB(0, 190, 200)),
	ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(1, Color3.fromRGB(190, 0, 255)),
})
kid.gotcha: With a list, the first time must be 0 and the last must be 1.

kid.simple: A ColorSequence is a color gradient: colors that blend from one to another along a timeline from 0 (start) to 1 (end). You describe it with ColorSequenceKeypoints, and Roblox blends smoothly between them. It colors particles, beams, trails, and UI gradients.
kid.analogy: It is like a sunset painted on a strip of paper: orange on the left, pink in the middle, purple on the right, all blended together.
whenToUse: ParticleEmitter.Color: fire that starts yellow and turns red
Trail.Color and Beam.Color: rainbow streaks
UIGradient.Color: a colorful gradient on a button or frame
kid.where: Works in any script. Make one with ColorSequence.new(color), ColorSequence.new(startColor, endColor), or ColorSequence.new({ keypoints }).

terms.gradient: A smooth blend from one color to another.
terms.keypoint: One dot on a timeline that says "at this moment, the value is this". Roblox draws a straight line between dots to fill in the moments in between.
terms.time (0 to 1): Where on the timeline a keypoint sits, as a fraction. 0 is the very start, 1 is the very end, 0.5 is halfway. For a particle that lives 2 seconds, time 0.5 means after 1 second.
terms.Color3: A color made of red, green, and blue amounts.
terms.ParticleEmitter: An object that shoots out lots of little images (particles) to make fire, smoke, sparkles, and similar effects.
terms.Trail: A streak that follows behind a moving object, like a comet tail.
terms.UIGradient: An object you put inside a UI element to color it with a gradient.

examples.title: A rainbow gradient on a button
examples.place: LocalScript in StarterGui (with a ScreenGui that has a TextButton named PlayButton)
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")
local button = playerGui:WaitForChild("ScreenGui"):WaitForChild("PlayButton")

-- The button's own color should be white so the gradient shows true colors
button.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.new(1, 1, 1)

local gradient = Instance.new("UIGradient")
gradient.Color = ColorSequence.new({
	ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0, Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0)),   -- left: red
	ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0.5, Color3.fromRGB(0, 255, 0)), -- middle: green
	ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(1, Color3.fromRGB(0, 0, 255)),   -- right: blue
})
gradient.Parent = button
explain: We find the button in the player's screen UI.
A UIGradient tints its parent, so a white background lets the colors show clearly.
Three keypoints: red at the start (left edge), green in the middle, blue at the end (right edge).
Between the keypoints Roblox blends the colors, so you see orange and yellow between red and green.

examples.title: Fire that turns from yellow to red
examples.code:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Anchored = true
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)
part.Parent = workspace

local fire = Instance.new("ParticleEmitter")
fire.Color = ColorSequence.new(Color3.fromRGB(255, 220, 0), Color3.fromRGB(255, 30, 0))
fire.Parent = part
explain: ColorSequence.new(start, finish) is a shortcut for two keypoints.
Each particle is yellow when it is born and slowly turns red as it gets older.

gotchas: The first keypoint must be at time 0 and the last at time 1.
Keypoints must be in time order, and you can have between 2 and 20 of them.
There is no built-in "what color is it at time 0.3?" function. You can write one that blends the two nearest keypoints.

datatype/ColorSequenceKeypoint.d:
The ColorSequenceKeypoint data type represents a single keypoint in a ColorSequence. Each keypoint has a time position between 0 and 1 and a Color3 value that defines the color at that point in the sequence. Properties that use a ColorSequence, such as ParticleEmitter.Color, Beam.Color, and Trail.Color, interpolate linearly between consecutive keypoints in RGB color space.

local keypoints = {
    ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0, Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0)),
    ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0.5, Color3.fromRGB(0, 255, 0)),
    ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(1, Color3.fromRGB(0, 0, 255)),
}
local colorSequence = ColorSequence.new(keypoints)
datatype/ColorSequenceKeypoint.s: A color and time value that represents a keypoint in a `Datatype.ColorSequence`.

m.d: The relative time at which this keypoint is positioned within the parent ColorSequence, expressed as a number from 0 to 1 where 0 is the beginning of the sequence and 1 is the end. Within a ColorSequence, the first keypoint must have a time of 0 and the last keypoint must have a time of 1; any intermediate keypoints must be in ascending time order. The engine linearly interpolates colors between consecutive keypoints in RGB color space based on their time positions. Defaults to 0.
m.s: The relative time at which the keypoint is located.

kid.simple: Where this color stop sits, from 0 (start) to 1 (end). The first stop in a sequence must be at 0 and the last at 1.
kid.example:
local kp = ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0.5, Color3.new(0, 1, 0))
print(kp.Time) --> 0.5

m.d: The Color3 color value at this keypoint's position in the sequence. When the engine evaluates a ColorSequence, it linearly interpolates between adjacent keypoints' color values in RGB color space based on time. Each component of the color (red, green, blue) must be between 0 and 1. Defaults to (0, 0, 0) (black).
m.s: The Color3 value of the keypoint.

kid.simple: The color (a Color3) at this stop.
kid.example:
local kp = ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0.5, Color3.new(0, 1, 0))
print(kp.Value) --> 0, 1, 0

m.d: Returns a ColorSequenceKeypoint with the given time and color. The time parameter should be a number between 0 and 1, where 0 represents the beginning of the sequence and 1 represents the end. The color parameter is a Color3 whose components must each be between 0 and 1.
m.s: Returns a ColorSequenceKeypoint from the given time and color.

p.s: The position of the keypoint along the sequence, a number between 0 and 1.
The color value at this keypoint.

kid.simple: Makes a color stop from a time (0 to 1) and a Color3.
kid.example:
local start = ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0, Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0))   -- red at the start
local middle = ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0.5, Color3.fromRGB(0, 255, 0)) -- green halfway

kid.simple: A ColorSequenceKeypoint is one color stop in a ColorSequence. It says "at this point (from 0 to 1), the color is this". Roblox blends smoothly between the stops.
kid.analogy: It is one blob of paint on a strip of paper. Put a few blobs along the strip and smear between them to get a gradient.
whenToUse: Building a ColorSequence with three or more colors
Reading the color stops of an existing ColorSequence
kid.where: Works in any script. Make one with ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(time, color) and put several in a list for ColorSequence.new.

terms.keypoint: One dot on a timeline that says "at this moment, the value is this". Roblox draws a straight line between dots to fill in the moments in between.
terms.time (0 to 1): Where on the timeline a keypoint sits, as a fraction. 0 is the very start, 1 is the very end, 0.5 is halfway. For a particle that lives 2 seconds, time 0.5 means after 1 second.
terms.Color3: A color made of red, green, and blue amounts, each from 0 to 1.
terms.RGB blending: Mixing two colors by moving each of red, green, and blue part of the way. Halfway between red (1, 0, 0) and blue (0, 0, 1) is (0.5, 0, 0.5), a purple.

examples.title: A trail with three colors
examples.code:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Anchored = true
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)
part.Parent = workspace

-- A Trail needs two Attachments to draw between
local a0 = Instance.new("Attachment")
a0.Position = Vector3.new(0, 0.5, 0)
a0.Parent = part
local a1 = Instance.new("Attachment")
a1.Position = Vector3.new(0, -0.5, 0)
a1.Parent = part

local trail = Instance.new("Trail")
trail.Attachment0 = a0
trail.Attachment1 = a1
trail.Color = ColorSequence.new({
	ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0, Color3.fromRGB(255, 255, 0)), -- yellow
	ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0.5, Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 150)), -- pink
	ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(1, Color3.fromRGB(0, 120, 255)), -- blue
})
trail.Parent = part
explain: Each ColorSequenceKeypoint has a time and a color.
Time 0 is yellow, time 0.5 is pink, time 1 is blue.
The trail only shows up while the part is moving, so try moving the part in Studio to see it.

gotchas: Time is a fraction from 0 to 1, not seconds.
The color must be a Color3 with parts from 0 to 1. Use Color3.fromRGB if you think in 0 to 255.

datatype/Content.d:
The Content data type represents a reference to asset content stored externally or as an object within the place, wrapping a single value of one of the supported ContentSourceType values.

Warning

Replication is not yet supported for Object values. When an Instance with a Content property containing a Object value is replicated, an unusable placeholder Object of the same type will be used instead of the Object itself, and any attempt to read or write the contents of that placeholder object will throw. These placeholder objects will render as a cyan and magenta checkerboard pattern.

This will be replaced with standard replication behavior in the future. For now, do not use EditableImage or EditableMesh as Content on the server on an Instance that can replicate to clients.
datatype/Content.s: Represents a reference to asset content stored externally or as an object within the place.

m.d: An empty Content value with Content.SourceType of None.
m.s: An empty `Content` value with `Datatype.Content.SourceType` of `Enum.ContentSourceType|None`.

kid.simple: An empty Content that points to nothing. Its SourceType is None. Use it to clear a content property or to check if one is empty.
kid.example:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")
local label = playerGui:WaitForChild("ScreenGui"):WaitForChild("ImageLabel")

if label.ImageContent == Content.none then
	print("No image set yet")
end

m.d: The source type of the contained value. Indicates which property contains a non‑nil value.
m.s: The source type of the contained value.

kid.simple: Tells you what kind of Content this is: None (empty), Uri (an asset link), Object (an object in the game), or Opaque. It also tells you which of Uri, Object, or Opaque has a value.
kid.example:
local c = Content.fromAssetId(1234567)
if c.SourceType == Enum.ContentSourceType.Uri then
	print("Points to an asset:", c.Uri)
end

m.d: A URI string if Content.SourceType is Uri, otherwise nil.
m.s: A URI `string` if `Datatype.Content.SourceType` is `Enum.ContentSourceType|Uri`, otherwise `nil`.

kid.simple: The asset link text, like "rbxassetid://1234567", if SourceType is Uri. Otherwise nil.
kid.example:
local c = Content.fromAssetId(1234567)
print(c.Uri) --> rbxassetid://1234567

m.d: A reference to a non-nil Object if Content.SourceType is Object, otherwise nil.
m.s: A reference to a non-`nil` `Class.Object` if `Datatype.Content.SourceType` is `Enum.ContentSourceType|Object`, otherwise `nil`.

kid.simple: The object this Content points to (like an EditableImage), if SourceType is Object. Otherwise nil.
kid.example:
local c = Content.fromAssetId(1234567)
print(c.Object) --> nil (this one is a Uri, not an Object)

m.d: A reference to a non-nil Opaque content if Content.SourceType is Opaque, otherwise nil.
m.s: A reference to a non-`nil` `Opaque` content if `Datatype.Content.SourceType` is `Enum.ContentSourceType|Opaque`, otherwise `nil`.

kid.simple: Holds a special kind of content when SourceType is Opaque, otherwise nil. Most scripts never need it.
kid.example:
local c = Content.none
print(c.Opaque) --> nil

m.d:
Returns a new Content with an asset URI string value referencing content external to the place.

Content.SourceType will be Uri, and Content.Uri will contain a non‑nil string value.

If uri is empty, Content.none will be returned instead.
m.s: Returns a new `Content` with an [asset URI](../../../projects/assets/index.md#asset-uris) `string` value referencing content external to the place.

p.s: The asset URI string.

kid.simple: Makes a Content from an asset link like "rbxassetid://1234567". An empty string gives Content.none.
kid.example:
local c = Content.fromUri("rbxassetid://0") -- replace 0 with a real asset ID
print(c.SourceType)

m.d:
Returns a new Content from a numeric asset ID. This is a convenience constructor equivalent to calling Content.fromUri("rbxassetid://" .. tostring(assetId)).

Content.SourceType will be Uri, and Content.Uri will contain the formatted rbxassetid:// URI string.

If assetId is 0, Content.none will be returned instead.

Throws if assetId is non‑finite, for example math.huge() or 0/0.
m.s: Returns a new `Content` from a numeric asset ID.

p.s: The numeric asset ID.

kid.simple: Makes a Content from an asset ID number. It is a shortcut for Content.fromUri("rbxassetid://" .. id). An ID of 0 gives Content.none.
kid.example:
local c = Content.fromAssetId(1234567) -- use your own asset ID
print(c.Uri) --> rbxassetid://1234567
kid.gotcha: math.huge or 0/0 are not real numbers for an ID and cause an error.

m.d:
Returns a new Content with a strong reference to an Object.

Content.SourceType will be Object, and Content.Object will contain a non‑nil Object reference.

Content.Object references are strong references that hold shared ownership of the Object. Any Content.Object reference will extend the lifetime of that Object and prevent it from being garbage collected.

Throws if object is nil.
m.s: Returns a new `Content` with a strong reference to an `Class.Object`.

p.s: The Object to reference.

kid.simple: Makes a Content that points to an object in the game, like an EditableImage you made with code. While the Content exists, the object will not be cleaned up.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript
local AssetService = game:GetService("AssetService")

local editable = AssetService:CreateEditableImage({ Size = Vector2.new(64, 64) })
if editable then
	local c = Content.fromObject(editable)
	print(c.SourceType) --> Enum.ContentSourceType.Object
end
kid.gotcha: Passing nil causes an error. Object Content does not copy from server to players yet, so use it on the client.

m.d: An empty Content value with Content.SourceType of None.
m.s: An empty `Content` value with `Datatype.Content.SourceType` of `Enum.ContentSourceType|None`.

kid.simple: An empty Content that points to nothing. Its SourceType is None. Use it to clear a content property or to check if one is empty.
kid.example:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")
local label = playerGui:WaitForChild("ScreenGui"):WaitForChild("ImageLabel")

if label.ImageContent == Content.none then
	print("No image set yet")
end

kid.simple: A Content points to something like an image, mesh, or sound for Roblox to show or play. It can point to an uploaded asset (with an asset ID or a link like rbxassetid://123) or to an object inside the game, like an EditableImage you are drawing on. SourceType tells you which kind it is.
kid.analogy: A Content is like a label on a box saying where to find the picture: either "it's in the Roblox warehouse, shelf 12345" (an asset ID) or "it's right here in this room" (an object in the game).
whenToUse: Setting content properties like ImageLabel.ImageContent from an asset ID
Showing an EditableImage you created with code
Checking whether a content property is empty (Content.none)
kid.where: Works in any script. Make one with Content.fromAssetId, Content.fromUri, or Content.fromObject, or use Content.none for empty.

terms.asset: A file stored by Roblox, like an image, mesh, sound, or font. Each one has an ID number.
terms.asset ID: The number for an uploaded asset, like 1234567.
terms.URI: A text link to an asset, like rbxassetid://1234567.
terms.EditableImage: An image you can draw on with code, pixel by pixel.
terms.replicate: Copy from the server to every player's game automatically. Content objects (like EditableImages) are not copied yet.
terms.server / client: The server is Roblox's computer running the game for everyone. The client is each player's own device.
terms.garbage collected: Cleaned up and deleted automatically by Roblox when nothing uses it anymore.

examples.title: Show an uploaded image
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local player = Players.LocalPlayer

local screenGui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
screenGui.Parent = player:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

local picture = Instance.new("ImageLabel")
picture.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(200, 200)
picture.Parent = screenGui

local IMAGE_ID = 0 -- replace 0 with your own image asset ID
picture.ImageContent = Content.fromAssetId(IMAGE_ID)

print(picture.ImageContent.SourceType) -- Enum.ContentSourceType.Uri (or None while the ID is 0)
explain: We make an ImageLabel 200 by 200 pixels.
Content.fromAssetId turns the number into a Content that points to rbxassetid://<your ID>.
If the ID is 0, you get Content.none (empty) instead.
SourceType tells us what kind of Content it is.

gotchas: Content made from an object (fromObject) does not copy from the server to players yet. Players see a cyan and magenta checkerboard. Do EditableImage and EditableMesh work in LocalScripts instead.
Content.fromAssetId(0) and Content.fromUri("") give Content.none (empty), not an error.
A Content made with fromObject keeps that object alive as long as the Content is used.

datatype/DateTime.d:
The DateTime data type represents a moment in time using a Unix timestamp. It can be used to easily format dates and times in specific locales. When converted to a string, a string conversion of the stored timestamp integer is returned. They don't store timezone values. Instead, timezones are considered when constructing and using DateTime objects.

DateTime objects are equal if and only if their UnixTimestampMillis properties are equal.

Time Value Table

The ToUniversalTime() and ToLocalTime() methods return a table of time-related values, such as Year, Month, and Day. The format of the table returned by these functions is described below, with each integer element in descending size order.

Name Range Notes
Year1400–9999—
Month1–12—
Day1–31—
Hour0–23—
Minute0–59—
Second0–59—
Millisecond0–999—

String Format

The DateTime object supports date/time conversion into a string through the FormatUniversalTime() and FormatLocalTime() methods. They both work the same except for which timezone the DateTime should be interpreted in.

The first argument passed to these methods must be a string representing one of the tokens shown below. The tokens are then replaced with a specific value depending on the provided locale.

local dt = DateTime.now()

-- The "dddd" token is replaced with the full day of the week
print("Today is " .. dt:FormatLocalTime("dddd", "en-us"))

-- For the "en-us" locale, the "LL" token equals "MMMM D, YYYY"
print("The date is " .. dt:FormatLocalTime("LL", "en-us"))
Composite Tokens

Depending on locale, these tokens replace to specific combinations of the elemental tokens described in the next section. This produces a correct date/time string depending on the locale. For example, in English, the date has the "[month] [day]" as in "June 11". In French, the date is in a "[day] [month]" format as in "11 juin". These special rules are handled for you automatically through the following composite tokens, so use these if you're displaying simple time and/or date information.

Token(s) Locale Examples (Format)

LT
en-us : 8:30 PM (h:mm A)
zh-cn : 20:30 (HH:mm)

zh-cn : 20:30:25 (HH:mm:ss)
Month (Number), Day, Year
L
en-us : 09/04/1986 (MM/DD/YYYY)
zh-cn : 1986/09/04 (YYYY/MM/DD)
l
en-us : 9/4/1986 (M/D/YYYY)
zh-cn : 1986/9/4 (YYYY/M/D)
Month (Name), Day, Year
LL
en-us : September 4, 1986 (MMMM D, YYYY)
zh-cn : 1986年9月4日 (YYYY年M月D日)
ll
en-us : Sep 4, 1986 (MMM D, YYYY)
zh-cn : 1986年9月4日 (YYYY年M月D日)
Month (Name), Day, Year, Time
LLL

Elemental Tokens

Each of these tokens replace to a single value and can be used as elements of a larger time string. Avoid using these if you only need simple date and time information, as the composite tokens are more appropriate for those purposes.

datatype/DateTime.s: A data type that represents a moment in time.

m.d: The number of seconds since January 1st, 1970 at 00:00 UTC (the Unix epoch). Range is -17,987,443,200 to 253,402,300,799, approximately years 1400–9999.
m.s: The number of **seconds** between January 1st, 1970 at 00:00 UTC (the Unix epoch).

kid.simple: This moment as a whole number of seconds since January 1, 1970 (UTC). Easy to save and to subtract.
kid.example:
local start = DateTime.now().UnixTimestamp
task.wait(3)
print(DateTime.now().UnixTimestamp - start) --> about 3

m.d: The number of milliseconds since January 1st, 1970 at 00:00 UTC (the Unix epoch). Range is -17,987,443,200,000 to 253,402,300,799,999, approximately years 1400–9999.
m.s: The number of **milliseconds** between January 1st, 1970 at 00:00 UTC (the Unix epoch).

kid.simple: This moment as a number of milliseconds (thousandths of a second) since January 1, 1970 (UTC). Two DateTimes are equal only if this number is the same.
kid.example:
local now = DateTime.now()
print(now.UnixTimestampMillis) -- like 1792699200123

m.d: Converts the value of this DateTime object to Universal Coordinated Time (UTC). The returned table contains the following keys: Year, Month, Day, Hour, Minute, Second, Millisecond. For more details, see the time value table in this data type's description. The values within this table could be passed to fromUniversalTime() to produce the original DateTime object.
m.s: Returns the components of the `Datatype.DateTime` in UTC.

kid.simple: Breaks the moment into a table of calendar parts in UTC: Year, Month, Day, Hour, Minute, Second, Millisecond.
kid.example:
local parts = DateTime.now():ToUniversalTime()
print(parts.Year, parts.Month, parts.Day, parts.Hour)

m.d: Converts the value of this DateTime object to local time. The returned table contains the following keys: Year, Month, Day, Hour, Minute, Second, Millisecond. For more details, see the time value table in this data type's description. The values within this table could be passed to fromLocalTime() to produce the original DateTime object.
m.s: Returns the components of the `Datatype.DateTime` in local time.

kid.simple: Breaks the moment into a table of calendar parts in the device's local time zone: Year, Month, Day, Hour, Minute, Second, Millisecond.
kid.example:
local parts = DateTime.now():ToLocalTime()
if parts.Hour >= 18 then
	print("Good evening!")
end

m.d:
Formats a date as a ISO 8601 date-time string. The value returned by this function could be passed to fromIsoDate() to produce the original DateTime object.

An example ISO 8601 date-time string would be 2020-01-02T10:30:45Z, which represents January 2nd 2020 at 10:30 AM, 45 seconds.
m.s: Returns the `Datatype.DateTime` as an ISO 8601 date-time string.

kid.simple: Turns the moment into ISO 8601 text in UTC, like "2020-01-02T10:30:45Z". DateTime.fromIsoDate can turn it back.
kid.example: print(DateTime.now():ToIsoDate()) -- like 2026-10-22T14:05:09Z

m.d:
Generates a string from the DateTime value interpreted as Universal Coordinated Time (UTC) and a format string. The format string should contain tokens, which will replace to certain date/time values described by the DateTime object. For more details, see the String Format section in this data type's description.

local dt = DateTime.now()
-- For en-us, the "LL" token equals "MMM D, YYYY", which gives "June 11, 2020"
print("The date is " .. dt:FormatUniversalTime("LL", "en-us"))
--> "The date is June 11, 2020"
m.s: Returns the DateTime's value in UTC formatted into a string.

p.s: A format string containing tokens that are replaced with date and time values, such as "LL" or "YYYY-MM-DD".
A BCP 47 locale identifier (such as "en-us") that determines language and formatting conventions.

kid.simple: Turns the moment into text using a pattern (like "YYYY-MM-DD" or "LL") and a language code (like "en-us"), in UTC time. Good when everyone should see the same time.
kid.example:
local t = DateTime.fromUniversalTime(2030, 1, 1)
print(t:FormatUniversalTime("LL", "en-us")) --> January 1, 2030

m.d:
Generates a string from the DateTime value interpreted as local time and a format string. The format string should contain tokens, which will replace to certain date/time values described by the DateTime object. For more details, see the String Format section in this data type's description.

local dt = DateTime.now()
-- For en-us, the "LL" token equals "MMM D, YYYY", which gives "June 11, 2020"
print("The date is " .. dt:FormatLocalTime("LL", "en-us"))
--> "The date is June 11, 2020"
m.s: Returns the `Datatype.DateTime` object's value in local time formatted into a string.

p.s: A format string containing tokens that are replaced with date and time values, such as "LL" or "YYYY-MM-DD".
A BCP 47 locale identifier (such as "en-us") that determines language and formatting conventions.

kid.simple: Turns the moment into text using a pattern and a language code, in the device's local time zone. Use it in a LocalScript to show players their own time.
kid.example:
local now = DateTime.now()
print(now:FormatLocalTime("dddd, h:mm A", "en-us")) -- like Thursday, 8:30 PM

m.d:
Returns a new DateTime representing the current moment in time, using the device's local clock. Most operating systems automatically sync their local time against online time servers, so this should be within a few hundred milliseconds. However, users can easily disable sync behavior and set the system time to anything they want; for synchronized time between client and server, use Workspace:GetServerTimeNow() instead.

When you need to precisely measure the time elapsed between two points in time, like when testing performance, use os.clock() instead.
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.DateTime` representing the current moment in time.

kid.simple: Gives a DateTime for right now, using the device's clock. Good for showing the time, but players can change their own clock.
kid.example:
local now = DateTime.now()
print(now.UnixTimestamp) -- seconds since January 1, 1970
kid.gotcha: For a time that matches between server and clients, use workspace:GetServerTimeNow() instead.

m.d:
Returns a new DateTime object from the given Unix timestamp, or the number of seconds since January 1st, 1970 at 00:00 (UTC).

This function only has granularity to 1 second. To represent sub-second timestamps, use DateTime.fromUnixTimestampMillis() instead.
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.DateTime` representing the given Unix timestamp.

p.s: The number of seconds since January 1st, 1970 at 00:00 UTC (the Unix epoch). Must be between -17,987,443,200 and 253,402,300,799 (approximately years 1400 to 9999).

kid.simple: Makes a DateTime from a number of seconds since January 1, 1970 (UTC). For example, 0 is that exact midnight, and 86400 is one day later.
kid.example:
local moment = DateTime.fromUnixTimestamp(86400)
print(moment:ToIsoDate()) --> 1970-01-02T00:00:00Z
kid.gotcha: It only counts whole seconds. Use fromUnixTimestampMillis for more detail.

m.d: Returns a new DateTime object from the given Unix timestamp, or the number of milliseconds since January 1st, 1970 at 00:00 (UTC).
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.DateTime` representing the given Unix timestamp in milliseconds.

p.s: The number of milliseconds since January 1st, 1970 at 00:00 UTC (the Unix epoch). Must be between -17,987,443,200,000 and 253,402,300,799,999 (approximately years 1400 to 9999).

kid.simple: Makes a DateTime from a number of milliseconds (thousandths of a second) since January 1, 1970 (UTC).
kid.example:
local moment = DateTime.fromUnixTimestampMillis(1500) -- 1.5 seconds after the start
print(moment.UnixTimestampMillis) --> 1500

m.d:
Returns a new DateTime using the given units from a UTC time. The values accepted are similar to those found in the time value table returned by ToUniversalTime().

  • Date units (year, month, day) that produce an invalid date will raise an error. For example, January 32nd or February 29th on a non-leap year.
  • Time units (hour, minute, second, millisecond) that are outside their normal range are valid. For example, 90 minutes will cause the hour to roll over by 1; -10 seconds will cause the minute value to roll back by 1.
  • Non-integer values are rounded down. For example, providing 2.5 hours will be equivalent to providing 2 hours, not 2 hours 30 minutes.
  • Omitted values are assumed to be their lowest value in their normal range, except for year which defaults to 1970.
m.s: Returns a new `Datatype.DateTime` using the given units from a UTC time.

p.s: The year value, between 1400 and 9999.
The month value, between 1 and 12.
The day of the month, between 1 and 31.
The hour value, between 0 and 23.
The minute value, between 0 and 59.
The second value, between 0 and 60.
The millisecond value, between 0 and 999.

kid.simple: Makes a DateTime from calendar parts (year, month, day, hour, minute, second, millisecond) in UTC, the world clock. Anything you leave out is the lowest value (year defaults to 1970). Extra minutes roll over: 90 minutes becomes 1 hour 30 minutes.
kid.example:
-- New Year's Day 2030 at midnight, world time
local newYear = DateTime.fromUniversalTime(2030, 1, 1)
print(newYear:ToIsoDate()) --> 2030-01-01T00:00:00Z
kid.gotcha: Impossible dates like month 13 or January 32 cause an error. Decimals are rounded down: 2.5 hours counts as 2.

m.d:
Returns a new DateTime using the given units from a local time. The values accepted are similar to those found in the time value table returned by ToLocalTime().

  • Date units (year, month, day) that produce an invalid date will raise an error. For example, January 32nd or February 29th on a non-leap year.
  • Time units (hour, minute, second, millisecond) that are outside their normal range are valid. For example, 90 minutes will cause the hour to roll over by 1; -10 seconds will cause the minute value to roll back by 1.
  • Non-integer values are rounded down. For example, providing 2.5 hours will be equivalent to providing 2 hours, not 2 hours 30 minutes.
  • Omitted values are assumed to be their lowest value in their normal range, except for year which defaults to 1970.
m.s: Returns a new `Datatype.DateTime` using the given units from a local time.

p.s: The year value, between 1400 and 9999.
The month value, between 1 and 12.
The day of the month, between 1 and 31.
The hour value, between 0 and 23.
The minute value, between 0 and 59.
The second value, between 0 and 60.
The millisecond value, between 0 and 999.

kid.simple: Like fromUniversalTime, but the calendar parts you give are in the local time zone of the device running the script.
kid.example:
-- October 22, 2026 at 6 PM in the device's own time zone
local t = DateTime.fromLocalTime(2026, 10, 22, 18, 0, 0)
print(t:FormatLocalTime("LLL", "en-us"))
kid.gotcha: On the server, local time means the server's time zone, not the player's.

m.d:
Returns a DateTime from an ISO 8601 date-time string in UTC time, such as those returned by ToIsoDate(). If the string parsing fails, the function returns nil.

An example ISO 8601 date-time string would be 2020-01-02T10:30:45Z, which represents January 2nd 2020 at 10:30 AM, 45 seconds.
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.DateTime` from an ISO 8601 date-time string (in UTC).

p.s: An ISO 8601 date-time string in UTC, such as "2020-01-02T10:30:45Z".

kid.simple: Makes a DateTime from ISO 8601 text in UTC, like "2020-01-02T10:30:45Z". If the text cannot be understood, it gives nil.
kid.example:
local t = DateTime.fromIsoDate("2020-01-02T10:30:45Z")
if t then
	print(t.UnixTimestamp)
end

kid.simple: A DateTime is one exact moment in time, like "June 11, 2020 at 3:45 PM". It can tell you the current time, turn times into nice text like "September 4, 1986", and convert between the player's own time zone and world time (UTC). Inside, it is just a count of milliseconds since January 1, 1970.
kid.analogy: A DateTime is like a stopwatch that started on January 1, 1970 and has been ticking ever since. The number on it is the moment. Then you can ask it to read that number out as a calendar date in any language or time zone.
whenToUse: Daily rewards: checking if a day has passed since the last claim
Showing the date or time on screen in the player's own format
Saving a time in a DataStore as a number and loading it later
Counting down to an event on a set date
kid.where: Works in any script on the server or client. Make one with DateTime.now(), DateTime.fromUnixTimestamp, DateTime.fromUniversalTime, DateTime.fromLocalTime, or DateTime.fromIsoDate.

terms.Unix timestamp: The number of seconds since midnight on January 1, 1970 (in UTC). For example, 86400 means exactly one day later: January 2, 1970.
terms.millisecond: One thousandth of a second. 1000 milliseconds = 1 second.
terms.UTC: Short for Coordinated Universal Time, the world's shared clock. It is the same everywhere, no matter your time zone.
terms.local time: The time on the player's own device clock, in their time zone. Two players in different countries see different local times for the same moment.
terms.time zone: A region of the world that uses the same clock time. When it is noon in London, it is morning in New York.
terms.ISO 8601: A standard way to write a date and time as text, like 2020-01-02T10:30:45Z. The Z at the end means UTC.
terms.format string: A pattern of special letters that get replaced with parts of the date. YYYY becomes the year, MM the month number, DD the day.
terms.locale: A code for a language and region, like "en-us" for American English. It controls things like month names and the order of day and month.
terms.dictionary: A Lua table where you look things up by name, like t.Year or t.Month.

examples.title: Show today's date in the player's own time zone
examples.code:
local now = DateTime.now()

-- "LL" is a ready-made pattern: like "September 4, 1986" in en-us
print("Today is " .. now:FormatLocalTime("LL", "en-us"))

-- "LT" is the short time, like "8:30 PM"
print("The time is " .. now:FormatLocalTime("LT", "en-us"))

-- Build your own pattern
print(now:FormatLocalTime("YYYY-MM-DD", "en-us")) -- like 2026-10-22
explain: DateTime.now() grabs the current moment.
FormatLocalTime turns it into text using the player's time zone. We run it in a LocalScript so it uses the player's device.
"LL" and "LT" are shortcuts for a long date and a short time.
"YYYY-MM-DD" builds a custom pattern: 4-digit year, 2-digit month, 2-digit day.

examples.title: Is it time for a daily reward?
examples.code:
local ONE_DAY = 24 * 60 * 60 -- 86400 seconds in a day

-- Pretend we loaded this from a DataStore (a Unix timestamp in seconds)
local lastClaim = DateTime.now().UnixTimestamp - 90000

local now = DateTime.now().UnixTimestamp
if now - lastClaim >= ONE_DAY then
	print("Reward ready! Claim it!")
	lastClaim = now -- save this back to the DataStore
else
	local secondsLeft = ONE_DAY - (now - lastClaim)
	print("Come back in", math.ceil(secondsLeft / 3600), "hours")
end
explain: UnixTimestamp is a plain number, which is easy to save in a DataStore.
We subtract the last claim time from now to get how many seconds have passed.
If at least 86400 seconds (one day) have passed, the reward is ready.
Otherwise we work out how many hours are left by dividing seconds by 3600.

gotchas: A player can change their device clock, so do not trust DateTime.now() on the client for rewards. Do reward checks on the server.
To measure how long code takes, use os.clock(), not DateTime.
FormatLocalTime and ToLocalTime use the time zone of the computer running the script. On the server, that is the server's zone, not the player's.
Dates that do not exist, like February 30, cause an error in fromUniversalTime and fromLocalTime.

datatype/DockWidgetPluginGuiInfo.d: The DockWidgetPluginGuiInfo data type describes details for a DockWidgetPluginGui. This data type is used when constructing a PluginGui via the plugin's Plugin:CreateDockWidgetPluginGuiAsync() method.

m.d: The initial enabled state of a PluginGui created using this DockWidgetPluginGuiInfo. If a PluginGui with the same ''pluginGuiId'' has previously been created in an earlier session of Roblox Studio, then it will reload that saved enabled state (unless InitialEnabledShouldOverrideRestore is true).
m.s: The enabled state of the `Class.PluginGui` if it does not have a saved state from a previous session.

m.d: If true, the value of InitialEnabled will override the previously saved enabled state of a PluginGui being created with this DockWidgetPluginGuiInfo. The previously saved enabled state is loaded based on the pluginGuiId argument of Plugin:CreateDockWidgetPluginGuiAsync().
m.s: If true, will override any saved enabled state with the `InitialEnabled` value.

m.d: The initial pixel width of a PluginGui created using this DockWidgetPluginGuiInfo, when the InitialDockState is set to Float.
m.s: The initial pixel width of the PluginGui when floating.

m.d: The initial pixel height of a PluginGui created using this DockWidgetPluginGuiInfo, when the InitialDockState is set to Float.
m.s: The initial pixel height of the PluginGui when floating.

m.d:
The minimum width of a PluginGui created using this DockWidgetPluginGuiInfo, in pixels.

Each platform has its own absolute minimum that Roblox will enforce. These variations exist to account for the contents of the title bar (which varies by platform) when the widget is floating. For example, on a Mac, the width can never be less than ~80 pixels to accommodate the close/minimize/maximize buttons.
m.s: The minimum pixel width of the PluginGui.

m.d: The minimum height of a PluginGui created using this DockWidgetPluginGuiInfo, in pixels.
m.s: The minimum pixel height of the PluginGui.

m.d: The main constructor function for the DockWidgetPluginGuiInfo.
m.s: Returns a new DockWidgetPluginGuiInfo object.

datatype/Enum.d: The Enum data type represents an individual enum in Roblox. An individual enum can be indexed through the Enums type, via the name of the enum itself.
datatype/Enum.s: A data type that represents an individual enum.

m.d: Returns an array of all the EnumItem options available for this enum.
m.s: Returns an array of all `Datatype.EnumItem` options available for this enum.

r.s: An array of all EnumItem values belonging to this enum.

kid.simple: Gives a list of every option (EnumItem) in this enum.
kid.example:
for _, item in Enum.PartType:GetEnumItems() do
	print(item.Name) -- Ball, Block, Cylinder, ...
end

m.d: Returns either the converted Enum or nil.
m.s: Converts an enum name to an `Datatype.Enum`.

p.s: The name of the EnumItem to look up in this enum.

r.s: The EnumItem whose Name matches the given string, or nil if no match exists.

kid.simple: Finds the option in this enum with the name you give, like "Wood". Gives nil if there is no option with that name.
kid.example:
local wood = Enum.Material:FromName("Wood")
print(wood) --> Enum.Material.Wood
print(Enum.Material:FromName("Chocolate")) --> nil

m.d: Returns either the converted Enum or nil.
m.s: Converts an enum value to an `Datatype.Enum`.

p.s: The integer value of the EnumItem to look up in this enum.

r.s: The EnumItem whose integer value matches the given number, or nil if no match exists.

kid.simple: Finds the option in this enum with the number value you give. Every EnumItem has a number; for example Enum.Material.Plastic is 256. Gives nil if no option has that number.
kid.example:
local plastic = Enum.Material:FromValue(256)
print(plastic) --> Enum.Material.Plastic

kid.simple: An Enum is a fixed list of named choices that Roblox gives you, like Enum.Material (Plastic, Wood, Grass, ...) or Enum.KeyCode (every keyboard key). Each choice in the list is an EnumItem. Using Enums instead of typing words avoids typos.
kid.analogy: An Enum is like a menu at a restaurant. Enum.Material is the menu of materials, and each dish on it (Wood, Grass, Ice) is an EnumItem. You can only order what is on the menu.
whenToUse: Listing every option in a list with GetEnumItems
Turning a saved name like "Wood" back into Enum.Material.Wood with FromName
Turning a saved number back into an EnumItem with FromValue
kid.where: Available everywhere. Get one by name from the global `Enum`, like Enum.Material or Enum.KeyCode.

terms.enum: Short for enumeration: a fixed list of named options.
terms.EnumItem: One option inside an enum, like Enum.Material.Wood.
terms.nil: Lua's word for "nothing". FromName and FromValue give nil if there is no match.
terms.array: A list in Lua, numbered 1, 2, 3, and so on.

examples.title: Give a part a random shape
examples.code:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Anchored = true
part.Size = Vector3.new(4, 4, 4)
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)
part.Parent = workspace

local shapes = Enum.PartType:GetEnumItems() -- Ball, Block, Cylinder, ...
local rng = Random.new()

while true do
	local pick = shapes[rng:NextInteger(1, #shapes)]
	part.Shape = pick
	print("Now I am a", pick.Name)
	task.wait(2)
end
explain: Enum.PartType is the enum (the whole menu of part shapes).
GetEnumItems gives a list of every shape in it.
Every 2 seconds we pick a random shape from the list and give it to the part.
pick.Name is the shape's name as text, like "Ball".

examples.title: Save a material as text and load it back
examples.code:
local saved = Enum.Material.Grass.Name -- "Grass" (easy to store)

-- Later, turn the text back into an EnumItem
local material = Enum.Material:FromName(saved)
if material then
	print("Loaded:", material) --> Enum.Material.Grass
end
explain: You cannot save an EnumItem directly in a DataStore, but you can save its Name (a string).
FromName looks up the item with that name in Enum.Material.
If the name does not exist, FromName gives nil, so we check before using it.

gotchas: Enum.Material (the list) and Enum.Material.Wood (one item) are different things. Properties want the item.
FromName and FromValue give nil when nothing matches. Always check before using the result.

datatype/EnumItem.d: The EnumItem data type represents an individual item in a Roblox enum.
datatype/EnumItem.s: An individual item in an enum.

m.d: The name of the EnumItem.
m.s: The name of the EnumItem.

kid.simple: The name of this option as text, like "Wood". Handy for printing or saving.
kid.example: print(Enum.Material.Wood.Name) --> Wood

m.d: The integral value assigned to the EnumItem.
m.s: The integral value assigned to the EnumItem.

kid.simple: The whole number that belongs to this option. Handy for saving, and Enum:FromValue can turn it back into the EnumItem.
kid.example:
print(Enum.Material.Plastic.Value) --> 256
print(Enum.KeyCode.E.Value)        --> 101

m.d: A reference to the parent Enum of the EnumItem.
m.s: A reference to the parent `Datatype.Enum` of the EnumItem.

kid.simple: The Enum list this option belongs to. Enum.Material.Wood.EnumType is Enum.Material.
kid.example:
local item = Enum.Material.Wood
print(item.EnumType == Enum.Material) --> true

kid.simple: An EnumItem is one option from an Enum list, like Enum.Material.Wood or Enum.KeyCode.E. You use them to set properties and to check what something is. Each one has a Name, a number Value, and knows which Enum it belongs to.
kid.analogy: If an Enum is a restaurant menu, an EnumItem is one dish on it. The dish has a name ("Pizza"), a menu number (#12), and you know which menu it came from.
whenToUse: Setting properties like part.Material = Enum.Material.Neon
Checking which key was pressed, like input.KeyCode == Enum.KeyCode.E
Saving an option as text (Name) or a number (Value)
kid.where: Available everywhere. Get one with Enum.<EnumName>.<ItemName>, like Enum.Material.Wood.

terms.enum: A fixed list of named options, like Enum.Material.
terms.integer: A whole number with no decimal part.

examples.title: Do something when the E key is pressed
examples.code:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")

UserInputService.InputBegan:Connect(function(input, gameProcessed)
	if gameProcessed then
		return -- the player was typing in chat, ignore
	end
	if input.KeyCode == Enum.KeyCode.E then
		print("You pressed E!")
		print(input.KeyCode.Name, input.KeyCode.Value) --> E 101
	end
end)
explain: InputBegan fires whenever the player presses a key or button.
gameProcessed is true when Roblox already used the key, like typing in chat.
input.KeyCode is an EnumItem. We compare it with Enum.KeyCode.E.
The EnumItem's Name is "E" and its Value is 101.

gotchas: Compare EnumItems directly (input.KeyCode == Enum.KeyCode.E), not their names as strings.
EnumItems from different enums are never equal, even if they share a name.

datatype/Enums.d: The Enums data type, more commonly known as Enum by its global variable in Luau), acts as the root access point for all available enums on Roblox. All enums on Roblox are indexed via their name through this data type, and developers can also utilize the GetEnums() method to get a list of all enums on Roblox.
datatype/Enums.s: A root access point of all `Datatype.Enum|Enums`.

m.d: Returns an array containing all available Enums on Roblox.
m.s: Returns an array of all `Datatype.Enum|Enums`.

kid.simple: Gives a list of every Enum that exists in Roblox.
kid.example:
for _, e in Enum:GetEnums() do
	print(e) -- prints each Enum, like Material or KeyCode
end

kid.simple: Enums is the big collection of every Enum in Roblox. You use it all the time without noticing: it is the global word `Enum` that you type before Enum.Material or Enum.KeyCode. It also has GetEnums to list every Enum that exists.
kid.analogy: If each Enum is a menu, Enums is the whole food court holding every menu. You walk up to the food court (Enum) and pick a menu by name (Material, KeyCode).
whenToUse: Getting any Enum by name, like Enum.Material
Listing every Enum that exists with Enum:GetEnums(), for example to explore what is available
kid.where: Available everywhere as the global variable `Enum`. You never make one yourself.

terms.global: Something you can use in any script without creating or requiring it first.
terms.enum: A fixed list of named options, like Enum.Material.
terms.array: A list in Lua, numbered 1, 2, 3, and so on.

examples.title: Count every Enum in Roblox
examples.code:
local allEnums = Enum:GetEnums()
print("Roblox has", #allEnums, "enums")

-- Print the first five names
for i = 1, 5 do
	print(allEnums[i])
end
explain: Enum here is the Enums collection.
GetEnums gives a list of every Enum, like Material, KeyCode, and EasingStyle.
#allEnums is how many there are, and the loop prints the first five.

gotchas: The global is spelled `Enum`, not `Enums`. Enums is just the name of its type.

datatype/Faces.d:
The Faces data type contains six booleans representing whether a feature is enabled for each face (NormalId) of a Part. In other words, this contains a boolean for each axes (X/Y/Z) in both directions (positive/negative). The Handles object uses this data type to enable whether a direction has a visible handle on a Part's face.

local handles = Instance.new("Handles")
handles.Faces = Faces.new(Enum.NormalId.Front, Enum.NormalId.Left)

Like most data types on Roblox, the Faces data type is immutable and you cannot assign to its properties once created.
datatype/Faces.s: A data type containing six booleans, each representing a face of a `Class.BasePart`.

m.d: Whether the top face (positive Y direction, corresponding to NormalId.Top) is included in this Faces value. Defaults to false when NormalId.Top is not passed to the Faces.new() constructor.
m.s: Whether the top face is included.

m.d: Whether the bottom face (negative Y direction, corresponding to NormalId.Bottom) is included in this Faces value. Defaults to false when NormalId.Bottom is not passed to the Faces.new() constructor.
m.s: Whether the bottom face is included.

m.d: Whether the left face (negative X direction, corresponding to NormalId.Left) is included in this Faces value. Defaults to false when NormalId.Left is not passed to the Faces.new() constructor.
m.s: Whether the left face is included.

m.d: Whether the right face (positive X direction, corresponding to NormalId.Right) is included in this Faces value. Defaults to false when NormalId.Right is not passed to the Faces.new() constructor.
m.s: Whether the right face is included.

m.d: Whether the back face (positive Z direction, corresponding to NormalId.Back) is included in this Faces value. Defaults to false when NormalId.Back is not passed to the Faces.new() constructor.
m.s: Whether the back face is included.

m.d: Whether the front face (negative Z direction, corresponding to NormalId.Front) is included in this Faces value. Defaults to false when NormalId.Front is not passed to the Faces.new() constructor.
m.s: Whether the front face is included.

m.d:
Creates a new Faces given some number of NormalId as arguments. Each NormalId provided indicates the property of the same name in the new Faces will be true.

  • The table.unpack() function can be used to unpack a table of NormalId to be included.
  • Passing values that are not a NormalId will do nothing; they are ignored silently.
m.s: Returns a `Faces` with the corresponding face of each passed `Enum.NormalId` as `true`.

p.s: Any number of NormalId values indicating which faces to enable in the new Faces.

datatype/FloatCurveKey.d:
A time-value pair used with FloatCurve instances.

The Interpolation property dictates the interpolation mode for the segment started by this key and ended by the next key on the curve. Each segment may use a different interpolation mode.

The LeftTangent and RightTangent properties apply to the cubic interpolation mode and define the desired tangent (slope) at the key. Different left and right values can be used to encode discontinuities in slope at the key. Attempting to set a RightTangent value on a key that doesn't use the cubic interpolation mode will result in a runtime error. It is possible to set the LeftTangent property on any key, as it will be used should the preceding segment use cubic interpolation.
datatype/FloatCurveKey.s: A time-value pair used with `Class.FloatCurve` instances.

m.d:
Specifies the interpolation mode used for the curve segment that begins at this key and ends at the next key on the FloatCurve. Each segment of the curve can use a different interpolation mode. The default value is KeyInterpolationMode.Cubic.

The available modes are:

  • Constant — the segment holds the value of this key until the next key.
  • Linear — the segment linearly interpolates between this key's value and the next key's value.
  • Cubic — the segment uses a cubic Hermite spline defined by this key's RightTangent and the next key's LeftTangent.

Changing this property to a non-cubic mode automatically clears the RightTangent of this key, because only cubic segments use a right tangent.
m.s: The key interpolation mode for the segment started by this `Datatype.FloatCurveKey`.

m.d: The time position of this FloatCurveKey along the curve's timeline. The default value is 0. Keys within a FloatCurve are kept sorted in ascending time order; if you insert a key at a time that already exists on the curve, the existing key at that time is replaced.
m.s: The time position of this `Datatype.FloatCurveKey`.

m.d: The numerical output value at this key's position on the curve. The default value is 0. When a FloatCurve is sampled at this key's Time, the curve evaluates to this value (subject to any interpolation with neighboring keys depending on the sampling time).
m.s: The value of this `Datatype.FloatCurveKey`.

m.d: The slope of the curve leaving this key toward the next key. The default value is nil, which means the tangent is automatically computed (an effective value of 0 is used during evaluation). This property can only be set when Interpolation is KeyInterpolationMode.Cubic; attempting to set it on a key with Constant or Linear interpolation raises a runtime error. Pairing a different RightTangent value on this key with a different LeftTangent value on the next key creates a discontinuity in slope (a "corner") at the next key.
m.s: The tangent to the right of this `Datatype.FloatCurveKey`.

m.d: The slope of the curve arriving at this key from the previous key. The default value is nil, which means the tangent is automatically computed (an effective value of 0 is used during evaluation). Unlike RightTangent, this property can be set on a key with any interpolation mode, because the preceding segment may itself use cubic interpolation and therefore needs a defined left tangent at this endpoint.
m.s: The tangent to the left of this `Datatype.FloatCurveKey`.

m.d: Creates a new FloatCurveKey at a given time and value. LeftTangent and RightTangent are left uninitialized and, if not initialized, tangent values of 0 will be used when evaluating the curve.
m.s: Returns a new `Datatype.FloatCurveKey` from the given time and value.
