kid.example:
local FONT_ID = 0 -- replace 0 with a real font asset ID number
local font = Font.fromId(FONT_ID, Enum.FontWeight.Medium)

kid.simple: A Font describes the lettering style for text on the screen. It has three parts: the font family (the overall design, like Fredoka One or Bangers), the weight (how thick the letters are, like Regular or Bold), and the style (Normal or Italic). You use it on the FontFace property of TextLabels, TextButtons, and TextBoxes.
kid.analogy: Picking a Font is like picking a marker: first the kind of marker (family), then how thick the tip is (weight), and whether you write slanted (italic).
whenToUse: Changing the lettering of a TextLabel, TextButton, or TextBox with FontFace
Making text bold or italic
Using a font from Roblox's built-in list by name, like "Bangers"
kid.where: Works in any script. Make one with Font.new, Font.fromName, Font.fromEnum, or Font.fromId. Text UI is usually changed in a LocalScript.

terms.font family: A whole set of matching letter designs. One family, like Roboto, has thin, normal, bold, and italic versions.
terms.weight: How thick the letters are, from Thin up through Regular, SemiBold, Bold, and Heavy (an Enum.FontWeight).
terms.style: Normal (straight up) or Italic (slanted), an Enum.FontStyle.
terms.asset ID: A link that points to a file Roblox stores, like rbxasset://fonts/families/Bangers.json for built-in fonts, or rbxassetid://12345 for uploaded ones.
terms.Enum.Font: The older list of fonts. Some properties and functions still need it. Font.fromEnum turns it into the newer Font.
terms.FontFace: The property on text objects that takes a Font.

examples.title: A bold, fun title
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local player = Players.LocalPlayer

local screenGui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
screenGui.Parent = player:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

local title = Instance.new("TextLabel")
title.Size = UDim2.fromScale(0.6, 0.15)
title.Position = UDim2.fromScale(0.2, 0.05)
title.BackgroundTransparency = 1
title.TextScaled = true
title.Text = "Welcome to My Obby!"
-- Built-in font "FredokaOne", bold weight, normal style
title.FontFace = Font.fromName("FredokaOne", Enum.FontWeight.Bold)
title.Parent = screenGui
explain: We make a TextLabel near the top of the screen.
Font.fromName("FredokaOne") turns the name into the asset rbxasset://fonts/families/FredokaOne.json.
Enum.FontWeight.Bold makes the letters thick.
Setting FontFace applies the font to the label.

examples.title: Make existing text italic
examples.place: LocalScript in StarterGui (with a ScreenGui that has a TextLabel named Info)
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")
local label = playerGui:WaitForChild("ScreenGui"):WaitForChild("Info")

local font = label.FontFace          -- get a copy of the current font
font.Style = Enum.FontStyle.Italic   -- change the copy
label.FontFace = font                -- put it back so the label updates
explain: label.FontFace gives you a copy of the Font.
Changing the copy does not change the label yet.
Setting label.FontFace = font again makes the label use the italic version.

gotchas: Changing label.FontFace.Weight directly does nothing visible. Copy the Font, change the copy, then set FontFace again.
Font.fromName names have no spaces: use "FredokaOne", not "Fredoka One".
Font.fromEnum(Enum.Font.Unknown) throws an error.

datatype/Instance.d: The Instance data type holds constructors for Instance objects.

m.d:
Creates a new Instance of type className. Abstract classes and services cannot be created with this constructor.

Note that when the Parent of an object is set, Luau listens to a variety of different property changes for replication, rendering, and physics. For performance reasons, it's recommended to set the instance's Parent property last when creating new objects, instead of specifying the second argument (parent) of this constructor.

local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

-- Set new instance's parent last (recommended)
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 10, 0)
part.Parent = Workspace

-- Set new instance's parent in constructor (discouraged)
local part = Instance.new("Part", Workspace)
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 10, 0)
m.s: Returns an `Class.Instance` of the specified class.

p.s: Class name of the new instance to create.
Optional object to parent the new instance to. Not recommended for performance reasons (see description above).

kid.simple: Creates a brand-new object of the kind you name, like `"Part"`, `"Folder"`, or `"Sound"`. It starts with no Parent, so it is not in the game until you set its Parent.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Anchored = true
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)
part.Parent = Workspace -- set Parent last (recommended)
kid.gotcha: There is an optional second argument for the parent, `Instance.new("Part", Workspace)`, but Roblox recommends setting `Parent` last instead because it is faster. You also cannot create services (like Workspace) or abstract classes (like BasePart) this way.

m.d:
Creates a new object with the same type and property values as an existing object. In most cases using Instance:Clone() is more appropriate, but this constructor is useful when implementing low‑level libraries or systems.

There are two behavioral differences between this constructor and the Instance:Clone() method:

  • This constructor will not copy any of the descendant Instances parented to the existing object.

  • This constructor will return a new object even if the existing object had Instance.Archivable set to false.
m.s: Returns an `Class.Instance` which is a copy of an existing `Class.Instance`.

p.s: The existing Instance to copy property values from.

kid.simple: Makes a new object of the same kind with the same property values as an existing one, but WITHOUT copying the things inside it. Most of the time you want `Clone` instead.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local original = Workspace:WaitForChild("Lamp")
local copy = Instance.fromExisting(original) -- same properties, no children
copy.Parent = Workspace
kid.gotcha: Unlike `Clone`, it ignores `Archivable` and never copies children.

kid.simple: Almost every thing in a Roblox game is an Instance: parts, scripts, sounds, lights, folders, even the Workspace itself. Every Instance has a Name, a Parent (the thing it sits inside), and can have children (things inside it). All those things sitting inside each other form a big family tree, which you see in the Explorer window. This page also covers `Instance.new`, the way your code makes brand-new objects.
kid.analogy: Instances are like folders and files on a computer. A folder (the parent) can hold files and other folders (its children). The full path to a file, like Workspace > House > Door, tells you exactly where it lives.
whenToUse: Create new things while the game runs with `Instance.new`, like spawning a coin.
Find things in the game tree with `FindFirstChild`, `WaitForChild`, or dot access.
Move things around the tree by changing `Parent`, or remove them with `Destroy`.
Copy a whole object and everything inside it with `Clone`.
Store your own extra info on an object with attributes (`SetAttribute`), or label it with tags (`AddTag`).
React when things are added or removed with events like `ChildAdded` and `Destroying`.
kid.where: Instance is the base of nearly every class, so every object in Server and client code has these members. You never make a plain Instance; instead you call `Instance.new("Part")` (or any other class name) to create a specific kind.

terms.instance: One object in the game, like one Part or one Script. Every object you see in the Explorer is an instance.
terms.class: The kind of an object, like Part, Script, or Sound. `ClassName` tells you which kind it is.
terms.parent: The object something sits directly inside. If Door is inside House, then House is Door's parent.
terms.child: An object that sits directly inside another one. Door is a child of House.
terms.descendant: Anything inside an object at any depth: its children, their children, and so on. A Knob inside Door inside House is a descendant of House.
terms.ancestor: Anything an object is inside, at any depth: its parent, its parent's parent, and so on, up to `game`. House and Workspace are both ancestors of Door.
terms.hierarchy: The whole family tree of objects inside each other. The Explorer window shows it.
terms.DataModel / game: The very top of the tree. In scripts it is called `game`. Services like Workspace and ReplicatedStorage are its children.
terms.nil: Luau's word for nothing or no value. A part whose Parent is nil is not in the game tree, so nobody can see it.
terms.yield: To pause the script and wait. `WaitForChild` yields until the child shows up.
terms.thread: One running piece of code. When a thread yields, only that piece pauses; the rest of the game keeps going.
terms.client: A player's own device (their computer, phone, or console). LocalScripts run there.
terms.server: Roblox's computer that runs the game for everyone in it. Scripts in ServerScriptService run there.
terms.replicate: To copy changes from the server to players' devices (or the other way) so everyone sees the same thing.
terms.event / signal: Something that announces "this just happened!". You `:Connect` a function to an event so your function runs every time it happens.
terms.callback: A function you hand to something else so it can call it later, for example the function you pass to `:Connect`.
terms.attribute: A custom value you stick on an object yourself, like `Coins = 5` or `IsLava = true`. It shows up in the Properties window.
terms.tag: A text label you put on objects, like "Lava", so you can find every object with that label at once.
terms.deprecated: Old and replaced by something newer. It may still work, but you should use the new version.
terms.Archivable: Whether an object can be copied by `Clone` and saved with the place.

examples.title: Make a new part from code
examples.code:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

-- 1. Create a brand-new Part. It is not in the world yet (its Parent is nil).
local part = Instance.new("Part")

-- 2. Set it up first
part.Name = "Gift"
part.Size = Vector3.new(4, 4, 4)
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 10, 0)
part.Anchored = true
part.BrickColor = BrickColor.new("Bright red")

-- 3. Set Parent LAST. This is the moment it appears in the world.
part.Parent = Workspace
explain: `Instance.new("Part")` creates a Part, but it is floating in nowhere-land (Parent is nil), so nobody sees it yet.
We set its name, size, position, and color while it is still invisible. That is faster for the game.
Setting `Parent = Workspace` puts it in the 3D world. It appears at (0, 10, 0), 10 studs above the center of the map.

examples.title: Dot access vs FindFirstChild vs WaitForChild
examples.code:
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

-- DOT ACCESS: short, but ERRORS if "Baseplate" does not exist
local baseplate = Workspace.Baseplate

-- FindFirstChild: looks once, right now. Gives nil if not found (no error)
local coin = Workspace:FindFirstChild("Coin")
if coin then
	print("Found a coin!")
else
	print("No coin right now")
end

-- WaitForChild: waits (pauses this script) until the child exists
-- Best on the client, because things from the server may arrive a little late
local remote = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("GiveCoin")
print("Remote is ready:", remote.Name)
explain: `Workspace.Baseplate` is quick to type, but if nothing named Baseplate is there, the script stops with an error.
`FindFirstChild("Coin")` checks one time. If there is no Coin, you get `nil` and can handle it with an `if`.
`WaitForChild("GiveCoin")` pauses until GiveCoin appears. On a player's device, objects from the server can show up a moment after the script starts, so waiting is safer.

examples.title: Walk the family tree
examples.code:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

-- Build a small tree:  Workspace > House > Door > Knob
local house = Instance.new("Model")
house.Name = "House"
local door = Instance.new("Part")
door.Name = "Door"
door.Anchored = true
local knob = Instance.new("Part")
knob.Name = "Knob"
knob.Anchored = true

knob.Parent = door   -- Knob is a CHILD of Door
door.Parent = house  -- Door is a CHILD of House
house.Parent = Workspace

print(knob.Parent.Name)                 --> Door (its parent)
print(#house:GetChildren())             --> 1 (just Door)
print(#house:GetDescendants())          --> 2 (Door and Knob)
print(knob:IsDescendantOf(house))       --> true (House is an ancestor)
print(knob:FindFirstAncestor("House"))  --> House
print(knob:GetFullName())               --> Workspace.House.Door.Knob
explain: Children are only the things directly inside. House has 1 child (Door).
Descendants count everything inside at any depth. House has 2 (Door and Knob).
Ancestors go the other way, upward: Knob's ancestors are Door, House, Workspace, and game.
`GetFullName` shows the whole path, like an address.

examples.title: Copy a coin and clean it up later
examples.code:
local ServerStorage = game:GetService("ServerStorage")
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

-- A Part named "CoinTemplate" is stored in ServerStorage
local template = ServerStorage:WaitForChild("CoinTemplate")

for i = 1, 5 do
	local coin = template:Clone()      -- copy it (and anything inside it)
	coin.Name = "Coin" .. i
	coin.Position = Vector3.new(i * 6, 3, 0) -- 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 studs along X
	coin.Parent = Workspace

	-- Remove each coin after 10 seconds
	task.delay(10, function()
		coin:Destroy()
	end)
end
explain: `Clone` makes a full copy, including everything inside the template.
The copies start with no Parent, so we set Position first, then Parent them to Workspace.
`Destroy` removes the coin for good and frees up memory.

examples.title: Use attributes to store your own values
examples.code:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local chest = Workspace:WaitForChild("Chest")

-- Store our own data on the chest
chest:SetAttribute("Gold", 50)

-- Run code whenever Gold changes
chest:GetAttributeChangedSignal("Gold"):Connect(function()
	print("Chest now has", chest:GetAttribute("Gold"), "gold")
end)

chest:SetAttribute("Gold", 75)  --> Chest now has 75 gold
explain: `SetAttribute` sticks a custom value named Gold onto the chest.
`GetAttributeChangedSignal("Gold")` gives an event that fires only when Gold changes.
Changing Gold to 75 makes the connected function print the new amount.

gotchas: Dot access (`Workspace.Coin`) errors if the child is missing. Use `FindFirstChild` and check for nil when something might not be there.
In LocalScripts, use `WaitForChild` for things that come from the server. They may not have arrived yet when your script starts.
Set `Parent` last when building a new object. Setting it first makes the game do extra work for every property you change after.
`WaitForChild` with no timeout can wait forever if you misspell the name. After 5 seconds it prints an "Infinite yield possible" warning in Output, which is a hint to check your spelling.
Names do not have to be unique. If two children are both called "Coin", `FindFirstChild("Coin")` just gives you one of them.
Names with spaces or that start with a number cannot use dot access. Use `parent["My Part"]` or `FindFirstChild("My Part")` instead.
`Clone` returns nil if the object's `Archivable` is false.
Use `Destroy`, not `Parent = nil`, when you are done with something forever. Destroy also disconnects its events and frees memory.

datatype/InstanceHandle.d:
The InstanceHandle data type is a weak reference to an Instance that might not be available locally. Use it to point at an instance that hasn't arrived yet, could stream out, or exists only on another machine, and to pick that instance up once it's there.

A handle always refers to the same target. To reach that target, call InstanceHandle:Wait(), which yields until the instance is available:

local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local part = Instance.new("Part")
local target = Instance.new("Part")
target.Name = "TargetPart"
part.Parent = Workspace
target.Parent = Workspace

part:SetAttribute("Target", target)

local handle = part:GetAttribute("Target")
local instance = handle:Wait(10)
if instance then
    print("Target is", instance.Name) --> Target is TargetPart
end

Prefer InstanceHandle:Wait() with a timeout so your code runs as soon as the instance shows up. Use InstanceHandle:Get() when you want an immediate answer and can handle nil, such as in code that runs every frame.

Examples

Attributes

Attributes use InstanceHandle instead of an ordinary instance reference. Since the handle itself is never nil, you can tell apart an attribute that is missing from one where the instance is not currently present:

local part = Instance.new("Part")

print(part:GetAttribute("Target")) --> nil

part:SetAttribute("Target", InstanceHandle.new(nil))
local handle = part:GetAttribute("Target")
print(handle:Get()) --> nil

InstanceHandle attributes also appear in Instance:GetAttributes(), which can't hold nil values.

Instance:GetAttributeChangedSignal() fires when the attribute is set to a new target or removed. It does not fire when the target streams in or out, or when the target is destroyed. To react to availability, combine the signal with InstanceHandle:Wait():

local part = Instance.new("Part")

part:GetAttributeChangedSignal("Target"):Connect(function()
    local handle = part:GetAttribute("Target")
    if not handle then
        return
    end

    local instance = handle:Wait(10)
    if instance then
        print("New target:", instance.Name)
    end
end)
Remote events

Pass a handle through a RemoteEvent to give the receiver a reference to an instance it doesn't have yet. The receiver waits for the instance instead of getting nothing.

In a server script, call this function with your remote event, the receiving player, and the model to send:

local function sendHandle(remoteEvent: RemoteEvent, player: Player, spawnedModel: Model)
    local handle = InstanceHandle.new(spawnedModel)
    remoteEvent:FireClient(player, handle)
end

In a client script, call this function with the same remote event to start listening before the server sends the handle:

local function receiveHandles(remoteEvent: RemoteEvent)
    remoteEvent.OnClientEvent:Connect(function(handle)
        local model = handle:Wait(10)
        if model then
            print("Received", model.Name)
        end
    end)
end

Ownership

A handle acts as a weak reference. It never keeps its target alive. The lifetime of the target is controlled by the rest of your experience: its parent and any ordinary references your scripts hold that prevent it from being garbage collected.

InstanceHandle:Get() and InstanceHandle:Wait() return an ordinary instance reference, which does keep the instance alive for as long as you hold it.

A handle is otherwise lightweight and needs no cleanup.

Equality

Two handles are equal when they refer to the same target, even if you created them separately and even after the target is gone. All empty handles are equal to each other. Each handle is still a distinct value.

local instance1 = Instance.new("Part")
local instance2 = Instance.new("Part")

local a = InstanceHandle.new(instance1)
local b = InstanceHandle.new(instance1)
local c = InstanceHandle.new(instance2)

print(a == b) --> true
print(a == c) --> false

Equality depends on target identity, so it still works when the target isn't currently available.
datatype/InstanceHandle.s: A lightweight, weak reference to an `Class.Instance` that might not be available locally.

m.d:
This method doesn't yield.

Get() returns nil when the handle is empty, when the target hasn't arrived on the client or server running the script, when the target is no longer available after streaming out, when the target has been garbage collected, and when the target isn't accessible to the calling script. Use InstanceHandle:Wait() to yield until the target arrives instead of checking once.
m.s: Returns the referenced `Class.Instance` if it's available locally, otherwise `nil`.

r.s: The referenced instance, or nil if it isn't available locally.

m.d:
Returns nil if the handle is empty, the target is inaccessible to the calling script, or timeout elapses first. Wait() returns immediately when the target is already available and when the handle is empty.

Pass a timeout whenever you can't guarantee that the target reaches the caller. A target that's destroyed before it replicates leaves a handle that never resolves, and a Wait() with no timeout never returns. A pending wait can't be cancelled: task.cancel() stops your coroutine, but the wait isn't unregistered until the target arrives or the timeout elapses.

timeout must be a number greater than zero. Throws if timeout is zero, negative, or not a number.
m.s: Yields until the referenced `Class.Instance` is available locally, then returns it.

p.s: How long to wait, in seconds. Must be greater than zero. Waits indefinitely when omitted.

r.s: The referenced instance, or nil if the handle is empty, the target is inaccessible to the calling script, or timeout elapses first.

m.d:
The handle refers to the instance weakly and doesn't extend its lifetime.

local target = Instance.new("Part")
target.Name = "TargetPart"

local handle = InstanceHandle.new(target)
local empty = InstanceHandle.new(nil)

print(handle:Get()) --> TargetPart
print(empty:Get()) --> nil

Throws if instance is neither an Instance nor nil.
m.s: Returns a new `Datatype.InstanceHandle` referring to the given `Class.Instance`.

p.s: The instance to refer to, or nil for an empty handle.

datatype/NumberRange.d:
The NumberRange represents a range of numbers.

NumberRange stores its NumberRange.Min and NumberRange.Max values as 32-bit floating-point numbers. Very large numbers or numbers requiring high decimal precision may lose accuracy.

m.d: The minimum value of the NumberRange, always less than or equal to the maximum.
m.s: The minimum value of the `Datatype.NumberRange`.

kid.simple: The smallest number in the range. Always less than or equal to Max.
kid.example:
local r = NumberRange.new(1, 4)
print(r.Min) --> 1

m.d: The maximum value of the NumberRange, always greater than or equal to the minimum.
m.s: The maximum value of the `Datatype.NumberRange`.

kid.simple: The biggest number in the range. Always greater than or equal to Min.
kid.example:
local r = NumberRange.new(1, 4)
print(r.Max) --> 4

m.d: Returns a new NumberRange with the minimum and maximum set to the value.
m.s: Returns a new `Datatype.NumberRange` with the minimum and maximum set to the `value`.

p.s: The number that both the minimum and maximum of the range are set to.

kid.simple: Makes a NumberRange. Give it one number to make Min and Max the same, or two numbers for Min and Max.
kid.example:
local exact = NumberRange.new(2)      -- Min 2, Max 2
local between = NumberRange.new(1, 4) -- Min 1, Max 4
print(between.Min, between.Max) --> 1 4
kid.gotcha: The first number must not be bigger than the second.

kid.simple: A NumberRange is a pair of numbers: a smallest (Min) and a biggest (Max). Roblox picks random numbers between them. It is mostly used in ParticleEmitters, like how long each particle lives or how fast it flies.
kid.analogy: It is like saying "bring between 3 and 5 friends". Each time, the number could be anything from 3 to 5.
whenToUse: ParticleEmitter.Lifetime: how many seconds each particle lasts
ParticleEmitter.Speed: how fast particles shoot out
ParticleEmitter.Rotation and RotSpeed: how much particles spin
Storing any "from this to that" range in your own code
kid.where: Works in any script. Make one with NumberRange.new(min, max) or NumberRange.new(value).

terms.range: All the numbers from a smallest to a biggest. The range 2 to 5 includes 2, 3.7, 5, and so on.
terms.Min: The smallest number in the range.
terms.Max: The biggest number in the range.
terms.ParticleEmitter: An object that shoots out lots of little images (particles) to make fire, smoke, sparkles, and similar effects.
terms.32-bit float: The way NumberRange stores numbers. It keeps about 7 digits of accuracy, so very big or very precise numbers get rounded a little.

examples.title: Sparkles that live a random amount of time
examples.code:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Anchored = true
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)
part.Parent = workspace

local emitter = Instance.new("ParticleEmitter")
emitter.Lifetime = NumberRange.new(1, 3) -- each particle lives 1 to 3 seconds
emitter.Speed = NumberRange.new(5)       -- every particle moves at exactly 5
emitter.Parent = part
explain: NumberRange.new(1, 3): each particle gets a random lifetime between 1 and 3 seconds, so they do not all vanish at once.
NumberRange.new(5): Min and Max are both 5, so every particle has the same speed.
Putting the emitter inside the part makes the sparkles come out of the part.

gotchas: Min must be smaller than or equal to Max. NumberRange.new(5, 1) causes an error.
You cannot change .Min or .Max after making it. Make a new NumberRange instead.

datatype/NumberSequence.d:
The NumberSequence data type represents a series of number values from 0 to 1. The number values are expressed using the NumberSequenceKeypoint type. This type is used in properties such as ParticleEmitter.Size and Beam.Transparency to define a numerical change over time.

Equality

Two NumberSequence objects are equivalent only if the values of their NumberSequenceKeypoint are equivalent, even if both would result in similar graphs.

Evaluation

The NumberSequence type does not have a built-in method for getting the value at a certain time/point because keypoints can have random envelopes. However, assuming the envelope values of your keypoints are all 0, you can use the following function to evaluate at a specific time.

local function evalNumberSequence(sequence: NumberSequence, time: number)
    -- If time is 0 or 1, return the first or last value respectively
    if time == 0 then
        return sequence.Keypoints[1].Value
    elseif time == 1 then
        return sequence.Keypoints[#sequence.Keypoints].Value
    end

    -- Otherwise, step through each sequential pair of keypoints
    for i = 1, #sequence.Keypoints - 1 do
        local currKeypoint = sequence.Keypoints[i]
        local nextKeypoint = sequence.Keypoints[i + 1]
        if time >= currKeypoint.Time and time < nextKeypoint.Time then
            -- Calculate how far alpha lies between the points
            local alpha = (time - currKeypoint.Time) / (nextKeypoint.Time - currKeypoint.Time)
            -- Return the value between the points using alpha
            return currKeypoint.Value + (nextKeypoint.Value - currKeypoint.Value) * alpha
        end
    end
end

local numberSequence = NumberSequence.new{
    NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(0, 0),
    NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(0.5, 1),
    NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(1, 0),
}

print(evalNumberSequence(numberSequence, 0.65))  --> 0.7
datatype/NumberSequence.s: A series of floats across a period of time.

m.d: An array containing NumberSequenceKeypoint values for the NumberSequence.
m.s: An array of `Datatype.NumberSequenceKeypoint` values in ascending order.

kid.simple: The list of NumberSequenceKeypoints that make up this sequence, in time order. You can read it to see each dot's time and value.
kid.example:
local seq = NumberSequence.new(1, 3)
for _, keypoint in seq.Keypoints do
	print(keypoint.Time, keypoint.Value)
end
--> 0 1
--> 1 3

m.d:
Returns a NumberSequence with the start and end values set to the provided n.

local numberSequence = NumberSequence.new(n)
-- Equivalent to
local numberSequence = NumberSequence.new{
    NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(0, n),
    NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(1, n)
}
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.NumberSequence` with the start and end values set to the provided `n`.

p.s: The constant value used for both the start and end keypoints of the sequence.

kid.simple: Makes a NumberSequence. Give it one number (same value the whole time), two numbers (a start value and an end value), or a list of NumberSequenceKeypoints for more control.
kid.example:
local steady = NumberSequence.new(0.5)    -- 0.5 the whole time
local grow = NumberSequence.new(1, 3)     -- 1 at the start, 3 at the end
local pulse = NumberSequence.new({
	NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(0, 0),
	NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(0.5, 1),   -- peak in the middle
	NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(1, 0),
})
kid.gotcha: With a list, it needs at least 2 keypoints, starting at time 0 and ending at time 1.

kid.simple: A NumberSequence is a number that changes over a timeline, from the start (time 0) to the end (time 1). You describe it with dots called keypoints, and Roblox draws straight lines between them. It is used for things like particles that grow, shrink, or fade over their life.
kid.analogy: It is like a volume plan for a song: "start quiet, get loud in the middle, and fade out at the end". You only say the volume at a few moments and the rest is filled in smoothly.
whenToUse: ParticleEmitter.Size: particles that start small and grow
ParticleEmitter.Transparency: particles that fade out
Beam.Transparency and Trail.Transparency
UIGradient.Transparency for see-through gradients on UI
kid.where: Works in any script. Make one with NumberSequence.new(n), NumberSequence.new(start, finish), or NumberSequence.new({ keypoints }).

terms.keypoint: One dot on a timeline that says "at this moment, the value is this". Roblox draws a straight line between dots to fill in the moments in between.
terms.time (0 to 1): Where on the timeline a keypoint sits, as a fraction. 0 is the very start, 1 is the very end, 0.5 is halfway. For a particle that lives 2 seconds, time 0.5 means after 1 second.
terms.interpolate: Fill in the in-between values. Halfway between 0 and 10 is 5.
terms.ParticleEmitter: An object that shoots out lots of little images (particles) to make fire, smoke, sparkles, and similar effects.
terms.Transparency: How see-through something is. 0 is fully solid, 1 is fully invisible.
terms.envelope: A random wiggle room around a keypoint's value. Value 2 with envelope 0.5 can come out anywhere from 1.5 to 2.5.

examples.title: Smoke that grows and fades away
examples.code:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Anchored = true
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)
part.Parent = workspace

local smoke = Instance.new("ParticleEmitter")

-- Size: starts at 1, grows to 4 by the end of each particle's life
smoke.Size = NumberSequence.new(1, 4)

-- Transparency: solid at first, still solid at 70%, invisible at the end
smoke.Transparency = NumberSequence.new({
	NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(0, 0),   -- time 0: fully solid
	NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(0.7, 0), -- time 0.7: still solid
	NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(1, 1),   -- time 1: fully invisible
})

smoke.Parent = part
explain: NumberSequence.new(1, 4) is a shortcut for two keypoints: size 1 at the start and size 4 at the end. Halfway through its life a particle is size 2.5.
The transparency sequence uses three keypoints. From time 0 to 0.7 the value stays 0 (solid).
From time 0.7 to 1 it goes from 0 to 1, so the smoke fades out in the last 30% of its life.
If a particle lives 2 seconds, it starts fading after 1.4 seconds.

gotchas: The first keypoint must be at time 0 and the last at time 1, or you get an error.
Keypoints must be in order of time, from smallest to biggest.
You can have at most 20 keypoints.
There is no built-in "give me the value at this time" function, because envelopes add randomness. You can write your own if all envelopes are 0.

datatype/NumberSequenceKeypoint.d: The NumberSequenceKeypoint data type represents keypoints within a NumberSequence with a particular time, value, and envelope size.
datatype/NumberSequenceKeypoint.s: Represents keypoint within a `Datatype.NumberSequence` with a particular time, value, and envelope size.

m.d: The amount of variance allowed from the value. For example, a value of 0.5 with an envelope of 0.1 could compute to between 0.4 and 0.6 at runtime. The most common use case for this property is to randomize the size of particles (within the envelope) from a ParticleEmitter.
m.s: The amount of variance allowed from the value.

kid.simple: How much random wiggle room the value has. Value 0.5 with envelope 0.1 can come out between 0.4 and 0.6. Mostly used to make particles different sizes.
kid.example:
local kp = NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(0, 1, 0.25)
print(kp.Envelope) --> 0.25

m.d: The relative time at which this keypoint is positioned within the parent NumberSequence, expressed as a number from 0 to 1 where 0 is the beginning of the sequence and 1 is the end. Within a NumberSequence, the first keypoint must have a time of 0 and the last keypoint must have a time of 1; any intermediate keypoints must be in ascending time order. The engine linearly interpolates values and envelopes between consecutive keypoints based on their time positions. Defaults to 0.
m.s: The relative time at which the keypoint is positioned.

kid.simple: Where this dot sits on the timeline, from 0 (start) to 1 (end). In a sequence the first dot must be at 0 and the last at 1.
kid.example:
local kp = NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(0.25, 3)
print(kp.Time) --> 0.25 (a quarter of the way through)

m.d: The base numeric value at this keypoint's position in the sequence. When the engine evaluates a NumberSequence, it linearly interpolates between adjacent keypoints' values based on time. If Envelope is greater than 0, the actual output at runtime may vary randomly within the range [Value − Envelope, Value + Envelope]. Defaults to 0.
m.s: The base value of the keypoint.

kid.simple: The number at this dot. Between dots, Roblox fills in the values with straight lines.
kid.example:
local kp = NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(0.25, 3)
print(kp.Value) --> 3

m.d: Returns a NumberSequenceKeypoint with the given time and value, with Envelope defaulting to 0 (no random variance). The time parameter should be a number between 0 and 1, and value can be any number.
m.s: Returns a keypoint with the specified time and value.

p.s: The relative time position of the keypoint within the sequence, expressed as a number from 0 to 1.
The base numeric value at this keypoint's time position.

kid.simple: Makes a keypoint from a time (0 to 1) and a value. You can add a third number, the envelope, for random wiggle room. Without it, the envelope is 0.
kid.example:
local plain = NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(0.5, 2)       -- halfway: value 2
local wobbly = NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(0.5, 2, 0.5) -- halfway: 1.5 to 2.5

kid.simple: A NumberSequenceKeypoint is one dot on a NumberSequence's timeline. It says "at this time (from 0 to 1), the value is this", and can also add some random wiggle room called an envelope.
kid.analogy: If a NumberSequence is a road trip plan, each keypoint is one stop: "at the halfway point, we are at the gas station".
whenToUse: Building a NumberSequence with more than two points
Adding random variety to particle sizes using the envelope
Reading the dots of an existing NumberSequence
kid.where: Works in any script. Make one with NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(time, value) or NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(time, value, envelope), then put several in a list for NumberSequence.new.

terms.keypoint: One dot on a timeline that says "at this moment, the value is this". Roblox draws a straight line between dots to fill in the moments in between.
terms.time (0 to 1): Where on the timeline a keypoint sits, as a fraction. 0 is the very start, 1 is the very end, 0.5 is halfway. For a particle that lives 2 seconds, time 0.5 means after 1 second.
terms.envelope: A random wiggle room around the value. Value 0.5 with envelope 0.1 can come out anywhere from 0.4 to 0.6. It must not be negative.
terms.interpolate: Fill in the in-between values. Halfway between 0 and 10 is 5.

examples.title: Particles of slightly different sizes
examples.code:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Anchored = true
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)
part.Parent = workspace

local emitter = Instance.new("ParticleEmitter")
emitter.Size = NumberSequence.new({
	NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(0, 1, 0.5), -- start: size 1, give or take 0.5
	NumberSequenceKeypoint.new(1, 0),      -- end: size 0 (shrinks away)
})
emitter.Parent = part
explain: The first keypoint is at time 0 with value 1 and envelope 0.5, so each particle starts somewhere between size 0.5 and 1.5.
The second keypoint is at time 1 with value 0, so every particle shrinks to nothing by the end.
The envelope makes the effect look more natural because not every particle is the same.

gotchas: Time must be between 0 and 1. It is a fraction of the whole timeline, not seconds.
Envelope must be 0 or more.

datatype/OverlapParams.d:
The OverlapParams data type stores parameters for use with WorldRoot boundary-querying functions, in particular WorldRoot:GetPartBoundsInBox(), WorldRoot:GetPartBoundsInRadius() and WorldRoot:GetPartsInPart(). The ExcludeInstances and IncludeInstances properties store a set of objects and their descendants that will be excluded and included from the query. The OverlapParams.CollisionGroup property can specify a collision group for the boundary query operation.

Unlike most data types in Luau, you can change all of the members of OverlapParams without creating a new object, allowing you to reuse the same object repeatedly.
datatype/OverlapParams.s: Stores parameters used in boundary-querying functions.

m.d: An optional array of instances whose descendants will be excluded from the query. This property can be used simultaneously with IncludeInstances to allow for mixed filtering, for example including a large folder but excluding specific child instances. If an instance matches both an exclude and include filter, exclusions take priority over inclusions.
m.s: An optional array of instances whose descendants will be excluded from the query.

kid.simple: A list of things to skip, along with everything inside them.
kid.example:
local params = OverlapParams.new()
params.ExcludeInstances = { workspace:WaitForChild("Baseplate") } -- ignore the floor

m.d:
An optional array of instances whose descendants will be included in the query. This property can be used simultaneously with ExcludeInstances to allow for mixed filtering. If an instance matches both an exclude and include filter, exclusions take priority over inclusions.

Setting IncludeInstances to nil versus an empty array ({}) has opposite effects. IncludeInstances = nil is the most permissive filter (includes everything), whereas IncludeInstances = {} is the most restrictive filter (includes nothing).
m.s: An optional array of instances whose descendants will be included in the query.

kid.simple: A list of the ONLY things that can be found (plus everything inside them). nil allows everything; an empty list {} allows nothing.
kid.example:
local params = OverlapParams.new()
params.IncludeInstances = { workspace:WaitForChild("Coins") } -- only find coins
kid.gotcha: nil and {} are opposites: nil = everything, {} = nothing.

m.d: The maximum amount of parts to be returned by the query. The default value of zero (0) represents no limit.
m.s: The maximum amount of parts to be returned by the query.

kid.simple: The most parts the check will return. 0 (the default) means no limit.
kid.example:
local params = OverlapParams.new()
params.MaxParts = 1 -- I only need to know if ANY part is there
local parts = workspace:GetPartBoundsInRadius(Vector3.new(0, 5, 0), 4, params)
print(#parts > 0)

m.d: Specifies a collision group for the operation. Parts in collision groups that are set to not collide with this group are ignored. If this property is omitted, the operation assumes the Default collision group.
m.s: The collision group used for the operation.

kid.simple: The name of a collision group the check pretends to belong to. Parts in groups set to NOT collide with it are skipped. If not set, it uses "Default".
kid.example:
local params = OverlapParams.new()
params.CollisionGroup = "Players" -- this group must exist in your game

m.d: Slightly increases the volume of the boundary-querying operation, clamped between 0 and 0.05 studs.
m.s: Slightly increases the volume of the boundary-querying operation.

kid.simple: Makes the checked area very slightly bigger so parts that are just barely touching still count. It can only be between 0 and 0.05 studs.
kid.example:
local params = OverlapParams.new()
params.Tolerance = 0.05 -- the biggest allowed

m.d: This property, if true, makes the boundary-querying operation use an intersected part's BasePart.CanCollide value in favor of its BasePart.CanQuery value when determining whether that part is included in the array of spatial query results.
m.s: Determines whether the boundary-querying operation considers a part's `Class.BasePart.CanCollide` property value over its `Class.BasePart.CanQuery` value.

kid.simple: If true, a part is found or skipped based on its CanCollide setting instead of CanQuery. So walk-through parts (CanCollide off) are skipped.
kid.example:
local params = OverlapParams.new()
params.RespectCanCollide = true

m.d: When enabled, the query will ignore all part collision properties and perform a brute-force check on every part. This will negatively impact performance and should not be used in live experiences.
m.s: When enabled, the query will ignore all part collision properties and perform a brute-force check on every part.

kid.simple: If true, ignores all the usual part settings and checks every part the slow way. Only for testing, never in a real game.
kid.example:
local params = OverlapParams.new()
params.BruteForceAllSlow = true -- testing only!

m.d: An array of objects whose descendants are used in filtering candidates. Note that this property has been superseded by ExcludeInstances and IncludeInstances which should be used for new work.
m.s: An array of objects whose descendants are used in filtering candidates.

kid.simple: The older way to filter: a list used as a skip list or an only-these list depending on FilterType. New code should use ExcludeInstances or IncludeInstances.
kid.gotcha: Replaced by ExcludeInstances and IncludeInstances for new work.

m.d: Determines whether the FilterDescendantsInstances array is used as an exclude or include list. Note that this property has been superseded by ExcludeInstances and IncludeInstances which should be used for new work.
m.s: Determines whether the `Datatype.OverlapParams.FilterDescendantsInstances|FilterDescendantsInstances` array is used as an exclude or include list.

kid.simple: Says whether FilterDescendantsInstances is a skip list (Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude) or an only-these list (Enum.RaycastFilterType.Include). Part of the older filter system.
kid.gotcha: New code should use ExcludeInstances or IncludeInstances.

m.d: Adds the instances provided to FilterDescendantsInstances. Note that this property has been superseded by ExcludeInstances and IncludeInstances which should be used for new work.
m.s: Adds the instances provided to `Datatype.OverlapParams.FilterDescendantsInstances|FilterDescendantsInstances`.

p.s: An instance or an array containing instances to add.

kid.simple: Adds one thing, or a list of things, to FilterDescendantsInstances without wiping what is already there. Part of the older filter system.
kid.example:
local params = OverlapParams.new()
params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
params:AddToFilter(workspace:WaitForChild("Baseplate"))
kid.gotcha: New code should use ExcludeInstances or IncludeInstances.

m.d: Returns a blank OverlapParams object. Unlike other data type constructors, this constructor does not have any parameters, so you should set its properties appropriately.
m.s: Returns a blank `Datatype.OverlapParams` object.

kid.simple: Makes a blank OverlapParams with no rules. It takes no arguments; set its properties afterwards.
kid.example:
local params = OverlapParams.new()
params.MaxParts = 10

kid.simple: OverlapParams is a settings box for the "what parts are inside this area?" functions, like workspace:GetPartBoundsInRadius, GetPartBoundsInBox, and GetPartsInPart. It tells them which parts to skip, which parts are allowed, and the most parts to return.
kid.analogy: It is like the rules for a game of tag inside a circle drawn on the ground: "count everyone inside the circle, but not the person who is It, and stop after 10 people".
whenToUse: Finding everything inside a bomb's blast radius, but not the bomb itself
Checking which players are standing in a zone
Limiting how many parts a check returns with MaxParts
Only checking parts inside one folder
kid.where: Works in any script on server or client. Make one with OverlapParams.new() (no arguments), set its properties, then pass it as the last argument to GetPartBoundsInRadius, GetPartBoundsInBox, or GetPartsInPart. You can reuse it.

terms.filter: A list of things the ray should skip (exclude) or the only things it may hit (include). Usually you exclude your own character so you do not hit yourself.
terms.descendant: Anything inside something else, at any depth: its children, their children, and so on. Excluding a character also excludes its arms, legs, hats, and so on.
terms.collision group: A named team of parts that you set up so some groups pass through each other. Queries can pretend to be in one of these groups.
terms.CanQuery: A part property. When false, raycasts and other spatial queries skip that part.
terms.CanCollide: A part property. When false, players and other parts can walk or fall through it.
terms.stud: Roblox's unit of distance. A default character is about 5 studs tall.
terms.overlap: When two things take up some of the same space, like a ball half inside a box.
terms.bounding box: The smallest invisible box that fits around a part. "Bounds" functions check these boxes, which is fast but not exact for round or rotated shapes.
terms.include: ONLY these things can be found.
terms.array: A list in Lua, written with curly braces like {partA, partB}.

examples.title: Explosion that finds everything nearby
examples.code:
local bomb = Instance.new("Part")
bomb.Shape = Enum.PartType.Ball
bomb.Anchored = true
bomb.Position = Vector3.new(0, 3, 0)
bomb.Parent = workspace

local params = OverlapParams.new()
params.ExcludeInstances = { bomb } -- don't find the bomb itself
params.MaxParts = 50                -- stop after 50 parts

task.wait(3) -- countdown

-- Find parts within 10 studs of the bomb
local parts = workspace:GetPartBoundsInRadius(bomb.Position, 10, params)
for _, part in parts do
	print("Caught in the blast:", part:GetFullName())
end
bomb:Destroy()
explain: We make a ball-shaped bomb and an OverlapParams.
ExcludeInstances skips the bomb so it does not find itself.
MaxParts = 50 means the list will never have more than 50 parts.
GetPartBoundsInRadius gives a list of every part whose box touches a 10-stud ball around the bomb.
We print each part's full name, then remove the bomb.

gotchas: IncludeInstances = {} (empty) finds nothing. Leave it nil to allow everything.
If something is in both lists, exclude wins.
MaxParts 0 means no limit, not zero parts.
Older code uses FilterDescendantsInstances and FilterType. New code should use ExcludeInstances and IncludeInstances.

datatype/PhysicalProperties.d:
The PhysicalProperties data type describes several physical properties of a BasePart: Density, Elasticity, and Friction. It is used in the similarly-named BasePart.CustomPhysicalProperties property.

Weighting Behavior

PhysicalProperties also provides weightings properties, ElasticityWeight and FrictionWeight. When two parts interact, the friction and elasticity between them are determined in the same way by the following pairwise weighted average function:

local function getActualFriction(partA, partB)
    return (partA.Friction * partA.FrictionWeight + partB.Friction * partB.FrictionWeight) / (partA.FrictionWeight + partB.FrictionWeight)
end

Although the formula above refers to the Friction and FrictionWeight of two parts, A and B, the formula is used in the same manner when determining Elasticity. Generally, when the weight of A is much greater than that of B, the actual value will be closer to A. If the weights are similar, the actual value will be close to the midpoint between their individual values.
datatype/PhysicalProperties.s: Describes properties that affect the physical behavior of a `Class.BasePart`.

m.d:
A value between 0 and 1 denoting how absorbent the material is to AudioEmitters. When using acoustic simulation, surfaces with higher absorption will result in less reverb than surfaces with lower absorption.

Note that this does not affect the degree to which audio transmits through surfaces; for that, see Density.
m.s: A value between `0` and `1` denoting how absorbent the material is to `Class.AudioEmitter|AudioEmitters`.

kid.simple: How much sound this surface soaks up, from 0 to 1, when Roblox simulates echoes for AudioEmitters. Higher means less echo, like a room with soft carpets. It does not change how much sound goes THROUGH the part (Density does that).
kid.example:
local carpet = PhysicalProperties.new(1, 0.5, 0, 1, 1, 0.9)
print(carpet.AcousticAbsorption) --> 0.9

m.d:
Density is defined as the amount of mass per unit volume. The more dense a part is, the more force it takes to accelerate it. Acceptable range is 0.0001 to 100.0 and values outside this range will be clamped.

When using acoustic simulation, parts with higher density will muffle occluded AudioEmitters more.
m.s: The mass per unit volume of the part.

kid.simple: How heavy the part is for its size. Higher density = heavier = harder to push or launch. Range 0.0001 to 100. With acoustic simulation, denser parts also muffle sounds behind them more.
kid.example:
local heavy = PhysicalProperties.new(50, 0.5, 0)
print(heavy.Density) --> 50

m.d: Friction is defined as the force that opposes the relative lateral motion of two solid surfaces in contact. The greater the friction on a part, the quicker it will decelerate when it rubs against another part with friction. Acceptable range is 0.0 to 2.0 and values outside this range will be clamped.
m.s: The deceleration of the part when rubbing against another part.

kid.simple: How grippy the part is when it rubs against another part. 0 is ice-slippery, 2 is the stickiest. Higher friction makes sliding things slow down faster.
kid.example:
local slippery = PhysicalProperties.new(1, 0, 0)
print(slippery.Friction) --> 0

m.d: Elasticity refers to a part's tendency to retain energy when colliding with another part. An Elasticity of 1 indicates that the part bounces with the same energy it had before a collision. Acceptable range is 0.0 to 1.0 and values outside this range will be clamped.
m.s: The amount of energy retained when colliding with another part.

kid.simple: How bouncy the part is. 0 means it lands with a thud. 1 means it bounces back with the same energy it had. Range 0 to 1.
kid.example:
local bouncy = PhysicalProperties.new(1, 0.3, 1)
print(bouncy.Elasticity) --> 1

m.d: The friction weight of two parts rubbing together creates a ratio used to calculate the actual friction between the two parts. The higher a part's FrictionWeight, the more its Friction is used. Acceptable range is 0.0 to 100.0 and values outside this range will be clamped.
m.s: The importance of the part's `Datatype.PhysicalProperties.Friction|Friction` property when calculating the friction with the colliding part.

kid.simple: How much this part's Friction counts when it rubs against another part. Roblox mixes both parts' friction, and the one with the bigger weight gets more say. Example: friction 0 with weight 100 against friction 1 with weight 1 gives about 0.01. Range 0 to 100.
kid.example:
local props = PhysicalProperties.new(1, 0, 0, 100, 1)
print(props.FrictionWeight) --> 100

m.d: The elasticity weight of two parts colliding creates a ratio used to calculate the actual elasticity between the two parts. The higher a part's ElasticityWeight, the more its Elasticity is used. Acceptable range is 0.0 to 100.0 and values outside this range will be clamped.
m.s: The importance of the part's `Datatype.PhysicalProperties.Elasticity|Elasticity` property when calculating the elasticity with the colliding part.

kid.simple: How much this part's Elasticity counts when it hits another part. The part with the bigger weight decides more of how bouncy the hit is. Range 0 to 100.
kid.example:
local props = PhysicalProperties.new(1, 0.3, 1, 1, 100)
print(props.ElasticityWeight) --> 100

m.d: Returns a PhysicalProperties container, with the density, friction, and elasticity specified for this material.
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.PhysicalProperties` with the default properties for the given material.

p.s: The Material for which to retrieve default physical properties.

kid.simple: Makes a PhysicalProperties. You can give it a Material (to copy that material's normal values), or numbers in this order: density, friction, elasticity, then optionally frictionWeight and elasticityWeight, then optionally acousticAbsorption.
kid.example:
local likeIce = PhysicalProperties.new(Enum.Material.Ice) -- copy Ice's values
local basic = PhysicalProperties.new(1, 0.5, 0.2)          -- density, friction, elasticity
local full = PhysicalProperties.new(1, 0.5, 0.2, 1, 1)     -- plus the two weights
local withSound = PhysicalProperties.new(1, 0.5, 0.2, 1, 1, 0.8) -- plus acoustic absorption

local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.CustomPhysicalProperties = basic
part.Parent = workspace

kid.simple: PhysicalProperties describes how a part acts in physics: how heavy it is for its size (Density), how grippy or slippery it is (Friction), and how bouncy it is (Elasticity). You set it on a part's CustomPhysicalProperties to make ice floors, bouncy balls, or super-heavy blocks.
kid.analogy: It is like choosing what a ball is made of. A bowling ball is heavy (high Density). A hockey puck on ice slides (low Friction). A rubber ball bounces (high Elasticity).
whenToUse: Making a slippery ice floor
Making a super-bouncy ball or trampoline
Making a part very heavy or very light so it is harder or easier to push
Making a room echo less with AcousticAbsorption
kid.where: Works in any script. Make one with PhysicalProperties.new(...) and set part.CustomPhysicalProperties to it. Set part.CustomPhysicalProperties = nil to go back to the material's normal values.

terms.density: How heavy something is for its size. A small block of lead is heavier than a big block of foam. Range 0.0001 to 100.
terms.friction: How much two surfaces grip when they rub. High friction = sticky, like rubber. Low friction = slippery, like ice. Range 0 to 2.
terms.elasticity: How bouncy something is. 0 = no bounce (thud). 1 = bounces back with all its energy. Range 0 to 1.
terms.weight (in FrictionWeight / ElasticityWe: Not how heavy the part is. It means "how much this part's value counts" when two parts touch. The part with the bigger weight gets more say.
terms.clamped: Pushed back inside the allowed range. A Friction of 5 becomes 2, because 2 is the most allowed.
terms.acoustic simulation: Roblox working out how sound echoes and gets muffled by surfaces around it.
terms.reverb: The echo you hear in a big empty room or a cave.
terms.Enum.Material: The list of materials a part can be made of, like Plastic, Wood, Ice, and Metal.

examples.title: A slippery ice floor
examples.code:
local floor = Instance.new("Part")
floor.Size = Vector3.new(40, 1, 40)
floor.Anchored = true
floor.Position = Vector3.new(0, 0.5, 0)
floor.Color = Color3.fromRGB(170, 220, 255)
floor.Parent = workspace

floor.CustomPhysicalProperties = PhysicalProperties.new(
	0.9,  -- density: about normal
	0,    -- friction: zero grip, super slippery
	0,    -- elasticity: no bounce
	100,  -- frictionWeight: MY friction wins when something touches me
	1     -- elasticityWeight: normal
)
explain: We make a big flat floor.
Friction 0 means nothing can grip it.
The other part touching the floor (like a player's foot) has its own friction too. frictionWeight 100 makes the floor's friction count much more, so the final friction is close to 0.
Walk on it and you will slide around.

examples.title: A super-bouncy ball
examples.code:
local ball = Instance.new("Part")
ball.Shape = Enum.PartType.Ball
ball.Size = Vector3.new(3, 3, 3)
ball.Position = Vector3.new(0, 30, 0)
ball.Parent = workspace

-- density 1, friction 0.3, elasticity 1 (max bounce), frictionWeight 1, elasticityWeight 100
ball.CustomPhysicalProperties = PhysicalProperties.new(1, 0.3, 1, 1, 100)
explain: The ball starts 30 studs up and falls.
Elasticity 1 is the bounciest allowed.
elasticityWeight 100 makes the ball's bounciness win over the floor's, so it keeps bouncing high.

gotchas: Values outside the allowed ranges are clamped, not errors. Friction 10 quietly becomes 2.
When two parts touch, Roblox mixes their friction (and their elasticity) using the weights. If your bouncy ball barely bounces, raise its ElasticityWeight.
PhysicalProperties values cannot be edited after you make them. Make a new one and set it again.

datatype/RBXScriptConnection.d:
The RBXScriptConnection data type is a special object returned by the Connect() method of an event (RBXScriptSignal). This is used primarily to disconnect a listener from an RBXScriptSignal.

local part = Instance.new("Part")
-- Store reference to the RBXScriptConnection so it can be disconnected later
local connection : RBXScriptConnection = part.Touched:Connect(function(otherPart)
    print("Hello world!")
end)
-- Disconnect when the connection is no longer needed
connection:Disconnect()
datatype/RBXScriptConnection.s: A connection between an `Datatype.RBXScriptSignal` and a function.

m.d: Describes whether or not the connection is still alive. This becomes false if Disconnect() is called.
m.s: The state of the RBXScriptConnection.

kid.simple: True while the link is active. Turns false after `:Disconnect()` (or after a `:Once` connection has fired).
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local conn = Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function() end)
print(conn.Connected) --> true
conn:Disconnect()
print(conn.Connected) --> false

m.d: Disconnects the connection from the event.
m.s: Disconnects the connection from the event.

kid.simple: Stops your function from running when the event fires. Safe to call more than once.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")

local frames = 0
local conn
conn = RunService.Heartbeat:Connect(function()
	frames += 1
	if frames >= 60 then
		print("Counted 60 frames, stopping")
		conn:Disconnect()
	end
end)

kid.simple: An RBXScriptConnection is the link between an event and your function. You get one back every time you call `:Connect` (or `:Once`). Keep it if you want to stop listening later with `:Disconnect()`.
kid.analogy: If connecting to an event is like subscribing to a newsletter, the connection is the 'unsubscribe' link. Keep it handy and click it when you do not want any more messages.
whenToUse: Stopping a function from running when an event fires, for example after a power-up ends.
Cleaning up listeners you no longer need so your game stays fast.
Checking if a link is still active with `.Connected`.
kid.where: Returned by `RBXScriptSignal:Connect`, `:Once` and `:ConnectParallel`. Also returned by `MessagingService:SubscribeAsync`. Works in Scripts and LocalScripts.

terms.event / signal: Something that can happen, like a touch or a click.
terms.connect: Attaching your function to an event.
terms.disconnect: Removing that attachment so your function stops running when the event fires.
terms.memory leak: When a game keeps holding onto things it no longer needs, using more and more memory over time. Old connections you forget to disconnect can cause this.

examples.title: A lava floor that turns off after 10 seconds
examples.place: Script inside a Part in Workspace
examples.code:
local part = script.Parent

-- Save the connection so we can stop it later
local connection = part.Touched:Connect(function(otherPart)
	local humanoid = otherPart.Parent:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
	if humanoid then
		humanoid.Health = 0
	end
end)

task.wait(10)
connection:Disconnect() -- lava is now safe to walk on
print("Still connected?", connection.Connected) --> false
explain: `:Connect` gives back a connection, which we save in a variable.
For 10 seconds, touching the part defeats players.
`connection:Disconnect()` unhooks the function, so touching does nothing now.

gotchas: Destroying an object disconnects its events automatically, but connections to things that live forever (like Players or RunService) stay until you disconnect them.
Disconnecting does not stop a function that is already running; it only stops future runs.

datatype/RBXScriptSignal.d: The RBXScriptSignal data type, more commonly known as an Event, provides a way for user-defined functions, called listeners, to call when something happens in the game. When an event happens, the RBXScriptSignal fires and calls any listeners that are connected to it. An RBXScriptSignal may also pass arguments to each listener to provide extra information about the event.
datatype/RBXScriptSignal.s: An object that runs connected functions upon a specific occurrence.

m.d: Establishes a function to be called when the event fires. Returns an RBXScriptConnection object associated with the connection.
m.s: Connects the given function to the event and returns an `Datatype.RBXScriptConnection` that represents it.

p.s: The callback function to invoke each time the event fires.

r.s: A connection object that can be used to disconnect the listener from the event.

kid.simple: Attaches a function to the event. Every time the event fires, your function runs and gets whatever the event passes (like the part that touched). Returns a connection you can disconnect later.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript inside a TextButton in StarterGui
local button = script.Parent

local connection = button.Activated:Connect(function()
	print("Button clicked!")
end)

m.d:
Establishes a function to be called when the event fires. Returns an RBXScriptConnection object associated with the connection. When the event fires, the signal callback is executed in a desynchronized state. Using ConnectParallel is similar to, but more efficient than, using Connect followed by a call to task.desynchronize() in the signal handler.

Note: Scripts that connect in parallel must be rooted under an Actor.
m.s: Connects the given function to the event and returns an `Datatype.RBXScriptConnection` that represents it.

p.s: The callback function to invoke when the event fires in a parallel execution context.

r.s: A connection object that can be used to disconnect the listener from the event.

kid.simple: An advanced version of `Connect` that runs your function in parallel (on another CPU core) for speed. Only works in scripts placed inside an Actor. Most games never need it.
kid.example:
-- Script inside an Actor in Workspace
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")

RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel(function()
	-- heavy math can go here, running in parallel
	local total = 0
	for i = 1, 1000 do
		total += i
	end
end)
kid.gotcha: In parallel mode you cannot change most things in the game. Call `task.synchronize()` before changing parts.

m.d: Establishes a function to be called when the event fires. Returns an RBXScriptConnection object associated with the connection. The behavior of Once is similar to Connect. However, instead of allowing multiple events to be received by the specified function, only the first event will be delivered. Using Once also ensures that the connection to the function will be automatically disconnected prior the function being called.
m.s: Connects the given function to the event (for a single invocation) and returns an `Datatype.RBXScriptConnection` that represents it.

p.s: The callback function to invoke the next time the event fires, after which it is automatically disconnected.

r.s: A connection object that can be used to disconnect the listener before it fires.

kid.simple: Like `Connect`, but your function runs only the next time the event fires, then disconnects automatically.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
	-- Only greet on their first spawn
	player.CharacterAdded:Once(function(character)
		print(player.Name .. " spawned for the first time")
	end)
end)

m.d: Yields the current thread until the signal fires and returns the arguments provided by the signal.
m.s: Yields the current thread until the signal fires and returns the arguments provided by the signal.

r.s: The arguments passed by the signal when it fires.

kid.simple: Pauses your script until the event fires, then gives back what the event sent. Handy for 'wait until X happens'.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local player = Players.LocalPlayer

-- Use the current character, or wait for one to spawn
local character = player.Character or player.CharacterAdded:Wait()
print("My character is ready:", character.Name)
kid.gotcha: If the event never fires, your script waits forever.

kid.simple: RBXScriptSignal is the official name for an event in Roblox, like `Touched`, `PlayerAdded` or `Activated`. An event is something that can happen. You attach a function to it with `:Connect`, and Roblox runs your function every time it happens.
kid.analogy: A signal is like a doorbell. `:Connect` is you saying 'every time the doorbell rings, I will go open the door'. `:Once` is 'I will answer it just the next time'. `:Wait` is standing by the door doing nothing else until it rings.
whenToUse: Any time you want code to run when something happens: a part is touched, a player joins, a button is clicked.
Waiting for something to happen before continuing (`:Wait`).
Running something only the first time an event happens (`:Once`).
kid.where: Signals are found on objects, like `part.Touched` or `Players.PlayerAdded`. Use them with a dot to get the event and a colon to call its method: `part.Touched:Connect(...)`. Works in Scripts and LocalScripts.

terms.event / signal: Something that can happen in the game, like a touch or a click. Roblox 'fires' the event when it happens.
terms.fire: When the event happens and Roblox runs all the connected functions.
terms.connect: Attaching your function to an event so it runs each time the event fires.
terms.connection: The object you get back from `:Connect`. You can keep it and call `:Disconnect()` later to stop listening.
terms.callback / handler: The function you connect to an event. Roblox calls it for you when the event fires.
terms.yield: To pause your script and wait. `:Wait()` pauses until the event fires.
terms.Actor / parallel: An advanced way to run code on several CPU cores at once. Only scripts inside an Actor object can use `ConnectParallel`. Beginners can skip it.

examples.title: Do something when a part is touched
examples.place: Script inside a Part in Workspace
examples.code:
local part = script.Parent

-- Touched is a signal. Connect a function to it.
part.Touched:Connect(function(otherPart)
	print(otherPart.Name .. " touched me!")
end)
explain: `part.Touched` is the event (signal).
`:Connect(function(otherPart) ... end)` attaches our function.
Every time something touches the part, Roblox runs the function and tells us what touched it.

examples.title: Connect, Once and Wait side by side
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

-- Runs for EVERY player who joins
Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
	print("Welcome, " .. player.Name)
end)

-- Runs only for the FIRST player who joins
Players.PlayerAdded:Once(function(player)
	print(player.Name .. " was the first one here!")
end)

-- Pauses this script until someone joins, then continues
local firstPlayer = Players.PlayerAdded:Wait()
print("Game can start now that " .. firstPlayer.Name .. " is here")
explain: `:Connect` keeps listening forever (until disconnected).
`:Once` listens one time, then stops by itself.
`:Wait` pauses the script and gives back what the event sent.

gotchas: Use a dot to get the event and a colon to use it: `part.Touched:Connect(...)`, not `part:Touched:Connect`.
Connections keep running until you disconnect them or the object is destroyed. Disconnect ones you no longer need to avoid slowdowns.
`:Wait()` stops the whole script until the event fires. If it never fires, the code after it never runs.
Pass a function to `:Connect`, not the result of calling one: `:Connect(onTouch)`, not `:Connect(onTouch())`.

datatype/Random.d: The Random data type generates pseudorandom numbers and directions.

m.d: Returns a pseudorandom integer uniformly distributed over [min, max], inclusive of both endpoints. If min is greater than max, the two values are swapped so the call still succeeds. Both arguments are truncated toward zero to whole numbers before sampling.
m.s: Returns a pseudorandom integer uniformly distributed over `[min, max]`.

p.s: The minimum integer value of the range (inclusive). Truncated toward zero to a whole number.
The maximum integer value of the range (inclusive). Truncated toward zero to a whole number.

kid.simple: Gives a random whole number from min to max, and both ends can come up. If you accidentally give the bigger number first, it swaps them for you.
kid.example:
local rng = Random.new()
local dice = rng:NextInteger(1, 6) -- 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6
print(dice)

m.d: Returns a uniform pseudorandom real number in the range of 0 to 1, inclusive.
m.s: Returns a pseudorandom number uniformly distributed over `[0, 1]`.

r.s: A pseudorandom number uniformly distributed over [0, 1].

kid.simple: Gives a random decimal number. With no arguments it is between 0 and 1. With min and max, it is between those two.
kid.example:
local rng = Random.new()
print(rng:NextNumber())        -- like 0.4821
print(rng:NextNumber(10, 20))  -- like 13.77

m.d:
Uniformly shuffles the array part of tb in-place using NextInteger to pick indices. If there are any nil "holes" in the array part of the table, Shuffle throws an error, since shuffling could change the length.

The hash part of tb is ignored. No metamethods of tb are invoked.

The shuffle is defined to be a Fisher-Yates shuffle so the number of NextInteger calls is guaranteed to be consistent between engine versions for a given size of table.
m.s: Uniformly shuffles a table in-place.

p.s: The table whose array part is shuffled in-place.

kid.simple: Mixes up the order of a list, right in place (the list itself is changed). Every order is equally likely.
kid.example:
local rng = Random.new()
local games = { "Obby", "Race", "Tag", "Hide and Seek" }
rng:Shuffle(games)
print(table.concat(games, ", ")) -- a new random order
kid.gotcha: The list must not have nil gaps in the middle, or it errors. It returns nothing, so do not write `games = rng:Shuffle(games)`.

m.d: Returns a unit vector with a pseudorandom direction. Vectors returned from this function are uniformly distributed over the unit sphere.
m.s: Returns a unit vector with a pseudorandom direction.

r.s: A unit vector with a pseudorandom direction.

kid.simple: Gives a random direction as a Vector3 arrow of length 1. Every direction in 3D is equally likely. Multiply it to make it longer.
kid.example:
local rng = Random.new()
local direction = rng:NextUnitVector()
-- A random spot 10 studs away from the center
local spot = Vector3.new(0, 10, 0) + direction * 10
print(spot)

m.d: Returns a new Random object whose internal state is copied from the original. After cloning, both the original and the clone produce the same sequence of pseudorandom values going forward, but they advance independently — consuming a value from one does not affect the other.
m.s: Returns a new Random object with the same state as the original.

r.s: A new Random object with the same internal state as the original.

kid.simple: Makes a copy of this random machine at exactly the same point in its recipe. From then on, both give the same next numbers, but using one does not change the other.
kid.example:
local rng = Random.new(7)
local copy = rng:Clone()
print(rng:NextInteger(1, 100) == copy:NextInteger(1, 100)) --> true

m.d:
Returns a new Random object. If you don't provide the seed parameter, Random uses a seed from an internal entropy source.

If you provide a seed, it should be within the range [-9007199254740991, 9007199254740991], and Random will round it down to the nearest integer. So seeds of 0, 0.99, and math.random() all produce identical generators. If you need to generate a seed and store it for later retrieval, use math.random(max).
m.s: Returns a new pseudorandom generator using an optional seed.

p.s: An optional number that initializes the pseudorandom number generator's internal state, truncated toward zero to a whole number. Should be within the range [-9007199254740991, 9007199254740991]; values outside this range are clamped to 0.

kid.simple: Makes a new random number machine. With no seed, Roblox picks a surprise starting point. With a seed number, you get the same results every time for that seed.
kid.example:
local surprise = Random.new()  -- different every time
local repeatable = Random.new(12345) -- same every time
kid.gotcha: Decimal seeds are cut down to whole numbers, so 7 and 7.9 are the same seed.

kid.simple: Random is a random number machine. You make one with Random.new(), then ask it for random whole numbers, random decimals, random directions, or to shuffle a list. If you give it a seed number, it gives the exact same "random" results every time, which is great for things like generating the same map twice.
kid.analogy: Random is like a deck of cards. Random.new() shuffles it in a surprise way. Random.new(42) always shuffles it in the same way, so if you and a friend both use 42, you draw the same cards in the same order.
whenToUse: Rolling dice or picking a random number for loot
Picking a random spawn point or player
Shuffling a list, like the order of mini-games
Making a procedural map that is the same every time for the same seed
kid.where: Works in any script on server or client. Make one with Random.new() or Random.new(seed). Keep it in a variable and reuse it instead of making a new one every time.

terms.pseudorandom: Numbers that look random but are made by a math recipe. With the same starting seed you get the same numbers.
terms.seed: The starting number for the recipe. Same seed = same sequence of results.
terms.integer: A whole number, like 3 or -7, with no decimal part.
terms.inclusive: The end numbers count too. NextInteger(1, 6) can give 1 and can give 6.
terms.unit vector: An arrow with a length of exactly 1. It only says which way, not how far.
terms.shuffle: Mix up the order of the items in a list.
terms.Vector3: Three numbers (X, Y, Z) for a position or direction in 3D.

examples.title: Roll a dice and pick a random prize
examples.code:
local rng = Random.new() -- a surprise seed each server

-- Roll a 6-sided dice
local roll = rng:NextInteger(1, 6)
print("You rolled a", roll)

-- Pick a random prize from a list
local prizes = { "Sword", "Shield", "Potion", "Hat" }
local prize = prizes[rng:NextInteger(1, #prizes)]
print("You won a", prize)

-- A random decimal between 0.5 and 2 for a size
local size = rng:NextNumber(0.5, 2)
print("Random size:", size)
explain: Random.new() with no seed gives different results each time the game runs.
NextInteger(1, 6) gives a whole number from 1 to 6, and both 1 and 6 are possible.
#prizes is how many items are in the list (4), so we pick a random spot from 1 to 4.
NextNumber(0.5, 2) gives a decimal, like 1.37.

examples.title: Same seed, same results
examples.code:
local a = Random.new(42)
local b = Random.new(42)

print(a:NextInteger(1, 100), b:NextInteger(1, 100)) -- the same two numbers
print(a:NextInteger(1, 100), b:NextInteger(1, 100)) -- the same again
explain: Both machines start with seed 42.
Because they follow the same recipe, they give the same numbers in the same order.
This is how games can rebuild the exact same random world from one saved seed.

gotchas: Do not make a new Random.new() every time you need a number. Make one and keep using it.
Seeds are rounded toward zero, so seeds 0 and 0.99 give the same results.
Shuffle only works on lists without gaps (no nil holes in the middle). It changes the list itself and returns nothing.

datatype/Ray.d: The Ray data type represents a half-line, finite in one direction but infinite in the other. It can be defined by a 3D point, where the line originates from, and a direction vector, which is the direction it goes in.
datatype/Ray.s: Represents a line with a starting point that casts infinitely in a specific direction.

m.d: The Ray with a normalized direction (the direction has a magnitude of 1).
m.s: The `Datatype.Ray` with a normalized direction (the direction has a magnitude of `1`).

kid.simple: A copy of this Ray whose direction has been shrunk or stretched to length exactly 1, still pointing the same way. A direction of (10, 0, 0) becomes (1, 0, 0).
kid.example:
local ray = Ray.new(Vector3.zero, Vector3.new(10, 0, 0))
print(ray.Unit.Direction) --> 1, 0, 0

m.d: The position of the origin.
m.s: The position of the origin.

kid.simple: The starting point of the Ray, as a Vector3 position.
kid.example:
local ray = Ray.new(Vector3.new(0, 10, 0), Vector3.new(0, -1, 0))
print(ray.Origin) --> 0, 10, 0

m.d: The direction vector of the Ray.
m.s: The direction vector of the `Datatype.Ray`.

kid.simple: The arrow that says which way the Ray points (and how long the arrow is), as a Vector3.
kid.example:
local ray = Ray.new(Vector3.new(0, 10, 0), Vector3.new(0, -5, 0))
print(ray.Direction) --> 0, -5, 0

m.d:
Returns a Vector3 projected onto the ray so that it is within the Ray line of sight.

Note: the Ray must be a unit ray for this method to behave as expected!
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.Vector3` projected onto the ray so that it is within the `Datatype.Ray` line of sight.

p.s: The point in 3D space to project onto the ray.

r.s: The point on the ray closest to the given point, or the ray origin if the projection falls behind it.

kid.simple: Gives the point on the Ray that is closest to the point you give it. If the point is behind the start of the Ray, you get the Ray's origin. The Ray must be a unit ray (use .Unit).
kid.example:
local unitRay = Ray.new(Vector3.zero, Vector3.new(1, 0, 0))
print(unitRay:ClosestPoint(Vector3.new(7, 2, 0)))  --> 7, 0, 0
print(unitRay:ClosestPoint(Vector3.new(-5, 2, 0))) --> 0, 0, 0 (behind the start)
kid.gotcha: Using a ray that is not unit length gives wrong answers. Call .Unit first.

m.d: Returns the distance between the given point and the point on the ray nearest to the given point (Ray.ClosestPoint(point)).
m.s: Returns the distance between the given point and the closest point on the `Datatype.Ray`.

p.s: The point in 3D space to measure distance from.

r.s: The shortest distance between the given point and the closest point on the ray.

kid.simple: Tells you how far a point is from the closest spot on the Ray, in studs.
kid.example:
local unitRay = Ray.new(Vector3.zero, Vector3.new(1, 0, 0))
print(unitRay:Distance(Vector3.new(7, 2, 0))) --> 2
