m.d: Returns a new Ray with given Origin and Direction.
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.Ray` with the given `Origin` and `Direction`.

p.s: The starting point of the ray in 3D space.
The direction vector of the ray. Does not need to be a unit vector.

kid.simple: Makes a Ray from an origin (start point) and a direction (which way it goes). The direction does not have to be length 1.
kid.example:
local ray = Ray.new(Vector3.new(0, 10, 0), Vector3.new(0, -1, 0)) -- start 10 studs up, point down
print(ray.Origin, ray.Direction)

kid.simple: A Ray is a math object for an invisible line that starts at one point (the origin) and shoots off forever in one direction. It can tell you the closest point on that line to some other spot, and how far away that spot is. To actually find what a laser hits in the world, you use workspace:Raycast instead, which takes an origin and a direction directly.
kid.analogy: A Ray is like a flashlight beam drawn on a map: it starts at the flashlight and goes straight out in one direction. Ray can tell you how close a treasure on the map is to the beam, but it does not light anything up by itself.
whenToUse: Finding the point on a line that is closest to something, like how close a player is to a laser beam
Measuring how far a spot is from a line
Getting a mouse ray from the camera with Camera:ScreenPointToRay, then using its Origin and Direction in workspace:Raycast
kid.where: Works in any script. Make one with Ray.new(origin, direction). Note: workspace:Raycast does NOT take a Ray object, but you can pass ray.Origin and ray.Direction to it.

terms.origin: The starting point of the ray: where the laser beam comes out. A Vector3 position like (0, 10, 0).
terms.direction: Which way the ray goes AND how far. It is a Vector3 arrow. Vector3.new(0, -50, 0) means "straight down, 50 studs long".
terms.magnitude: The length of a Vector3 arrow. The magnitude of (0, -50, 0) is 50. For a raycast, this length is how far the ray checks: anything farther away is ignored.
terms.Vector3: Three numbers (X, Y, Z) that describe a position or an arrow in the 3D world. Y is up and down.
terms.unit vector: An arrow with a length of exactly 1. It only tells you which way, not how far. `.Unit` turns any arrow into one.
terms.stud: Roblox's unit of distance. A default character is about 5 studs tall.
terms.project onto: Slide a point sideways onto the line until it touches it, landing at the closest spot on the line.

examples.title: How close is a point to a laser line?
examples.code:
-- A line starting at (0, 5, 0) going along the X direction
local ray = Ray.new(Vector3.new(0, 5, 0), Vector3.new(10, 0, 0))

-- ClosestPoint and Distance need a unit ray (direction length 1)
local unitRay = ray.Unit

local spot = Vector3.new(4, 8, 0)
print(unitRay:ClosestPoint(spot)) --> 4, 5, 0
print(unitRay:Distance(spot))     --> 3
explain: The ray starts at (0, 5, 0) and points along +X.
ray.Unit makes the same ray but with a direction of length 1, which ClosestPoint needs.
The spot (4, 8, 0) is 3 studs above the line. The closest place on the line is directly under it at (4, 5, 0).
Distance gives that gap: 3 studs.

examples.title: Turn a Ray into a real raycast
examples.code:
local ray = Ray.new(Vector3.new(0, 50, 0), Vector3.new(0, -100, 0))

-- workspace:Raycast wants the origin and direction separately
local result = workspace:Raycast(ray.Origin, ray.Direction)
if result then
	print("Hit", result.Instance.Name, "at", result.Position)
else
	print("Hit nothing")
end
explain: The Ray starts 50 studs up and points 100 studs straight down.
workspace:Raycast does the real work of checking parts in the world.
If something is in the way, result has information about the hit. If not, result is nil.

gotchas: ClosestPoint and Distance only work correctly on a unit ray. Use ray.Unit first.
A Ray by itself never hits parts. Use workspace:Raycast(origin, direction) for that.
Ray values cannot be changed after they are made. Make a new Ray instead.

datatype/RaycastParams.d:
The RaycastParams data type stores parameters for WorldRoot:Raycast() operations. The ExcludeInstances and IncludeInstances properties store a set of objects and their descendants that will be excluded and included from the query. The RaycastParams.IgnoreWater property can be used to ignore Terrain water, and the RaycastParams.CollisionGroup property can specify a collision group for the raycasting operation.

This object is different from the similarly named RaycastResult which provides the results of a raycast.

Unlike most data types in Luau, you can change all of the members of RaycastParams without creating a new object, allowing you to reuse the same object repeatedly.
datatype/RaycastParams.s: A container for parameters used in raycasting operations.

m.d: An optional array of instances whose descendants will be excluded from the query. This property can be used simultaneously with IncludeInstances to allow for mixed filtering, for example including a large folder but excluding specific child instances. If an instance matches both an exclude and include filter, exclusions take priority over inclusions.
m.s: An optional array of instances whose descendants will be excluded from the query.

kid.simple: A list of things the ray should skip, along with everything inside them. Usually you put the player's own character here.
kid.example:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local character = Players.LocalPlayer.Character or Players.LocalPlayer.CharacterAdded:Wait()

local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.ExcludeInstances = { character } -- never hit myself
kid.gotcha: If something is in both ExcludeInstances and IncludeInstances, it is excluded.

m.d:
An optional array of instances whose descendants will be included in the query. This property can be used simultaneously with ExcludeInstances to allow for mixed filtering. If an instance matches both an exclude and include filter, exclusions take priority over inclusions.

Setting IncludeInstances to nil versus an empty array ({}) has opposite effects. IncludeInstances = nil is the most permissive filter (includes everything), whereas IncludeInstances = {} is the most restrictive filter (includes nothing).
m.s: An optional array of instances whose descendants will be included in the query.

kid.simple: A list of the ONLY things the ray may hit (plus everything inside them). Leave it nil to allow everything. Setting it to an empty list {} allows nothing at all.
kid.example:
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.IncludeInstances = { workspace:WaitForChild("Targets") } -- only targets count
kid.gotcha: nil means "include everything", but {} means "include nothing". They are opposites.

m.d: Determines whether the water material is considered when raycasting against Terrain.
m.s: Determines whether the water material is considered when raycasting against `Class.Terrain`.

kid.simple: If true, the ray passes through Terrain water as if it were not there. If false, water can be hit.
kid.example:
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.IgnoreWater = true -- see the lake floor, not the water surface

m.d: Specifies a collision group for the raycasting operation. Parts in collision groups that are set to not collide with this group are ignored. If this property is omitted, the raycast assumes the Default collision group.
m.s: The collision group used for the operation.

kid.simple: The name of a collision group the ray pretends to belong to. Parts in groups set to NOT collide with that group are skipped. If you do not set it, the ray uses the "Default" group.
kid.example:
local params = RaycastParams.new()
-- "Ghosts" must already exist as a collision group in your game
params.CollisionGroup = "Ghosts"

m.d: This property, if true, makes the raycast operation use an intersected part's CanCollide value in favor of its CanQuery value when determining whether that part is included in the RaycastResult.
m.s: Determines whether the raycast operation considers a part's `Class.BasePart.CanCollide|CanCollide` property value over its `Class.BasePart.CanQuery|CanQuery` value.

kid.simple: If true, the ray decides whether to hit a part by its CanCollide setting instead of its CanQuery setting. So parts players can walk through (CanCollide off) are skipped.
kid.example:
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.RespectCanCollide = true -- ignore walk-through decorations

m.d: When enabled, the query will ignore all part collision properties and perform a brute-force check on every part. This will negatively impact performance and should not be used in live experiences.
m.s: When enabled, the query will ignore all part collision properties and perform a brute-force check on every part.

kid.simple: If true, the ray ignores all the usual part settings and checks every single part the slow way. It is only for testing; do not use it in a real game because it hurts performance.
kid.example:
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.BruteForceAllSlow = true -- testing only!
kid.gotcha: Leave this false in published games.

m.d:
Expands the cast shape uniformly in every direction. Must be finite and greater than or equal to 0. Defaults to 0.

Margin applies to WorldRoot:Shapecast(), WorldRoot:Blockcast(), WorldRoot:Spherecast() and WorldRoot:Raycast(). The expanded shape is what the maximum-size limit is checked against, so a large Margin can make an otherwise valid cast throw.

Setting a non-zero Margin on a WorldRoot:Raycast() makes the operation behave as a sphere cast of that radius.
m.s: Expands the cast shape uniformly in every direction.

kid.simple: Makes the cast shape a bit fatter in every direction, in studs. Default is 0. On a normal raycast, a Margin turns the thin laser into a ball of that radius (a sphere cast), so it is easier to hit things.
kid.example:
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.Margin = 1 -- the laser is now a ball 1 stud in radius
local result = workspace:Raycast(Vector3.new(0, 5, 0), Vector3.new(0, 0, -50), params)
kid.gotcha: Must be 0 or more. A huge Margin can make the cast too big and throw an error.

m.d:
Scales the cast shape over the length of the cast. Must be finite and greater than or equal to -1. Defaults to 0, which casts the shape at a constant size.

The shape starts at its original size and is scaled by 1 + SizeGradient by the end of the cast, interpolating in between. A SizeGradient of 0.5 finishes the cast 50% larger, -0.5 finishes it at half size, and -1 shrinks it away entirely.

SizeGradient scales the shape's own size, not Margin, so a cast with both keeps its margin at a constant width along the way. WorldRoot:Spherecast() is the exception: radius and margin are one and the same for a sphere, so both scale together.
m.s: Scales the cast shape over the length of the cast, tapering the swept volume.

kid.simple: Makes the cast shape grow or shrink as it travels, for shape casts like Spherecast and Blockcast. Default 0 keeps the size the same. 0.5 ends 50% bigger, -0.5 ends at half size, -1 shrinks to nothing.
kid.example:
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.SizeGradient = 1 -- the ball ends twice as big as it started
-- A 2-stud ball pushed 40 studs forward
local result = workspace:Spherecast(Vector3.new(0, 5, 0), 2, Vector3.new(0, 0, -40), params)
kid.gotcha: Must be -1 or more.

m.d: An array of objects whose descendants are used to filter raycasting candidates. Note that this property has been superseded by ExcludeInstances and IncludeInstances which should be used for new work.
m.s: An array of objects whose descendants are used to filter raycasting candidates.

kid.simple: The older way to filter: a list of things used as either a skip list or an only-these list, depending on FilterType. New code should use ExcludeInstances or IncludeInstances instead.
kid.gotcha: Replaced by ExcludeInstances and IncludeInstances for new work.

m.d: Determines whether the FilterDescendantsInstances array is used as an exclude or include list. Note that this property has been superseded by ExcludeInstances and IncludeInstances which should be used for new work.
m.s: Determines whether the `Datatype.RaycastParams.FilterDescendantsInstances|FilterDescendantsInstances` array is used as an exclude or include list.

kid.simple: Says whether the FilterDescendantsInstances list is a skip list (Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude) or an only-these list (Enum.RaycastFilterType.Include). It is part of the older filter system.
kid.gotcha: New code should use ExcludeInstances or IncludeInstances instead.

m.d: Adds the instances provided to FilterDescendantsInstances. Note that this property has been superseded by ExcludeInstances and IncludeInstances which should be used for new work.
m.s: Adds the instances provided to `Datatype.RaycastParams.FilterDescendantsInstances|FilterDescendantsInstances`.

p.s: An instance or an array containing instances to add.

kid.simple: Adds one thing, or a list of things, to the FilterDescendantsInstances list without replacing what is already there. Part of the older filter system.
kid.example:
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
params:AddToFilter(workspace:WaitForChild("Decorations"))
params:AddToFilter({ workspace:WaitForChild("Effects") })
kid.gotcha: New code should put things in ExcludeInstances or IncludeInstances instead.

m.d: Returns a blank RaycastParams object. Unlike other data type constructors, this constructor does not have any parameters, so you should set its properties appropriately.
m.s: Returns a blank `Datatype.RaycastParams`.

kid.simple: Makes a blank RaycastParams with no rules set. It takes no arguments, so you set its properties afterwards.
kid.example:
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.IgnoreWater = true

kid.simple: RaycastParams is a settings box you hand to workspace:Raycast (and the other cast functions). It tells the invisible laser beam what to skip and what it is allowed to hit. The most common use is telling the ray to ignore your own character so it does not hit yourself.
kid.analogy: RaycastParams is like the rules you give a friend playing "I spy": "don't count anything in my backpack, and don't count water". The friend still looks, but follows your rules.
whenToUse: Ignoring the player's own character when shooting a laser or checking what is in front of them
Only letting a ray hit things inside one folder (like Enemies)
Ignoring Terrain water
Making a ray pretend to be in a collision group
kid.where: Works in any script on server or client. Make one with RaycastParams.new() (no arguments), set its properties, then pass it as the third argument: workspace:Raycast(origin, direction, params). You can reuse the same one many times.

terms.raycast: Shooting an invisible laser beam through the 3D world and asking "what does it hit first?". Roblox tells you what part it hit, where, and how far away.
terms.origin: The starting point of the ray: where the laser beam comes out. A Vector3 position like (0, 10, 0).
terms.direction: Which way the ray goes AND how far. It is a Vector3 arrow. Vector3.new(0, -50, 0) means "straight down, 50 studs long".
terms.magnitude: The length of a Vector3 arrow. The magnitude of (0, -50, 0) is 50. For a raycast, this length is how far the ray checks: anything farther away is ignored.
terms.filter: A list of things the ray should skip (exclude) or the only things it may hit (include). Usually you exclude your own character so you do not hit yourself.
terms.descendant: Anything inside something else, at any depth: its children, their children, and so on. Excluding a character also excludes its arms, legs, hats, and so on.
terms.nil: Lua's word for "nothing". workspace:Raycast gives nil when the ray hits nothing.
terms.collision group: A named team of parts that you set up so some groups pass through each other. Queries can pretend to be in one of these groups.
terms.CanQuery: A part property. When false, raycasts and other spatial queries skip that part.
terms.CanCollide: A part property. When false, players and other parts can walk or fall through it.
terms.LookVector: A unit arrow pointing the way a part or character is facing. Multiply it by a number to make it that long: LookVector * 50 is a 50-stud arrow forward.
terms.stud: Roblox's unit of distance. A default character is about 5 studs tall.
terms.exclude: Skip these things. The ray goes right through them.
terms.include: ONLY these things can be hit. Everything else is skipped.
terms.array: A list in Lua, written with curly braces like {partA, partB}.
terms.sphere cast: Like a raycast, but instead of a thin laser you push a ball through the world and see what it bumps into first.
terms.shape cast: Pushing a shape (a part, a block, or a ball) through the world to see what it bumps into first. Blockcast, Spherecast, and Shapecast do this.

examples.title: Raycasting step by step: what is in front of me?
examples.code:
local character = script.Parent
local rootPart = character:WaitForChild("HumanoidRootPart")

-- Step 4: the filter. Skip my own character.
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.ExcludeInstances = { character }

while true do
	-- Step 1: origin = where the laser starts (my body)
	local origin = rootPart.Position

	-- Steps 2 and 3: direction = which way AND how far.
	-- LookVector is length 1, so * 20 makes it 20 studs long.
	local direction = rootPart.CFrame.LookVector * 20

	-- Step 5: shoot the ray
	local result = workspace:Raycast(origin, direction, params)

	if result then
		print("In front of me:", result.Instance.Name, math.floor(result.Distance), "studs away")
	end
	task.wait(1)
end
explain: Step 1, origin: the ray starts at my HumanoidRootPart, the middle of my character.
Step 2, direction: LookVector is an arrow pointing where I face, with length 1.
Step 3, length: the length (magnitude) of the direction is how far the ray checks. LookVector * 20 is 20 studs long, so anything farther than 20 studs is ignored.
Step 4, filter: without ExcludeInstances the ray would start inside my own body and hit me first. Excluding my character also skips all its descendants (arms, legs, hats).
Step 5, result: workspace:Raycast gives back a RaycastResult if it hit something, or nil if nothing was within 20 studs.
We check once a second with task.wait(1).

examples.title: Only hit enemies
examples.place: Script in ServerScriptService (with a Folder named Enemies in Workspace)
examples.code:
local enemies = workspace:WaitForChild("Enemies")

local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.IncludeInstances = { enemies } -- only things inside Enemies count
params.IgnoreWater = true

local origin = Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)
local direction = Vector3.new(100, 0, 0) -- 100 studs along +X

local result = workspace:Raycast(origin, direction, params)
if result then
	print("Hit enemy part:", result.Instance:GetFullName())
end
explain: IncludeInstances = { enemies } means walls, trees, and everything else are ignored. Only parts inside the Enemies folder can be hit.
IgnoreWater = true lets the ray pass through Terrain water.
The ray starts at (0, 5, 0) and checks 100 studs along the X direction.

gotchas: Forgetting to exclude your own character means the ray often hits you first.
IncludeInstances = {} (an empty list) means the ray can hit NOTHING. Leave it as nil if you want to hit everything.
If a part is in both the exclude and include lists, exclude wins.
The direction's length is the ray's range. Vector3.new(0, -1, 0) only checks 1 stud down. Multiply by a bigger number for more range (up to 15,000 studs).
Older code uses FilterDescendantsInstances and FilterType. New code should use ExcludeInstances and IncludeInstances.

datatype/RaycastResult.d:
The RaycastResult data type stores the result of a successful raycasting operation performed by WorldRoot:Raycast(). It contains the properties listed below.

This object should not be confused with the similarly-named RaycastParams which is used to perform a raycast.
datatype/RaycastResult.s: Stores results from a raycast operation.

m.d: The distance between the ray origin and the intersection point.
m.s: The distance between the ray origin and the intersection point.

kid.simple: How far it is, in studs, from the ray's starting point (origin) to the spot it hit.
kid.example:
local result = workspace:Raycast(Vector3.new(0, 20, 0), Vector3.new(0, -50, 0))
if result then
	print("Hit something", result.Distance, "studs below")
end

m.d: The BasePart or Terrain cell that the ray intersected.
m.s: The `Class.BasePart` or `Class.Terrain` cell that the ray intersected.

kid.simple: The thing that was hit: a part (BasePart) or the Terrain.
kid.example:
local result = workspace:Raycast(Vector3.new(0, 20, 0), Vector3.new(0, -50, 0))
if result then
	print("Hit:", result.Instance.Name)
end

m.d: The Material at the intersection point. For normal parts this is the BasePart.Material; for Terrain this can vary depending on terrain data.
m.s: The `Enum.Material` at the intersection point.

kid.simple: What the surface is made of at the hit spot, like Enum.Material.Grass. For normal parts it is the part's Material. For Terrain it is whatever terrain is at that spot.
kid.example:
local result = workspace:Raycast(Vector3.new(0, 20, 0), Vector3.new(0, -50, 0))
if result and result.Material == Enum.Material.Ice then
	print("Careful, it's slippery!")
end

m.d: The world space point at which the intersection occurred, usually a point directly on the surface of the BasePart or Terrain cell.
m.s: The world space point at which the intersection occurred.

kid.simple: The exact point in the world where the ray hit, usually right on the surface of the part or terrain. It is a world position, measured from the world's center.
kid.example:
local result = workspace:Raycast(Vector3.new(0, 20, 0), Vector3.new(0, -50, 0))
if result then
	print("Hit at", result.Position)
end

m.d: The normal vector of the intersected face.
m.s: The normal vector of the intersected face.

kid.simple: An arrow of length 1 that points straight out of the surface that was hit. A flat floor gives (0, 1, 0), meaning "up". A wall facing you gives an arrow pointing back toward you. Useful for bouncing things or placing decals flat.
kid.example:
local result = workspace:Raycast(Vector3.new(0, 20, 0), Vector3.new(0, -50, 0))
if result then
	print("Surface faces:", result.Normal) --> 0, 1, 0 on a flat floor
end

kid.simple: A RaycastResult is the report you get back when a raycast hits something. It tells you which part was hit, exactly where, how far away, what material it was, and which way the surface was facing. If the ray hits nothing, you get nil instead of a RaycastResult.
kid.analogy: It is like the report from a game of laser tag: "you hit the blue wall, 12 meters away, at this spot, and it was made of metal".
whenToUse: Finding which part a laser or bullet hit
Placing something exactly where the player clicked or aimed
Checking what is under a character's feet (grass, ice, water)
Lining up an object flat against a wall using the Normal
kid.where: You never make one yourself. workspace:Raycast(origin, direction, params) gives one back on a hit, or nil on a miss. Works on server and client.

terms.raycast: Shooting an invisible laser beam through the 3D world and asking "what does it hit first?". Roblox tells you what part it hit, where, and how far away.
terms.origin: The starting point of the ray: where the laser beam comes out. A Vector3 position like (0, 10, 0).
terms.direction: Which way the ray goes AND how far. It is a Vector3 arrow. Vector3.new(0, -50, 0) means "straight down, 50 studs long".
terms.normal: An arrow of length 1 sticking straight out of a surface, like a flagpole on the ground. On a flat floor the normal points straight up: (0, 1, 0).
terms.nil: Lua's word for "nothing". workspace:Raycast gives nil when the ray hits nothing.
terms.Vector3: Three numbers (X, Y, Z) that describe a position or an arrow in the 3D world. Y is up and down.
terms.stud: Roblox's unit of distance. A default character is about 5 studs tall.
terms.world space: Positions measured from the center of the whole world (0, 0, 0), not from some part.
terms.Material: What a surface is made of, like Grass, Wood, Ice, or Water (an Enum.Material).
terms.Terrain: Roblox's built-in landscape made of grass, rock, water, and so on, instead of separate parts.

examples.title: What am I standing on?
examples.code:
local character = script.Parent
local rootPart = character:WaitForChild("HumanoidRootPart")

local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.ExcludeInstances = { character } -- do not hit myself

while true do
	-- Shoot 10 studs straight down from my middle
	local result = workspace:Raycast(rootPart.Position, Vector3.new(0, -10, 0), params)

	if result then
		print("Standing on", result.Instance.Name)
		print("Material:", result.Material.Name)
		print("Floor is", result.Distance, "studs below me")
	else
		print("Nothing below me, I must be in the air!")
	end
	task.wait(2)
end
explain: The ray starts at the middle of the character and goes 10 studs straight down.
If it hits, result.Instance is the part (or Terrain) below.
result.Material tells you if it is Grass, Ice, Sand, and so on.
result.Distance is how far from the start of the ray to the hit point.
If nothing is within 10 studs, result is nil and we know the player is in the air.

examples.title: Pop a marker just above whatever you hit
examples.code:
local origin = Vector3.new(0, 50, 0)
local direction = Vector3.new(0, -100, 0) -- straight down, 100 studs

local result = workspace:Raycast(origin, direction)
if result then
	local marker = Instance.new("Part")
	marker.Shape = Enum.PartType.Ball
	marker.Size = Vector3.new(1, 1, 1)
	marker.Anchored = true
	marker.CanCollide = false
	-- Start at the hit point, then move half a stud out of the surface
	marker.Position = result.Position + result.Normal * 0.5
	marker.Parent = workspace
end
explain: The ray drops from 50 studs up and checks 100 studs down.
result.Position is the exact spot on the surface that was hit.
result.Normal points straight out of that surface, length 1. On a flat floor it is (0, 1, 0).
Adding result.Normal * 0.5 moves the ball half a stud away from the surface, so it sits on top instead of half buried. If the floor is at height 0, the ball ends up at height 0.5.

gotchas: Always check `if result then` before using it. A miss gives nil, and nil.Instance causes an error.
result.Instance can be Terrain, not just a Part. Check result.Instance:IsA("BasePart") or result.Instance == workspace.Terrain if it matters.

datatype/Rect.d:
Rect describes a rectangle on a 2D plane. It is constructed using two corners, either two Vector2 positions or four numbers:

local rect1 = Rect.new(Vector2.new(10, 10), Vector2.new(80, 80))
local rect2 = Rect.new(10, 10, 80, 80)

This data type is used in the ImageLabel.SliceCenter property which determines the center area of a scaled image.
datatype/Rect.s: A value that represents a two-dimensional rectangle.

m.d: The horizontal span of the rectangle, equal to Max.X - Min.X. This value is always non-negative because the constructor normalizes the input coordinates so that Min is component-wise less than or equal to Max. Defaults to 0 for a Rect created with no arguments.
m.s: The width of the **Rect**.

kid.simple: How wide the rectangle is: Max.X minus Min.X. Rect.new(10, 10, 80, 80) is 70 wide. Never negative.
kid.example:
local r = Rect.new(10, 20, 110, 70)
print(r.Width) --> 100

m.d: The vertical span of the rectangle, equal to Max.Y - Min.Y. This value is always non-negative because the constructor normalizes the input coordinates so that Min is component-wise less than or equal to Max. Defaults to 0 for a Rect created with no arguments.
m.s: The height of the **Rect**.

kid.simple: How tall the rectangle is: Max.Y minus Min.Y. Never negative.
kid.example:
local r = Rect.new(10, 20, 110, 70)
print(r.Height) --> 50

m.d: The top-left corner of the rectangle as a Vector2. When you construct a Rect with two positions, this property returns the component-wise minimum of those positions regardless of the order they were passed in. Defaults to (0, 0) for a Rect created with no arguments.
m.s: The coordinates of the top-left corner.

kid.simple: The top-left corner as a Vector2. It always has the smaller X and Y, even if you passed the corners in the other order.
kid.example:
local r = Rect.new(Vector2.new(80, 80), Vector2.new(10, 10)) -- backwards on purpose
print(r.Min) --> 10, 10

m.d: The bottom-right corner of the rectangle as a Vector2. When you construct a Rect with two positions, this property returns the component-wise maximum of those positions regardless of the order they were passed in. Defaults to (0, 0) for a Rect created with no arguments.
m.s: The coordinates of the bottom-right corner.

kid.simple: The bottom-right corner as a Vector2. It always has the bigger X and Y.
kid.example:
local r = Rect.new(10, 10, 80, 80)
print(r.Max) --> 80, 80

m.d: Constructs a new Rect with two zero Vector2 positions.
m.s: Returns a new **Rect** with zero `Datatype.Vector2` positions.

kid.simple: Makes a Rect. With nothing, both corners are (0, 0). With two Vector2s, they are the two corners. With four numbers, they are minX, minY, maxX, maxY.
kid.example:
local empty = Rect.new()                                   -- 0 by 0
local a = Rect.new(Vector2.new(10, 10), Vector2.new(80, 80))
local b = Rect.new(10, 10, 80, 80)                         -- same as a
print(a.Width, b.Height) --> 70 70

kid.simple: A Rect is a flat 2D rectangle, described by two corners: Min (top-left) and Max (bottom-right). It is mostly used in UI images, for example to say which middle part of an image is allowed to stretch (ImageLabel.SliceCenter).
kid.analogy: A Rect is like drawing a box on a piece of paper by putting one finger on the top-left corner and another on the bottom-right corner.
whenToUse: ImageLabel.SliceCenter or ImageButton.SliceCenter for 9-slice images that stretch without blurry corners
Storing a rectangle area in your own UI code
kid.where: Works in any script. Make one with Rect.new(), Rect.new(minVector2, maxVector2), or Rect.new(minX, minY, maxX, maxY).

terms.Vector2: Two numbers (X, Y) for a spot or size on a flat surface, like a screen or image.
terms.Min: The top-left corner (smallest X and smallest Y).
terms.Max: The bottom-right corner (biggest X and biggest Y). Remember, in 2D UI, Y gets bigger as you go DOWN.
terms.9-slice: A trick for stretching an image like a rounded button: the 4 corners stay the same size, the edges stretch one way, and the middle stretches both ways. SliceCenter says where the middle is.
terms.pixel: One tiny dot of an image or screen.

examples.title: A stretchy rounded panel with 9-slice
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local player = Players.LocalPlayer

local screenGui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
screenGui.Parent = player:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

local panel = Instance.new("ImageLabel")
panel.Size = UDim2.fromScale(0.4, 0.3)
panel.Position = UDim2.fromScale(0.3, 0.35)
panel.Image = "rbxassetid://0" -- replace 0 with your own 100 x 100 pixel image ID
panel.ScaleType = Enum.ScaleType.Slice
-- The middle area is from pixel (10, 10) to pixel (90, 90) of the image
panel.SliceCenter = Rect.new(10, 10, 90, 90)
panel.Parent = screenGui
explain: We make an ImageLabel and set ScaleType to Slice so it uses 9-slice stretching.
Rect.new(10, 10, 90, 90) says the middle of the image goes from (10, 10) to (90, 90).
So the 10-pixel border on each side (the corners and edges) does not get blurry when the panel grows.
Change the image ID to an image you uploaded.

gotchas: Rect is for flat 2D areas. For a 3D box, use Region3 or a CFrame and Size.
If you give the corners in the wrong order, Rect fixes it for you: Min is always the smaller numbers.
Rect values cannot be changed after they are made. Make a new one.

datatype/Region3.d:
The Region3 data type describes a volume in 3D space similar to an axis-aligned rectangular prism. It is commonly used with Terrain functions and functions that detect parts within a volume, such as WorldRoot:FindPartsInRegion3().

The prism's center is accessible using the Region3.CFrame property and the prism's size is accessible through the Region3.Size property. Note that the components of this property may be negative.

The Region3:ExpandToGrid() method returns a new Region3 whose bounds comply with a provided resolution value. The resulting volume may be equal to or greater than the original volume, but never smaller.

See also:

  • Region3int16
datatype/Region3.s: Describes a rectangular volume in 3D space.

m.d: The CFrame representing the center position and orientation of the Region3. The position component is the midpoint of the min and max vectors passed to Region3.new(), computed as (min + max) / 2. Because a Region3 is always axis-aligned, the rotation component of the returned CFrame is always the identity (no rotation). This property is read-only.
m.s: The center location and rotation of the `Datatype.Region3`.

kid.simple: The middle of the box (and a rotation, which is always none). The middle is halfway between the two corners. Corners (0, 0, 0) and (10, 20, 10) give a middle of (5, 10, 5). Read-only.
kid.example:
local region = Region3.new(Vector3.new(0, 0, 0), Vector3.new(10, 20, 10))
print(region.CFrame.Position) --> 5, 10, 5

m.d: The size of the Region3 as a Vector3, equal to max - min from the constructor arguments. Individual components may be negative if the corresponding component of min is greater than max in the call to Region3.new(). This property is read-only.
m.s: The 3D size of the `Datatype.Region3`.

kid.simple: How big the box is in X, Y, and Z, worked out as max corner minus min corner. Can be negative if the corners were given in the wrong order. Read-only.
kid.example:
local region = Region3.new(Vector3.new(0, 0, 0), Vector3.new(10, 20, 10))
print(region.Size) --> 10, 20, 10

m.d: Expands the Region3 based on the provided resolution and returns the expanded Region3 aligned to the Terrain voxel grid.
m.s: Expands the `Datatype.Region3` to fit a grid based on the provided resolution.

p.s: The grid resolution to align the region bounds to, in studs. Must be a positive number.

r.s: A new Region3 whose minimum bounds are floored and maximum bounds are ceiled to the nearest multiple of resolution.

kid.simple: Gives a new Region3 grown outward so its corners land on a grid of the size you pick. The low corner rounds down and the high corner rounds up, so the box can only get bigger, never smaller. Used before Terrain functions, which need a 4-stud grid.
kid.example:
local region = Region3.new(Vector3.new(1, 1, 1), Vector3.new(6, 6, 6))
local snapped = region:ExpandToGrid(4)
print(snapped.Size) --> 8, 8, 8 (corners became 0 and 8)

m.d:
Returns a new Region3 given the Vector3 bounds of the rectangular prism volume.

Note that the order of the provided bounds matters: by switching them, the polarity of the size components will switch. It is possible to create a Region3 with a negative volume.
m.s: Returns a new `Datatype.Region3` using the provided vectors as boundaries.

p.s: The lower corner of the rectangular volume.
The upper corner of the rectangular volume.

kid.simple: Makes a Region3 box from two corners: min (the low corner) and max (the high corner).
kid.example:
local region = Region3.new(Vector3.new(-5, 0, -5), Vector3.new(5, 10, 5))
print(region.Size) --> 10, 10, 10
kid.gotcha: Order matters. Region3.new(high, low) gives a negative size.

kid.simple: A Region3 is an invisible 3D box in the world, described by two opposite corners. Its sides always line up with the world's X, Y, and Z directions, so it can never be tilted. It is mostly used with Terrain, for example to fill an area with grass or water.
kid.analogy: A Region3 is like a shoebox you place in the world by saying where two opposite corners go. The box is always sitting straight, never tipped over.
whenToUse: Filling an area with Terrain using workspace.Terrain:FillRegion
Reading or clearing Terrain in an area
Describing a simple straight box zone
kid.where: Works in any script. Make one with Region3.new(minCorner, maxCorner). For finding parts in a box, the newer workspace:GetPartBoundsInBox (with OverlapParams) is usually a better choice.

terms.axis-aligned: The box's edges point exactly along X, Y, and Z. It cannot be rotated.
terms.min corner: The corner with the smallest X, Y, and Z numbers (bottom, left, back).
terms.max corner: The corner with the biggest X, Y, and Z numbers (top, right, front).
terms.CFrame: A position plus a rotation. For a Region3 the rotation is always none.
terms.voxel: A tiny 3D cube that Terrain is built from, like a pixel but in 3D. Roblox Terrain voxels are 4 studs on each side.
terms.resolution: The size of the grid squares to line up with, in studs. Terrain usually uses 4.
terms.Vector3: Three numbers (X, Y, Z) that describe a position or size in the 3D world.

examples.title: Make a patch of grass terrain
examples.code:
local Terrain = workspace.Terrain

-- A box from (0, 0, 0) to (16, 8, 16)
local region = Region3.new(Vector3.new(0, 0, 0), Vector3.new(16, 8, 16))

-- Line it up with the 4-stud terrain grid
region = region:ExpandToGrid(4)

-- Fill it with grass, using 4-stud voxels
Terrain:FillRegion(region, 4, Enum.Material.Grass)

print(region.CFrame.Position) --> 8, 4, 8 (the middle of the box)
print(region.Size)            --> 16, 8, 16
explain: Region3.new takes the low corner (0, 0, 0) and the high corner (16, 8, 16).
ExpandToGrid(4) makes sure the corners sit on multiples of 4, which Terrain needs. These corners already do, so nothing changes here.
FillRegion fills the box with Grass terrain.
The middle of the box is halfway between the corners: (8, 4, 8). The size is high corner minus low corner: (16, 8, 16).

gotchas: Give the low corner first and the high corner second. Swapping them makes a box with negative size.
A Region3 cannot be rotated. For a tilted box, use workspace:GetPartBoundsInBox with a CFrame instead.
Terrain functions like FillRegion need the region lined up with the 4-stud grid. Use ExpandToGrid(4) first.

datatype/Region3int16.d:
Not to be confused with Region3, a separate class that fulfills a different purpose.

The Region3int16 data type represents a volume in 3D space similar to an axis-aligned rectangular prism. It uses two Vector3int16 to store the volume's bounds in the Min and Max properties. It is constructed using Region3int16.new(Min, Max), given the two Vector3int16 bounds. This data type features no functions or operations.

Calculating Center and Size

This data type differs from Region3 in that it stores its bounds directly, rather than through a center and size combination. Nonetheless, it is possible to calculate these dimensions using Min and Max:

local region = Region3int16.new(Vector3int16.new(0, 0, -3), Vector3int16.new(4, 4, 4))
local size = region.Max - region.Min
local center = (region.Max + region.Min) / 2

Conversion to Region3

The following function can be used to convert a Region3int16 into a similar Region3. It does this by converting the Min and Max properties, which are Vector3int16, into Vector3 used with Region3.new().

local function Region3int16toRegion3(region16)
    return Region3.new(
        Vector3.new(region16.Min.X, region16.Min.Y, region16.Min.Z),
        Vector3.new(region16.Max.X, region16.Max.Y, region16.Max.Z)
    )
end

See also:

  • Region3, a similar data type
datatype/Region3int16.s: Represents a Region3 stored as two boundaries as opposed to position and size components.

m.d: The lower bound of the Region3int16, as passed to Region3int16.new().
m.s: The lower bound of the `Datatype.Region3int16`.

m.d: The upper bound of the Region3int16, as passed to Region3int16.new().
m.s: The upper bound of the `Datatype.Region3int16`.

m.d: Returns a new Region3int16 from the provided boundaries.
m.s: Returns a new Region3int16 from the provided boundaries.

p.s: The lower bound of the region.
The upper bound of the region.

datatype/RotationCurveKey.d:
A time-value pair used with RotationCurve instances.

The Interpolation property dictates the interpolation mode for the segment started by this key and ended by the next key on the curve. Each segment may use a different interpolation mode.

The LeftTangent and RightTangent properties apply to the cubic interpolation mode and define the desired tangent (slope) at the key. Different left and right values can be used to encode discontinuities in slope at the key. Attempting to set a RightTangent value on a key that doesn't use the cubic interpolation mode will result in a runtime error. It is possible to set the LeftTangent property on any key, as it will be used should the preceding segment use cubic interpolation.
datatype/RotationCurveKey.s: A time-value pair used with `Class.RotationCurve` instances.

m.d:
Defines the interpolation mode used for the curve segment that begins at this key and ends at the next key. Possible values are KeyInterpolationMode.Constant (holds the key's value until the next key), KeyInterpolationMode.Linear (linearly interpolates between this key and the next using spherical linear interpolation), and KeyInterpolationMode.Cubic (uses a cubic hermite spline shaped by RightTangent and the next key's LeftTangent). Defaults to KeyInterpolationMode.Cubic.

Setting this property to a non-cubic mode automatically clears RightTangent (because tangent slope is only meaningful in cubic segments).
m.s: The key interpolation mode for the segment started by this `Datatype.RotationCurveKey`.

m.d: The time position of this RotationCurveKey along the curve's timeline, in seconds. Keys within a RotationCurve are kept sorted by ascending time; inserting a key at the same time as an existing key replaces the existing key. Defaults to 0.
m.s: The time position of this `Datatype.RotationCurveKey`.

m.d: The rotation stored at this key, represented as a CFrame. Only the rotational component of the CFrame is used; the positional component is ignored. Defaults to CFrame.identity.
m.s: The `Datatype.CFrame` value of this `Datatype.RotationCurveKey`.

m.d: The outgoing tangent (slope) at this key, controlling the shape of the cubic segment that extends toward the next key. Defaults to 0. This property can only be set when Interpolation is KeyInterpolationMode.Cubic; attempting to set it on a key with a different interpolation mode raises a runtime error. Returns nil if the tangent has not been explicitly assigned.
m.s: The tangent to the right of this `Datatype.RotationCurveKey`.

m.d: The incoming tangent (slope) at this key, controlling the shape of the cubic segment arriving from the previous key. Defaults to 0. Unlike RightTangent, this property can be set on a key regardless of its own interpolation mode, because the preceding segment may use cubic interpolation and needs a defined slope at its endpoint. Returns nil if the tangent has not been explicitly assigned.
m.s: The tangent to the left of this `Datatype.RotationCurveKey`.

m.d: Creates a new RotationCurveKey at a given time with a given CFrame. LeftTangent and RightTangent are left uninitialized and, if not initialized, tangent values of 0 will be used when evaluating the curve.
m.s: Returns a new `Datatype.RotationCurveKey` at a given time with a given `Datatype.CFrame`.

p.s: Time at which to create the new RotationCurveKey.
CFrame of the new RotationCurveKey.
The interpolation mode for the segment started by this key. Defaults to KeyInterpolationMode.Cubic.

datatype/Secret.d: The Secret data type stores the secret content returned by HttpService:GetSecret(). It cannot be printed or logged, but can be modified using built-in functions:

m.d: Returns a secret formed by concatenating the supplied string to the secret content, for example prepending "Bearer" to the API key.
m.s: Prepends a string to the secret content.

p.s: The string to prepend to the secret content.

r.s: A new Secret with the prefix prepended to the original secret value.

m.d: Returns a secret formed by concatenating the original secret and the supplied string parameter. Useful when creating a URL containing a key and query parameters.
m.s: Appends a string to the secret content.

p.s: The string to append to the secret content.

r.s: A new Secret with the suffix appended to the original secret value.

datatype/SecurityCapabilities.d:
An immutable set of SecurityCapability values that controls which engine APIs and actions a script inside a sandboxed container can access. Assign a SecurityCapabilities value to an instance's Capabilities property to restrict the scripts beneath it.

Capability enforcement takes effect when Workspace.SandboxedInstanceMode is set to SandboxedInstanceMode.Experimental.

m.d: Returns a new set of capabilities with zero or more additions. If you add SecurityCapability items that are already present, they are not duplicated.
m.s: Returns a new set of capabilities with zero or more additions.

p.s: Zero or more SecurityCapability values to add to the set.

r.s: A new set containing the union of the original capabilities and the specified additions.

m.d: Returns a new set of capabilities with zero or more deletions. SecurityCapability items not present in the original set are ignored.
m.s: Returns a new set of capabilities with zero or more deletions.

p.s: Zero or more SecurityCapability values to remove from the set.

r.s: A new set with the specified capabilities removed.

m.d: Returns whether a set of capabilities contains the specified SecurityCapability items. The set must contain all provided items to return true.
m.s: Returns whether a set of capabilities contains the specified `Enum.SecurityCapability` items.

p.s: Zero or more SecurityCapability values to check for membership in the set.

m.d:
Returns a new set of capabilities from zero or more SecurityCapability items.

local capabilities = SecurityCapabilities.new(Enum.SecurityCapability.Players,
    Enum.SecurityCapability.Animation,
    Enum.SecurityCapability.Basic)

local newScript = Instance.new("Script")
newScript.Capabilities = capabilities
m.s: Returns a new set of capabilities from zero or more `Enum.SecurityCapability` items.

p.s: Zero or more SecurityCapability values to include in the new set.

m.d: Returns a new set of capabilities from the capabilities of the calling function.
m.s: Returns a new set of capabilities from the capabilities of the calling function.

datatype/SharedTable.d:
Represents a table-like data structure that can be shared across execution contexts. While it can be used for various sorts of general data storage, it is designed especially for use with Parallel Luau, where it can be used to share state across scripts parented under different Actor instances.

There are a couple idiomatic ways to communicate shared tables between scripts. One method is to store and retrieve SharedTable objects in the SharedTableRegistry. The registry lets any script in the same data model get or set a SharedTable by name. Another method is to use Actor:SendMessage() to send a shared table to another Actor inside a message.

Like a Luau table, a SharedTable object stores a set of key-value element pairs. Unlike a Luau table, only selected types of objects may be stored in a SharedTable, similar to other restrictions you'll find elsewhere in the Roblox Engine.

Keys must either be (1) a string or (2) a nonnegative integer number less than 232. Other kinds of keys are not supported.

Values must have one of the following types: Boolean, Number, Vector, String, SharedTable, or a serializable data type. The ability to store a SharedTable as a value in another SharedTable permits the construction of nested and recursive data structures.

SharedTable objects are distinct and different SharedTable objects never compare equal, even if they have contents that would compare equal.

Like a Luau table, a SharedTable object may be frozen, in which case it is read-only. An attempt to modify a frozen SharedTable will raise an error. A frozen SharedTable can be created by first creating a (non-frozen, modifiable) SharedTable with the desired contents, and then calling SharedTable.cloneAndFreeze() to create a frozen clone of it.
datatype/SharedTable.s: Provides sharable, table-like storage for key/value pairs.

m.d:
Returns a new, empty SharedTable.

local st = SharedTable.new()
m.s: Returns a new, empty `Datatype.SharedTable`.

m.d:
Atomically removes all of the elements from a SharedTable.

If the SharedTable is frozen, the operation fails and an error will be raised.

local st = SharedTable.new({"a", "b", "c"})
assert(SharedTable.size(st) == 3)

SharedTable.clear(st)
assert(SharedTable.size(st) == 0)
m.s: Removes all of the elements from the `Datatype.SharedTable`.

p.s: The SharedTable to clear.

m.d:
Creates a clone of a SharedTable and returns the clone.

If the optional deep argument is not present, or if it is present and its value is false, then a shallow clone is created. A shallow clone copies only the top-level SharedTable object. If any value in the SharedTable itself is a SharedTable, then both the original SharedTable and the clone SharedTable will refer to the same SharedTable.

The shallow clone operation is atomic, so the clone SharedTable will contain a consistent snapshot of the state in the original SharedTable, even if it is being modified concurrently from other scripts.

If the optional deep argument is present and its value is true, then a deep clone is created. A deep clone recursively copies a structure of SharedTable objects, such that there is no state shared between the original SharedTable and the clone.

The clone of each SharedTable within the graph of SharedTable objects is atomic, but the deep clone as a whole is not atomic. Thus, the clone of each SharedTable within the graph will contain a consistent snapshot of the state of the original SharedTable object from which it was cloned, but the states of different SharedTable objects may be inconsistent if the graph is being modified concurrently from other scripts.

The SharedTable object(s) being cloned may be frozen (read-only) or not. Regardless, the newly created clones are not frozen (and are thus modifiable). To create frozen clones, use the SharedTable.cloneAndFreeze function.

To illustrate the difference between a shallow clone and a deep clone, consider the following samples. This first sample creates a shallow clone and the second creates a deep clone.
m.s: Creates and returns a clone of the provided `Datatype.SharedTable`.

p.s: The SharedTable object to clone.
Whether to create a deep clone (true) or a shallow clone (false).

m.d:
Creates a frozen (read-only) clone of a SharedTable and returns the clone. The behavior of this function is the same as the behavior of clone, except that the clone is frozen.

If a deep clone is requested, then all of the cloned SharedTable objects are frozen.
m.s: Creates and returns a frozen (read-only) clone of the provided `Datatype.SharedTable`.

p.s: The SharedTable object to clone.
Whether to create a deep clone (true) or a shallow clone (false).

m.d:
Atomically increments the value of an element. An element with the specified key must exist in the SharedTable, and it must be of type number. The specified delta is added to the value, and the original value is returned.

The SharedTable.update function can also be used for this purpose; this increment function exists for convenience and performance (in general, increment is much faster than update, so it should be preferred where possible). The following two function calls have the same effect:

local st = SharedTable.new()
st["x"] = 1

local oldValue = SharedTable.increment(st, "x", 1)

SharedTable.update(st, "x", function(v)
    oldValue = v
    return v + 1
end)

If the SharedTable is frozen, the operation fails and an error will be raised.
m.s: Adds `delta` to the value with the provided key and returns the original value.

p.s: The SharedTable object to be updated.
The key of the element in the SharedTable object to be updated.
The value to be added to the element in the SharedTable.

r.s: The original value of the element, before delta was added to it.

m.d:
Returns true if the SharedTable is frozen (read-only).

local st1 = SharedTable.new({"a", "b", "c"})
assert(not SharedTable.isFrozen(st1))

local st2 = SharedTable.cloneAndFreeze(st1)
assert(SharedTable.isFrozen(st2))
m.s: Returns `true` if the `Datatype.SharedTable` is frozen (read-only).

p.s: The SharedTable object whose frozen state is to be queried.

m.d:
Returns the number of elements stored in the SharedTable. Note that if other scripts are concurrently modifying the SharedTable, the returned size may no longer be correct after it is returned, since other scripts may have added or removed elements from the SharedTable.

local st = SharedTable.new({"a", "b", "c"})
assert(SharedTable.size(st) == 3)

st[2] = nil
assert(SharedTable.size(st) == 2)
m.s: Returns the number of elements stored in the `Datatype.SharedTable`.

p.s: The SharedTable object whose size is to be queried.

m.d:
Atomically updates the value of an element.

When a SharedTable is accessed concurrently from scripts running in different execution contexts, it is possible for their accesses to interleave unpredictably. Because of this, code like the following is generally incorrect, because the value may have changed between the read on the first line and the update on the second line:

local st = SharedTable.new({ x = "a" })
local oldValue = st["x"]
st["x"] = oldValue .. ",x"
print(st["x"]) --> a,x

The update function makes it possible to perform an atomic update to an element. It takes a function that it will call with the current value of the element. The function can then compute and return the new value. Note that the function may be called multiple times if the SharedTable is being concurrently modified from other scripts.

If the SharedTable is frozen, the operation fails and an error will be raised.
m.s: Updates the value with the provided key via the provided update function.

p.s: The SharedTable object to be updated.
The key of the element in the SharedTable object to be updated.
The function that will be called to compute the new value for the element.

datatype/TweenInfo.d: The TweenInfo data type stores parameters for TweenService:Create() to specify the behavior of the tween. The properties of a TweenInfo cannot be written to after its creation.

m.d: The direction in which the tween executes.
m.s: The direction in which the tween executes.

kid.simple: Which end of the tween the easing style happens at. In puts the effect at the start, Out at the end (the default), and InOut at both ends. Example: Bounce with Out bounces when it lands. Read-only.
kid.example:
local info = TweenInfo.new(1, Enum.EasingStyle.Bounce, Enum.EasingDirection.Out)
print(info.EasingDirection) --> Enum.EasingDirection.Out

m.d: Duration of the tween, in seconds.
m.s: Duration of the tween, in seconds.

kid.simple: How many seconds one play of the tween takes. Time 2 means the part takes 2 seconds to reach its goal. Read-only.
kid.example:
local info = TweenInfo.new(2)
print(info.Time) --> 2

m.d: Time of delay until the tween begins, in seconds.
m.s: Time of delay until the tween begins, in seconds.

kid.simple: How many seconds to wait after tween:Play() before the movement actually starts. Read-only.
kid.example:
local info = TweenInfo.new(1, Enum.EasingStyle.Quad, Enum.EasingDirection.Out, 0, false, 3)
print(info.DelayTime) --> 3 (waits 3 seconds first)

m.d: Number of times the tween repeats. -1 indicates indefinite repetition.
m.s: Number of times the tween repeats.

kid.simple: How many extra times the tween repeats after the first play. 0 plays once, 3 plays 4 times in total, -1 repeats forever. Read-only.
kid.example:
local info = TweenInfo.new(1, Enum.EasingStyle.Linear, Enum.EasingDirection.Out, -1)
print(info.RepeatCount) --> -1 (forever)

m.d: The style in which the tween executes.
m.s: The style in which the tween executes.

kid.simple: The shape of the motion. Linear is a steady speed. Sine and Quad are smooth. Back overshoots a little. Bounce bounces at the end. Elastic wobbles like a rubber band. Read-only.
kid.example:
local info = TweenInfo.new(1, Enum.EasingStyle.Elastic)
print(info.EasingStyle) --> Enum.EasingStyle.Elastic

m.d: Whether or not the tween interpolates in reverse tween once the initial tween completes.
m.s: Whether or not the tween interpolates in reverse tween once the initial tween completes.

kid.simple: If true, once the tween reaches its goal it plays backwards to where it started, like a door that opens and then closes. Read-only.
kid.example:
local info = TweenInfo.new(1, Enum.EasingStyle.Quad, Enum.EasingDirection.Out, 0, true)
print(info.Reverses) --> true

m.d: Creates a new TweenInfo from the provided parameters. This constructor raises an error if easingStyle is EasingStyle.Bezier or EasingStyle.Spring.
m.s: Creates a new `Datatype.TweenInfo` from the provided parameters.

p.s: Duration for the tween, in seconds.
Easing style for the tween.
The direction in which the tween executes.
Number of times the tween should repeat. -1 repeats indefinitely.
Whether the tween should reverse to the starting values once it reaches its targets.
Time of delay until the tween begins, in seconds.

kid.simple: Makes a new TweenInfo. All six settings are optional and go in this order: time (seconds, default 1), easingStyle (default Quad), easingDirection (default Out), repeatCount (default 0, -1 for forever), reverses (default false), delayTime (seconds, default 0).
kid.example:
-- Every setting, one by one
local info = TweenInfo.new(
	1.5,                       -- takes 1.5 seconds
	Enum.EasingStyle.Bounce,   -- bouncy motion
	Enum.EasingDirection.Out,  -- the bounce happens at the end
	2,                         -- repeat 2 more times
	false,                     -- do not play backwards
	1                          -- wait 1 second before starting
)
local simple = TweenInfo.new(0.5) -- just a half-second tween, defaults for the rest
kid.gotcha: Passing Enum.EasingStyle.Bezier or Enum.EasingStyle.Spring throws an error.

kid.simple: A TweenInfo is the instruction card for a tween. A tween is a smooth animation that slides a property (like a part's position, size, or color) from where it is now to a new value. TweenInfo says how long it takes, what style of motion to use, how many times to repeat, whether to go back, and how long to wait before starting.
kid.analogy: TweenInfo is like the settings on a playground swing ride: how long one swing takes, whether it starts slow or fast, how many times it swings, whether it swings back, and how long you wait before it starts. The ride (the tween) follows the card.
whenToUse: Making a door slide open smoothly
Making a platform float up and down forever
Fading a part or UI in and out
Making a menu slide onto the screen
kid.where: Works in any script. Make one with TweenInfo.new(...) and give it to TweenService:Create(object, tweenInfo, goals). Get TweenService with game:GetService("TweenService").

terms.tween: A smooth change of a property from one value to another over time, made by TweenService. Short for "in-between".
terms.easing: How the speed changes during the tween. Linear moves at the same speed the whole time. Others start slow, end slow, bounce, or overshoot.
terms.EasingStyle: The shape of the motion, like Linear, Sine, Quad, Back, Bounce, or Elastic.
terms.EasingDirection: Which end the easing style happens at: In (at the start), Out (at the end), or InOut (both ends).
terms.Enum: A fixed list of named choices Roblox gives you, like Enum.EasingStyle.Bounce.
terms.TweenService: The Roblox service that creates and plays tweens.
terms.read-only: You can look at the value but not change it. To change TweenInfo settings, make a new TweenInfo.

examples.title: A floating platform that bobs up and down forever
examples.code:
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")

-- Make the platform
local platform = Instance.new("Part")
platform.Size = Vector3.new(8, 1, 8)
platform.Anchored = true -- tweens work best on anchored parts
platform.Position = Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)
platform.Parent = workspace

local tweenInfo = TweenInfo.new(
	2,                          -- time: each trip takes 2 seconds
	Enum.EasingStyle.Sine,      -- easingStyle: smooth, gentle curve
	Enum.EasingDirection.InOut, -- easingDirection: slow at start AND end
	-1,                         -- repeatCount: -1 means repeat forever
	true,                       -- reverses: come back down after going up
	0.5                         -- delayTime: wait half a second before starting
)

-- Goal: move up to a height of 15
local goal = { Position = Vector3.new(0, 15, 0) }
local tween = TweenService:Create(platform, tweenInfo, goal)
tween:Play()
explain: time = 2: going from height 5 to height 15 takes 2 seconds.
easingStyle = Sine: the motion follows a soft wave shape instead of a stiff straight line.
easingDirection = InOut: it eases in at the start and out at the end, so it speeds up gently and slows down gently.
repeatCount = -1: it never stops repeating. A number like 3 would repeat 3 more times after the first play.
reverses = true: after reaching the goal it plays backwards to where it started, so the platform comes back down.
delayTime = 0.5: it waits half a second before it begins moving.
TweenService:Create builds the tween from the part, the TweenInfo, and a table of goal values. tween:Play() starts it.

examples.title: Slide a menu onto the screen
examples.place: LocalScript in StarterGui (with a ScreenGui that has a Frame named Menu)
examples.code:
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")
local menu = playerGui:WaitForChild("ScreenGui"):WaitForChild("Menu")

-- Start off-screen to the left
menu.Position = UDim2.fromScale(-0.5, 0.25)

-- Only time and style given; the rest use their defaults
local tweenInfo = TweenInfo.new(0.6, Enum.EasingStyle.Back)

local tween = TweenService:Create(menu, tweenInfo, {
	Position = UDim2.fromScale(0.25, 0.25),
})
tween:Play()
explain: The menu starts at X Scale -0.5, which is off the left side of the screen.
TweenInfo.new(0.6, Enum.EasingStyle.Back) lasts 0.6 seconds and uses Back, which overshoots a tiny bit and then settles, like a spring.
Things you leave out use defaults: direction Out, repeat 0, reverses false, delay 0.
The tween slides the menu to X Scale 0.25 so it lands on screen.

gotchas: You cannot change a TweenInfo after making it. If you need a different time, make a new TweenInfo.
The order of the six settings matters: time, easingStyle, easingDirection, repeatCount, reverses, delayTime.
RepeatCount 0 means play once (no extra repeats). -1 means forever. A forever tween runs until you call tween:Cancel().
Enum.EasingStyle.Bezier and Enum.EasingStyle.Spring cause an error in TweenInfo.new.
If physics is moving a part (it is not Anchored), physics and the tween fight. Anchor parts you tween.

datatype/UDim.d:
The UDim data type represents a one-dimensional value with two components: a relative scale and an absolute offset in logical pixels. At evaluation time, the engine computes the final pixel value as Scale * referenceMeasurement + Offset, where the reference measurement is typically the size of a parent GuiObject along the corresponding axis.

UDim values appear individually in properties such as UICorner.CornerRadius, UIPadding.PaddingTop, and UIStroke.Thickness, or paired as a UDim2 for two-dimensional sizing and positioning.

-- 50% of the parent plus 10 extra logical pixels
local dimension = UDim.new(0.5, 10)
datatype/UDim.s: Represents a one-dimensional value with two components, a relative scale and an absolute offset.

m.d: The relative scale component of the UDim, expressed as a fraction of a reference measurement (typically the corresponding axis of a parent GuiObject). A value of 1 represents the full reference measurement, 0.5 represents half, and 0 means the scale contributes nothing to the resolved pixel value. Defaults to 0 when not specified in the constructor. This property is read-only.
m.s: The relative scale component of the `Datatype.UDim`.

kid.simple: The fraction part of the UDim. 1 means the whole parent size, 0.5 means half, 0 means this part adds nothing. On a 1000-pixel parent, Scale 0.25 = 250 pixels. It is read-only.
kid.example:
local size = UDim.new(0.25, 0)
print(size.Scale) --> 0.25 (a quarter of the parent)

m.d: The absolute offset component of the UDim in pixels. This value is added to the resolved scale portion (Scale * referenceMeasurement) to produce the final pixel measurement. The offset is stored as an integer. Defaults to 0 when not specified in the constructor. This property is read-only.
m.s: The absolute offset component of the `Datatype.UDim`.

kid.simple: The exact-pixels part of the UDim. It is added after the Scale part is worked out. Offset 20 is always 20 pixels, no matter the screen. It is read-only.
kid.example:
local size = UDim.new(0.5, 20)
print(size.Offset) --> 20 (always 20 pixels extra)

m.d:
Returns a new UDim from the given Scale and Offset components. Both parameters are optional and default to 0 when omitted; calling UDim.new() with no arguments produces a UDim equivalent to UDim.new(0, 0).

local fullScale = UDim.new(1, 0)    -- 100% of parent, no pixel offset
local fixedPixels = UDim.new(0, 200) -- 0% scale, 200 pixel offset
local mixed = UDim.new(0.5, 20)      -- 50% of parent plus 20 pixels
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.UDim` from the given components.

p.s: The relative scale component, expressed as a fraction of the reference measurement (for example, 0.5 for 50% of the parent size along the corresponding axis). Defaults to 0.
The absolute pixel offset added after the scale is applied. Stored as an integer. Defaults to 0.

kid.simple: Makes a new UDim from a Scale (fraction of the parent) and an Offset (exact pixels). Both are optional and start at 0, so UDim.new() is the same as UDim.new(0, 0).
kid.example:
local full = UDim.new(1, 0)    -- all of the parent, no extra pixels
local fixed = UDim.new(0, 200) -- always 200 pixels
local mixed = UDim.new(0.5, 20) -- half the parent, plus 20 pixels
print(mixed) --> 0.5, 20
kid.gotcha: The order is Scale first, then Offset. UDim.new(20, 0.5) means 20 times the parent plus 0 pixels, which is huge.

m.d: Produces a UDim whose Scale is the sum of the two operands' scales and whose Offset is the sum of their offsets. Each component is added independently: UDim.new(a.Scale + b.Scale, a.Offset + b.Offset).
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.UDim` representing the sum of the two `Datatype.UDim` values.

kid.simple: Adds two UDims. The Scales are added together and the Offsets are added together, separately. UDim.new(0.5, 10) + UDim.new(0.25, 5) gives UDim.new(0.75, 15).
kid.example:
local a = UDim.new(0.5, 10)
local b = UDim.new(0.25, 5)
print(a + b) --> 0.75, 15

m.d: Produces a UDim whose Scale is the difference of the two operands' scales and whose Offset is the difference of their offsets. Each component is subtracted independently: UDim.new(a.Scale - b.Scale, a.Offset - b.Offset).
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.UDim` representing the difference between the two `Datatype.UDim` values.

kid.simple: Subtracts one UDim from another. Scale minus Scale, and Offset minus Offset, separately. UDim.new(1, 0) - UDim.new(0, 20) gives UDim.new(1, -20), which means "the whole parent, minus 20 pixels".
kid.example:
local full = UDim.new(1, 0)
local margin = UDim.new(0, 20)
print(full - margin) --> 1, -20 (whole parent minus 20 pixels)

kid.simple: A UDim is one measurement for on-screen UI, like a width, a height, or how round a corner is. It is made of two numbers: a Scale (a fraction of the parent's size) and an Offset (exact pixels). Roblox adds them together to get the final size in pixels. Two UDims together make a UDim2, which is what you use for Size and Position.
kid.analogy: A UDim is like saying how much pizza you want as "half the pizza plus 2 extra bites". The half part (Scale) depends on how big the pizza is. The 2 bites part (Offset) is always the same.
whenToUse: Setting how round corners are with UICorner.CornerRadius
Setting space inside a frame with UIPadding (PaddingTop, PaddingLeft, and so on)
Setting space between items with UIListLayout.Padding
Reading one axis (X or Y) out of a UDim2
kid.where: Works in any script (Script, LocalScript, or ModuleScript). Make one with UDim.new(scale, offset). UI usually runs in LocalScripts because each player has their own screen.

terms.Scale: A fraction of the parent's size. 0 means nothing, 0.5 means half, 1 means all of it. On a screen 1000 pixels wide, Scale 0.5 = 500 pixels. On a phone 400 pixels wide, the same Scale 0.5 = 200 pixels. It grows and shrinks with the screen.
terms.Offset: An exact number of pixels that never changes. Offset 20 is always 20 pixels, on a giant monitor or a tiny phone.
terms.pixel: One tiny dot on the screen. A normal computer screen is around 1920 pixels wide; a phone held sideways might be around 800.
terms.parent: The thing a UI object sits inside. For a Frame directly inside a ScreenGui, the parent is the whole screen. For a button inside a Frame, the parent is that Frame.
terms.GuiObject: Any 2D thing you can see on the screen in Roblox UI, like a Frame, TextLabel, TextButton, or ImageLabel.
terms.read-only: You can look at the value but you cannot change it directly. To get a different value, make a new one.
terms.final pixel value: The real size Roblox draws. It is worked out as Scale x (parent size) + Offset. Example: UDim.new(0.5, 10) inside a 400-pixel-wide parent = 0.5 x 400 + 10 = 210 pixels.
terms.UICorner: An object you put inside a Frame or button to round its corners.
terms.UIPadding: An object you put inside a Frame to add empty space between its edges and the things inside it.

examples.title: Round the corners of a button
examples.place: LocalScript in StarterGui (with a ScreenGui that has a TextButton named PlayButton)
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local player = Players.LocalPlayer
local playerGui = player:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

-- Find the button (change these names to match your game)
local screenGui = playerGui:WaitForChild("ScreenGui")
local button = screenGui:WaitForChild("PlayButton")

-- Make a UICorner and put it inside the button
local corner = Instance.new("UICorner")
corner.CornerRadius = UDim.new(0, 12) -- 0 scale, 12 pixels: always 12 pixels round
corner.Parent = button
explain: We get the LocalPlayer and wait for their PlayerGui, which is where their screen UI lives.
We find the ScreenGui and the button inside it.
UDim.new(0, 12) means Scale 0 (no fraction) and Offset 12 (exactly 12 pixels).
Putting the UICorner inside the button makes its corners round by 12 pixels on every device.

examples.title: See how Scale and Offset add up
examples.code:
local width = UDim.new(0.5, 10) -- half the parent, plus 10 pixels

-- Pretend the parent is 1000 pixels wide
local parentWidth = 1000
local pixels = width.Scale * parentWidth + width.Offset
print(pixels) --> 510

-- Now pretend the parent is a small phone, 400 pixels wide
parentWidth = 400
pixels = width.Scale * parentWidth + width.Offset
print(pixels) --> 210
explain: Scale 0.5 means half of the parent. Offset 10 means 10 more pixels.
On a 1000-pixel parent: 0.5 x 1000 = 500, plus 10 = 510 pixels.
On a 400-pixel parent: 0.5 x 400 = 200, plus 10 = 210 pixels.
The Scale part changed with the size. The Offset part (10) stayed the same.

gotchas: Scale is a fraction, not a percent. Use 0.5 for half, not 50. UDim.new(50, 0) would be 50 times the parent size.
Offset is always a whole number of pixels. UDim.new(0, 10.7) stores 10, not 10.7.
You cannot change .Scale or .Offset after making a UDim. Make a new one with UDim.new instead.

datatype/UDim2.d:
The UDim2 data type represents a two-dimensional value where each dimension is composed of a relative scale and an absolute offset in logical pixels. It is a combination of two UDim data types representing the X and Y dimensions. The most common usages for UDim2 are setting the Size and Position of GuiObjects.

local guiObject = Instance.new("Frame")
guiObject.Size = UDim2.new(0, 300, 1, 0)  -- 300 logical pixels wide; full height of parent
guiObject.Position = UDim2.new(0, 50, 0, 0)  -- 50 logical pixels from the left
print(guiObject.Size) --> {0, 300}, {1, 0}
datatype/UDim2.s: Represents a two-dimensional value where each dimension is composed of a relative scale and an absolute offset.

m.d:
The UDim component for the horizontal axis. The returned UDim has a .Scale (relative fraction) and .Offset (absolute logical pixels). This property is equivalent to UDim2.Width.

local pos = UDim2.new(0.5, 10, 1, 0)
print(pos.X.Scale)   -- 0.5
print(pos.X.Offset)  -- 10
m.s: The **X** dimension scale and offset of the `Datatype.UDim2`.

kid.simple: The left-to-right part of the UDim2, as a UDim with its own .Scale and .Offset. Same as UDim2.Width.
kid.example:
local pos = UDim2.new(0.5, 10, 1, 0)
print(pos.X.Scale)  --> 0.5
print(pos.X.Offset) --> 10

m.d:
The UDim component for the vertical axis. The returned UDim has a .Scale (relative fraction) and .Offset (absolute logical pixels). This property is equivalent to UDim2.Height.

local pos = UDim2.new(0.5, 10, 1, 0)
print(pos.Y.Scale)   -- 1
print(pos.Y.Offset)  -- 0
m.s: The **Y** dimension scale and offset of the `Datatype.UDim2`.

kid.simple: The top-to-bottom part of the UDim2, as a UDim with its own .Scale and .Offset. Same as UDim2.Height.
kid.example:
local pos = UDim2.new(0.5, 10, 1, 0)
print(pos.Y.Scale)  --> 1
print(pos.Y.Offset) --> 0

m.d: A synonym for UDim2.X. Returns the UDim component for the horizontal axis, containing both .Scale and .Offset.
m.s: The **X** dimension scale and offset of the `Datatype.UDim2`.

kid.simple: Another name for UDim2.X. It reads nicely when the UDim2 is a Size, like frame.Size.Width.
kid.example:
local size = UDim2.new(0.3, 0, 0, 40)
print(size.Width.Scale) --> 0.3 (same as size.X.Scale)

m.d: A synonym for UDim2.Y. Returns the UDim component for the vertical axis, containing both .Scale and .Offset.
m.s: The **Y** dimension scale and offset of the `Datatype.UDim2`.

kid.simple: Another name for UDim2.Y. It reads nicely when the UDim2 is a Size, like frame.Size.Height.
kid.example:
local size = UDim2.new(0.3, 0, 0, 40)
print(size.Height.Offset) --> 40 (same as size.Y.Offset)

m.d: Returns a UDim2 interpolated linearly between this UDim2 and the given goal. The alpha value should be a number between 0 and 1.
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.UDim2` interpolated linearly between the value and the given goal.

p.s: The target UDim2 to interpolate toward.
A value between 0 (returns this UDim2) and 1 (returns goal) controlling the interpolation.

r.s: A UDim2 where each axis is independently interpolated between this value and goal by the fraction alpha.

kid.simple: Gives you a UDim2 part of the way between this one and a goal. alpha 0 gives this one, 1 gives the goal, 0.5 gives exactly halfway. Each of the four numbers is worked out separately. Handy for making your own UI animations.
kid.example:
local startPos = UDim2.fromScale(0, 0.5)
local endPos = UDim2.fromScale(1, 0.5)
local halfway = startPos:Lerp(endPos, 0.5)
print(halfway) --> {0.5, 0}, {0.5, 0}
kid.gotcha: For smooth UI movement, TweenService or GuiObject:TweenPosition is often easier than calling Lerp every frame yourself.

m.d: Returns a new UDim2 with both dimensions set to zero — equivalent to UDim2.new(0, 0, 0, 0). All four components (X scale, X offset, Y scale, Y offset) default to 0.
m.s: Returns a new `Datatype.UDim2` with the coordinates of two zero `Datatype.UDim` components representing each axis.

kid.simple: Makes a new UDim2. You can give it nothing (all zeros), four numbers (xScale, xOffset, yScale, yOffset), or two UDims (one for X, one for Y). Every number you leave out is 0.
kid.example:
local zero = UDim2.new() -- same as UDim2.new(0, 0, 0, 0)
-- Half the parent wide plus 20 pixels, full parent tall
local size = UDim2.new(0.5, 20, 1, 0)
-- Same idea, built from two UDims
local same = UDim2.new(UDim.new(0.5, 20), UDim.new(1, 0))
print(size == same) --> true
kid.gotcha: Remember the order: X scale, X offset, Y scale, Y offset.

m.d:
Returns a new UDim2 with the given scalar coordinates and no offsets. Equivalent to:

local xScale, yScale = 0.5, 0.25
print(UDim2.fromScale(xScale, yScale) == UDim2.new(xScale, 0, yScale, 0)) --> true
m.s: Returns a new `Datatype.UDim2` with the given scale components and no offsets.

p.s: The relative scale for the horizontal (X) axis.
The relative scale for the vertical (Y) axis.

kid.simple: A shortcut that makes a UDim2 using only Scale (fractions of the parent), with both Offsets set to 0. UDim2.fromScale(0.5, 0.25) is the same as UDim2.new(0.5, 0, 0.25, 0). Great for UI that should look the same on every screen.

m.d:
Returns a new UDim2 with the given offset coordinates and no scaling. Equivalent to:

local xOffset, yOffset = 100, 50
print(UDim2.fromOffset(xOffset, yOffset) == UDim2.new(0, xOffset, 0, yOffset)) --> true
m.s: Returns a new `Datatype.UDim2` with the given offset components and no scaling.

p.s: The absolute logical pixel offset for the horizontal (X) axis.
The absolute logical pixel offset for the vertical (Y) axis.

kid.simple: A shortcut that makes a UDim2 using only Offset (exact pixels), with both Scales set to 0. UDim2.fromOffset(100, 50) is the same as UDim2.new(0, 100, 0, 50). Good for things that must stay an exact size, like a small icon.
kid.gotcha: Big fromOffset sizes can be too large for small phone screens.

m.d:
Adds both the scale and offset of each axis independently: the result's X scale is the sum of both X scales, the result's X offset is the sum of both X offsets, and likewise for Y.

local a = UDim2.new(0.5, 10, 0, 20)
local b = UDim2.new(0.25, 5, 1, 0)
local c = a + b  -- UDim2.new(0.75, 15, 1, 20)
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.UDim2` with components that are the sum of the respective components of the two `Datatype.UDim2` objects.

kid.simple: Adds two UDim2s. Each of the four numbers is added to its partner: X scales together, X offsets together, and the same for Y. Useful for nudging a position, like adding UDim2.fromOffset(0, 10) to move something 10 pixels down.

m.d:
Subtracts both the scale and offset of each axis independently: the result's X scale is the first X scale minus the second, the result's X offset is the first X offset minus the second, and likewise for Y.

local a = UDim2.new(1, 100, 1, 50)
local b = UDim2.new(0.5, 30, 0, 10)
local c = a - b  -- UDim2.new(0.5, 70, 1, 40)
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.UDim2` with components that are the difference of the respective components of the two `Datatype.UDim2` objects.

kid.simple: Subtracts one UDim2 from another, number by number: X scale minus X scale, X offset minus X offset, and the same for Y.

A UDim2 tells Roblox where a piece of UI goes on the screen and how big it is. It has an X part (left to right) and a Y part (top to bottom), and each part has a Scale and an Offset. Scale is a fraction of the parent's size, and Offset is exact pixels. You use it for the Size and Position of things like Frames, TextLabels, and buttons.
kid.analogy: Think of hanging a poster on a wall. Scale is like saying "put it halfway across the wall", which works on any wall size.
