Offset is like saying "move it 20 centimeters to the left", which is the same distance on a small wall or a big wall. A UDim2 lets you say both at once, for both across and up-down.
whenToUse: Setting the Size of a Frame, TextLabel, ImageLabel, or button
Setting the Position of UI on the screen
Centering a box on the screen
Animating UI moving or growing with TweenService
kid.where: Works in any script, but UI is usually changed from a LocalScript (in StarterGui or StarterPlayerScripts), because each player has their own screen. Make one with UDim2.new, UDim2.fromScale, or UDim2.fromOffset.

terms.Scale: A fraction of the parent's size. 0 means nothing, 0.5 means half, 1 means all of it. On a screen 1000 pixels wide, Scale 0.5 = 500 pixels. On a phone 400 pixels wide, the same Scale 0.5 = 200 pixels. It grows and shrinks with the screen.
terms.Offset: An exact number of pixels that never changes. Offset 20 is always 20 pixels, on a giant monitor or a tiny phone.
terms.pixel: One tiny dot on the screen. A normal computer screen is around 1920 pixels wide; a phone held sideways might be around 800.
terms.parent: The thing a UI object sits inside. For a Frame directly inside a ScreenGui, the parent is the whole screen. For a button inside a Frame, the parent is that Frame.
terms.GuiObject: Any 2D thing you can see on the screen in Roblox UI, like a Frame, TextLabel, TextButton, or ImageLabel.
terms.read-only: You can look at the value but you cannot change it directly. To get a different value, make a new one.
terms.X: The left-to-right direction on the screen. X = 0 is the left edge.
terms.Y: The top-to-bottom direction on the screen. Y = 0 is the TOP edge, and bigger Y goes down.
terms.Position: Where a UI object's top-left corner sits inside its parent (unless you change AnchorPoint).
terms.AnchorPoint: A GuiObject property that picks which spot of the object is placed at Position. (0, 0) is the top-left corner (the default), (0.5, 0.5) is the middle.
terms.interpolate / lerp: Find a value part of the way between two values. Halfway (0.5) between 0 and 10 is 5.
terms.TweenService: A Roblox service that smoothly animates a property from one value to another over time.

examples.title: Scale vs Offset on a real screen
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local player = Players.LocalPlayer

-- Make a ScreenGui to hold our boxes
local screenGui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
screenGui.Parent = player:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

-- Box A uses SCALE: half the screen wide, a tenth of the screen tall
local boxA = Instance.new("Frame")
boxA.Size = UDim2.fromScale(0.5, 0.1)
boxA.Position = UDim2.fromScale(0, 0) -- top-left corner
boxA.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(0, 170, 255)
boxA.Parent = screenGui

-- Box B uses OFFSET: always 500 x 60 pixels
local boxB = Instance.new("Frame")
boxB.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(500, 60)
boxB.Position = UDim2.new(0, 0, 0.2, 0) -- 20% down from the top
boxB.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(255, 85, 0)
boxB.Parent = screenGui
explain: On a computer screen 1000 pixels wide, box A is 0.5 x 1000 = 500 pixels wide, and box B is also 500 pixels wide. They look the same.
Now open the game on a phone that is only 400 pixels wide.
Box A becomes 0.5 x 400 = 200 pixels wide. It still fills exactly half the screen.
Box B is still 500 pixels wide, which is wider than the whole 400-pixel phone screen, so it gets cut off.
That is why Scale works on phones and pure Offset often does not: Scale grows and shrinks with the screen, Offset never changes.

examples.title: Center a box with UDim2.new(0.5, -50, 0.5, -25)
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local player = Players.LocalPlayer

local screenGui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
screenGui.Parent = player:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

local box = Instance.new("Frame")
box.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(100, 50) -- always 100 wide, 50 tall
-- Go to the middle (0.5), then back up by half the box size
box.Position = UDim2.new(0.5, -50, 0.5, -25)
box.Parent = screenGui
explain: The box is 100 pixels wide and 50 pixels tall.
Position says where the box's TOP-LEFT corner goes.
X part: Scale 0.5, Offset -50. On a 1000-pixel-wide screen that is 0.5 x 1000 - 50 = 450 pixels from the left.
Y part: Scale 0.5, Offset -25. On a 600-pixel-tall screen that is 0.5 x 600 - 25 = 275 pixels from the top.
So the box covers 450 to 550 across and 275 to 325 down. Its middle is (500, 300), the exact center of the screen.
The -50 and -25 are half of the box's width and height. That shift is what makes the box's middle (not its corner) land in the center.
An easier way: set box.AnchorPoint = Vector2.new(0.5, 0.5) and box.Position = UDim2.fromScale(0.5, 0.5).

examples.title: A health bar that fills part of its background
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local player = Players.LocalPlayer

local screenGui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
screenGui.ResetOnSpawn = false -- keep the bar when the character respawns
screenGui.Parent = player:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

-- Gray background bar: 40% of the screen wide, 20 pixels tall
local background = Instance.new("Frame")
background.Size = UDim2.new(0.4, 0, 0, 20)
background.Position = UDim2.new(0.3, 0, 1, -40) -- 40 pixels up from the bottom
background.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(60, 60, 60)
background.Parent = screenGui

-- Green fill INSIDE the background
local fill = Instance.new("Frame")
fill.Size = UDim2.fromScale(1, 1) -- start full
fill.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(0, 200, 0)
fill.Parent = background

local function update(humanoid)
	local percent = humanoid.Health / humanoid.MaxHealth
	-- X scale is a fraction of the BACKGROUND, because the fill is inside it
	fill.Size = UDim2.fromScale(percent, 1)
end

local function onCharacter(character)
	local humanoid = character:WaitForChild("Humanoid")
	update(humanoid)
	humanoid.HealthChanged:Connect(function()
		update(humanoid)
	end)
end

if player.Character then
	onCharacter(player.Character)
end
player.CharacterAdded:Connect(onCharacter)
explain: The background is 0.4 of the screen wide (Scale) and exactly 20 pixels tall (Offset).
Its Y position is Scale 1 (the very bottom) with Offset -40, so it sits 40 pixels above the bottom on every screen.
The green fill is inside the background, so its Scale is a fraction of the background, not the screen.
If health is 75 out of 100, percent is 0.75 and the fill covers three quarters of the bar.

gotchas: The order of UDim2.new is (xScale, xOffset, yScale, yOffset), not (x, y, width, height). Mixing up the order is the number one mistake.
Scale is a fraction from 0 to 1, not a percent. 50% is 0.5.
Pure Offset sizes can look fine in Studio and then be too big or too small on phones. Test with the Device Emulator in Studio.
Y = 0 is the top of the screen, not the bottom. To place something near the bottom, use Y Scale 1 with a negative Offset, like UDim2.new(0, 0, 1, -50).
Scale is always a fraction of the PARENT. A Frame inside another Frame uses the outer Frame's size, not the screen's.

datatype/User.d:
The User data type represents a user's scoped identity within a specific domain, such as an experience or OAuth application. It encapsulates a domain user ID alongside the domain metadata that uniquely identifies that user within that domain.

Unlike a numeric user ID alone, a User value carries its domain context, making it unambiguous across experiences and apps. It is the standard identifier for referencing users in new experience code and is available from Player.User.

Domain User IDs

User IDs on Roblox are domain-scoped: a single account has a unique domain user ID for each experience or app it interacts with. This ensures that user activity in one experience cannot be correlated with activity in another by a third party using the user ID alone.

A domain user ID is an integer that is unique within a given domain (identified by DomainType and domain ID). Domain user IDs are guaranteed not to collide with existing global user IDs.

Serialization

User supports round-trip string serialization via ToString() and fromString(). A User serialized with ToString() and deserialized with fromString() produces an identical value. The encoded string is stable, URL-safe, and compact. Use it when persisting or transmitting user identity across systems.

Users vs. Players

A User represents persistent identity, not live server presence. It can reference any account in the domain, whether or not that user is currently connected. Use Player when you need the in-server instance.
datatype/User.s: Represents a user's domain-scoped identity within a specific domain.

m.d: The domain user ID for this user within the associated domain. This is an integer that uniquely identifies the user within the specific domain type and domain ID combination.
m.s: The domain user ID, unique within this domain.

m.d: The DomainType that identifies the kind of domain this domain user ID belongs to. Currently supported values are DomainType.EXPERIENCE and DomainType.OAUTH.
m.s: The type of domain that this domain user ID belongs to.

m.d: The identifier of the specific domain instance that this user ID is scoped to. For DomainType.EXPERIENCE, this is the universe ID. For DomainType.OAUTH, this is the application ID.
m.s: The identifier of the specific domain instance.

m.d:
Serializes this User into a string that encodes the domain type, domain ID, and domain user ID. The result is stable, URL-safe, and compact. Use this when storing or transmitting user identity.

The string can be converted back to a User via fromString().
m.s: Serializes this `Datatype.User` into a stable string representation.

r.s: A stable, URL-safe encoded string representing the domain type, domain ID, and domain user ID that can be deserialized back with fromString().

m.d: Creates a new User from the given domain user ID, using the current experience as the domain. The ID must be a valid domain user ID (above the global user ID range).
m.s: Creates a `Datatype.User` from a domain user ID within the current experience.

p.s: The domain-scoped user ID to construct the User from. Must be above the global user ID range.

m.d: Deserializes a User from a string previously produced by ToString().
m.s: Creates a `Datatype.User` from its serialized string form.

p.s: A string previously produced by ToString().

datatype/ValueCurveKey.d:
A time-value pair used with ValueCurve instances.

The Interpolation property dictates the interpolation mode for the segment started by this key and ended by the next key on the curve. Each segment may use a different interpolation mode.

The LeftTangent and RightTangent properties apply to the cubic interpolation mode and define the desired tangent (slope) at the key. Different left and right values can be used to encode discontinuities in slope at the key. Attempting to set a RightTangent value on a key that doesn't use the cubic interpolation mode will result in a runtime error. It is possible to set the LeftTangent property on any key, as it will be used should the preceding segment use cubic interpolation.
datatype/ValueCurveKey.s: A time-value pair used with `Class.ValueCurve` instances.

m.d:
Specifies the interpolation mode used for the curve segment that begins at this key and ends at the next key on the ValueCurve. Each segment of the curve can use a different interpolation mode. The default value is KeyInterpolationMode.Constant.

The available modes are:

  • Constant — the segment holds the value of this key until the next key.
  • Linear — the segment linearly interpolates between this key's value and the next key's value.
  • Cubic — the segment uses a cubic Hermite spline defined by this key's RightTangent and the next key's LeftTangent.

Not all value types support Linear or Cubic interpolation. Non-numerical types such as strings, booleans, and enums revert to Constant interpolation regardless of this setting.

Changing this property to a non-cubic mode automatically clears the RightTangent of this key, because only cubic segments use a right tangent.
m.s: The key interpolation mode for the segment started by this `Datatype.ValueCurveKey`.

m.d: The time position of this ValueCurveKey along the curve. Defaults to 0. Keys within a ValueCurve are stored sorted by their time values; the time determines where in the animation timeline this key's value applies.
m.s: The time position of this `Datatype.ValueCurveKey`.

m.d: The value stored in this ValueCurveKey. Defaults to nil. Can hold any supported Luau type, including numbers, booleans, strings, Vector2, Vector3, CFrame, UDim, UDim2, NumberRange, NumberSequence, ColorSequence, and enums. All keys on a single ValueCurve must hold values of the same type; attempting to insert a key whose value type differs from existing keys produces an error.
m.s: The value of this `Datatype.ValueCurveKey`.

m.d: The outgoing tangent (slope) at this key, used when the Interpolation is KeyInterpolationMode.Cubic. Defaults to nil (unset); when unset, an effective tangent of 0 is used during curve evaluation. Attempting to set this property on a key whose interpolation mode is not Cubic throws a runtime error. This property is automatically cleared when Interpolation is changed to a non-cubic mode.
m.s: The tangent to the right of this `Datatype.ValueCurveKey`.

m.d: The incoming tangent (slope) at this key, used when the preceding segment uses KeyInterpolationMode.Cubic interpolation. Defaults to nil (unset); when unset, an effective tangent of 0 is used during curve evaluation. Unlike RightTangent, this property can be set on any key regardless of its own interpolation mode, because it defines the slope at the endpoint of the preceding cubic segment.
m.s: The tangent to the left of this `Datatype.ValueCurveKey`.

m.d: Creates a new ValueCurveKey at a given time and value. LeftTangent and RightTangent are left uninitialized and, if not initialized, tangent values of '0' will be used when evaluating the curve.
m.s: Returns a new `Datatype.ValueCurveKey` from the given time and value.

p.s: Time at which to create the new ValueCurveKey.
Value of the new ValueCurveKey.
The interpolation mode for the curve segment starting at this key. Defaults to KeyInterpolationMode.Constant if omitted.

datatype/Vector2.d:
The Vector2 data type represents a 2D value with direction and magnitude. Some applications include GUI elements and 2D mouse positions.

Math Operations

The following math operations are valid for the Vector2 data type:

Operation Description
Datatype.Vector2 + Datatype.Vector2 Produces a Datatype.Vector2 with each component of the second added to the corresponding component of the first.
Datatype.Vector2 - Datatype.Vector2 Produces a Datatype.Vector2 with each component of the second subtracted from the corresponding component of the first.
Datatype.Vector2 * Datatype.Vector2 Produces a Datatype.Vector2 with each component of the second multiplied by the corresponding component of the first.
Datatype.Vector2 / Datatype.Vector2 Produces a Datatype.Vector2 with each component of the first divided by the corresponding component of the second.
Datatype.Vector2 * number Produces a Datatype.Vector2 with each component multiplied by the number.
Datatype.Vector2 / number Produces a Datatype.Vector2 with each component divided by the number.
datatype/Vector2.s: Represents a 2D value with direction and magnitude.

m.d:
The x-coordinate of the Vector2, corresponding to the first argument passed to Vector2.new(). This property is read-only.

local v = Vector2.new(3, 4)
print(v.X)  --> 3
m.s: The x-coordinate of the `Datatype.Vector2`.

kid.simple: The first number: how far across (left to right).
kid.example: print(Vector2.new(3, 4).X) --> 3

m.d:
The y-coordinate of the Vector2, corresponding to the second argument passed to Vector2.new(). This property is read-only.

local v = Vector2.new(3, 4)
print(v.Y)  --> 4
m.s: The y-coordinate of the `Datatype.Vector2`.

kid.simple: The second number: how far down on the screen (or up, in your own 2D math).
kid.example: print(Vector2.new(3, 4).Y) --> 4

m.d:
The length (magnitude) of the Vector2, computed as math.sqrt(X^2 + Y^2). This property is read-only.

local v = Vector2.new(3, 4)
print(v.Magnitude)  --> 5
m.s: The length of the `Datatype.Vector2`.

kid.simple: The LENGTH of the arrow: square root of (X*X + Y*Y). Subtract two points and take the Magnitude to get the distance between them.
kid.example:
print(Vector2.new(3, 4).Magnitude) --> 5
local a, b = Vector2.new(10, 10), Vector2.new(13, 14)
print((b - a).Magnitude) --> 5  (5 pixels apart)

m.d:
A normalized copy of the Vector2 — one that has the same direction as the original but a magnitude of 1. If the vector has zero magnitude the result is undefined (contains nan values). This property is read-only.

local v = Vector2.new(3, 4)
print(v.Unit)             --> 0.6, 0.8
print(v.Unit.Magnitude)   --> 1
m.s: A normalized copy of the `Datatype.Vector2`.

kid.simple: A copy of the arrow with length exactly 1, pointing the same way. Use it when you only need the direction.
kid.example:
local v = Vector2.new(3, 4)
print(v.Unit)           --> 0.6, 0.8
print(v.Unit.Magnitude) --> 1
kid.gotcha: A (0, 0) vector has no direction, so `.Unit` gives NaN.

m.d:
Returns the 2D cross product of this vector with other, computed as self.X * other.Y - self.Y * other.X. Unlike Vector3:Cross() which returns a vector, the 2D cross product returns a scalar representing the signed magnitude of the perpendicular (Z) component. The result is positive when other is counter-clockwise from self, negative when clockwise, and zero when the vectors are parallel.

local a = Vector2.new(1, 0)
local b = Vector2.new(0, 1)
print(a:Cross(b))  -->  1
print(b:Cross(a))  --> -1
m.s: Returns the cross product of the two vectors.

p.s: The vector to compute the cross product against.

r.s: The signed scalar magnitude of the perpendicular component, computed as self.X * other.Y - self.Y * other.X.

kid.simple: The 2D cross product. Gives ONE number: X1*Y2 - Y1*X2. Positive means the second arrow is turned counter-clockwise from the first, negative means clockwise, 0 means they lie on the same line.
kid.example:
local a = Vector2.new(1, 0)
local b = Vector2.new(0, 1)
print(a:Cross(b)) -->  1
print(b:Cross(a)) --> -1

m.d: Returns a new vector from the absolute values of the original's components. For example, a vector of (-2, 4) returns a vector of (2, 4).
m.s: Returns a new vector from the absolute values of the original's components.

r.s: A new vector whose components are the absolute values of the original's components.

kid.simple: Removes minus signs from both numbers. (-2, 4) becomes (2, 4).
kid.example: print(Vector2.new(-2, 4):Abs()) --> 2, 4

m.d: Returns a new vector from the ceiling of the original's components. For example, a vector of (-2.6, 5.1) returns a vector of (-2, 6).
m.s: Returns a new vector from the ceiling of the original's components.

r.s: A new vector whose components are the ceiling (rounded up) of the original's components.

kid.simple: Rounds both numbers UP to whole numbers. (-2.6, 5.1) becomes (-2, 6).
kid.example: print(Vector2.new(-2.6, 5.1):Ceil()) --> -2, 6

m.d: Returns a new vector from the floor of the original's components. For example, a vector of (-2.6, 5.1) returns a vector of (-3, 5).
m.s: Returns a new vector from the floor of the original's components.

r.s: A new vector whose components are the floor (rounded down) of the original's components.

kid.simple: Rounds both numbers DOWN to whole numbers. (-2.6, 5.1) becomes (-3, 5).
kid.example: print(Vector2.new(-2.6, 5.1):Floor()) --> -3, 5

m.d: Returns a new vector from the sign (-1, 0, or 1) of the original's components. For example, a vector of (-2.6, 5.1) returns a vector of (-1, 1).
m.s: Returns a new vector from the sign (-1, 0, or 1) of the original's components.

r.s: A new vector whose components are the sign (-1, 0, or 1) of the original's components.

kid.simple: Turns each number into -1 (negative), 0 (zero) or 1 (positive). (-2.6, 5.1) becomes (-1, 1).
kid.example: print(Vector2.new(-2.6, 5.1):Sign()) --> -1, 1

m.d: Returns the angle in radians between the two vectors. Specify true for the optional isSigned boolean if you want a signed angle. By default, the method returns the absolute value. Signed angles are a negative when going clockwise. Values are in the range [0, pi] for absolute angles and [-pi, pi] for signed angles.
m.s: Returns the angle in radians between the two vectors.

p.s: The vector to measure the angle to.
Whether to return a signed angle (negative when clockwise) instead of the absolute value.

kid.simple: The angle between two arrows in radians. Normally always positive (0 to pi). Pass `true` as the second value to get a signed angle, which is negative when the turn is clockwise.
kid.example:
local a = Vector2.new(1, 0)
local b = Vector2.new(0, 1)
print(math.deg(a:Angle(b))) --> 90
print(math.deg(b:Angle(a, true))) -- signed: about -90 (clockwise)

m.d:
Returns the scalar dot product of this vector and v, computed as self.X * v.X + self.Y * v.Y. The result equals the product of the two magnitudes multiplied by the cosine of the angle between them. A positive value means the vectors point in roughly the same direction; zero means they are perpendicular; negative means they point in roughly opposite directions.

local a = Vector2.new(1, 0)
local b = Vector2.new(0, 1)
print(a:Dot(b))  --> 0  (perpendicular)
print(a:Dot(a))  --> 1  (parallel, equal to Magnitude^2)
m.s: Returns a scalar dot product of the two vectors.

p.s: The vector to compute the dot product with.

kid.simple: One number that says how much two arrows point the same way: X1*X2 + Y1*Y2. With 1-length arrows: 1 = same way, 0 = right angle, -1 = opposite.
kid.example:
local a = Vector2.new(1, 0)
print(a:Dot(Vector2.new(0, 1)))  --> 0  (right angle)
print(a:Dot(Vector2.new(-1, 0))) --> -1 (opposite)

m.d:
Returns a Vector2 linearly interpolated between this Vector2 and the given goal v by the fraction alpha, using the formula self + (v - self) * alpha. An alpha of 0 returns self, an alpha of 1 returns v, and values between 0 and 1 return a point in between. Note that alpha is not clamped to [0, 1] — values outside that range extrapolate beyond the two endpoints.

local a = Vector2.new(0, 0)
local b = Vector2.new(4, 8)
print(a:Lerp(b, 0.5))  --> 2, 4
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.Vector2` linearly interpolated between this `Datatype.Vector2` and the given goal by the given alpha.

p.s: The goal vector to interpolate toward.
The interpolation fraction, where 0 returns this vector and 1 returns v.

kid.simple: Finds a point part-way from this vector to `v`. `alpha` 0 is the start, 1 is the end, 0.5 is halfway. Great for sliding a 2D thing smoothly.
kid.example:
local a = Vector2.new(0, 0)
local b = Vector2.new(4, 8)
print(a:Lerp(b, 0.5))  --> 2, 4
print(a:Lerp(b, 0.25)) --> 1, 2
kid.gotcha: `alpha` is not limited to 0 to 1. Values outside that go past the ends.

m.d:
Returns a Vector2 with each component as the highest among the respective components of the provided Vector2 objects.

local a = Vector2.new(1, 2)
local b = Vector2.new(2, 1)

print(a:Max(b)) -- Vector2.new(2, 2)
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.Vector2` with each component as the highest among the respective components of the provided `Datatype.Vector2` objects.

p.s: One or more Vector2 objects to compare against.

kid.simple: Picks the BIGGER X and the BIGGER Y from all the vectors you give it. You can pass more than one.
kid.example: print(Vector2.new(1, 2):Max(Vector2.new(2, 1))) --> 2, 2

m.d:
Returns a Vector2 with each component as the lowest among the respective components of the provided Vector2 objects.

local a = Vector2.new(1, 2)
local b = Vector2.new(2, 1)

print(a:Min(b)) -- Vector2.new(1, 1)
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.Vector2` with each component as the lowest among the respective components of the provided `Datatype.Vector2` objects.

p.s: One or more Vector2 objects to compare against.

kid.simple: Picks the SMALLER X and the SMALLER Y from all the vectors you give it. You can pass more than one.
kid.example: print(Vector2.new(1, 2):Min(Vector2.new(2, 1))) --> 1, 1

m.d:
Returns true if the X and Y components of the other Vector2 are within epsilon units of each corresponding component of this Vector2. The comparison is per-component: both math.abs(self.X - other.X) and math.abs(self.Y - other.Y) must be less than or equal to epsilon. The optional epsilon parameter defaults to 1e-5 (0.00001) and must be a positive value no greater than 0.1.

local a = Vector2.new(1, 2)
local b = Vector2.new(1.000009, 2.000009)
print(a:FuzzyEq(b))           --> true  (within default 1e-5)
print(a:FuzzyEq(b, 0.000001)) --> false (tighter epsilon)
m.s: Returns `true` if the X and Y components of the other `Datatype.Vector2` are within epsilon units of each corresponding component of this `Datatype.Vector2`.

p.s: The vector to compare against.
The maximum difference allowed for each component to still be considered equal.

kid.simple: Checks if two Vector2s are ALMOST equal: each number must be within `epsilon` of its partner (default 0.00001). Useful because tiny rounding errors make `==` unreliable.
kid.example:
local a = Vector2.new(1, 2)
local b = Vector2.new(1.000009, 2.000009)
print(a:FuzzyEq(b))           --> true
print(a:FuzzyEq(b, 0.000001)) --> false
kid.gotcha: `epsilon` must be a positive number no bigger than 0.1.

m.d:
Returns a Vector2 from the given x and y components. Both parameters default to 0 if not provided.

local a = Vector2.new(3, 4)
print(a.X, a.Y)  --> 3  4

-- Omitted arguments default to 0
local b = Vector2.new()
print(b.X, b.Y)  --> 0  0
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.Vector2` from the given x and y components.

p.s: The x-coordinate of the new vector (defaults to 0).
The y-coordinate of the new vector (defaults to 0).

kid.simple: Makes a new Vector2 from an X and a Y number. Anything left out is 0.
kid.example:
local a = Vector2.new(3, 4)
print(a.X, a.Y) --> 3 4
local b = Vector2.new() --> 0, 0

m.d:
A Vector2 with a magnitude of zero.

This API member is a constant, and must be accessed through the Vector2 global as opposed to an individual Vector2 object.

print(Vector2.zero)  --> 0, 0
m.s: A `Datatype.Vector2` with a magnitude of zero.

kid.simple: A ready-made Vector2 of (0, 0).
kid.example: local origin = Vector2.zero -- 0, 0

m.d:
A Vector2 with a value of 1 on every axis.

This API member is a constant, and must be accessed through the Vector2 global as opposed to an individual Vector2 object.

print(Vector2.one)  --> 1, 1
m.s: A `Datatype.Vector2` with a value of 1 on every axis.

kid.simple: A ready-made Vector2 of (1, 1).
kid.example: print(Vector2.one * 5) --> 5, 5

m.d:
A Vector2 with a value of 1 on the X axis.

This API member is a constant, and must be accessed through the Vector2 global as opposed to an individual Vector2 object.

print(Vector2.xAxis)  --> 1, 0
m.s: A `Datatype.Vector2` with a value of 1 on the X axis.

kid.simple: A ready-made Vector2 of (1, 0): a 1-long arrow pointing along +X (to the right on screen).
kid.example: print(Vector2.xAxis * 10) --> 10, 0

m.d:
A Vector2 with a value of 1 on the Y axis.

This API member is a constant, and must be accessed through the Vector2 global as opposed to an individual Vector2 object.

print(Vector2.yAxis)  --> 0, 1
m.s: A `Datatype.Vector2` with a value of 1 on the Y axis.

kid.simple: A ready-made Vector2 of (0, 1): a 1-long arrow pointing along +Y (DOWN on the screen).
kid.example: print(Vector2.yAxis * 10) --> 0, 10

m.d:
Produces a Vector2 with each component of the second added to the corresponding component of the first.

print(Vector2.new(1, 2) + Vector2.new(3, 4))  --> 4, 6

print(Vector2.new(8, 15) / Vector2.new(4, 5))  --> 2, 3

Produces a Vector2 with each component multiplied by the number (scalar multiplication).

kid.example: print(Vector2.new(3, 4) * 2) --> 6, 8

Produces a Vector2 with each component divided by the number (scalar division).

print(Vector2.new(8, 12) / 4)  --> 2, 3

kid.simple: Divides both numbers by the same amount. Dividing a size by 2 finds the halfway point, like the middle of a GUI box.

A Vector2 is two numbers grouped together: X and Y. It is the flat, 2D cousin of Vector3. Roblox uses it mostly for things on your screen: where the mouse is, where a button sits, and how big a GUI box is in pixels. It can mean a SPOT on a flat surface or an ARROW (a direction with a length).
kid.analogy: A Vector2 is like a spot on a sheet of graph paper: how far across (X) and how far down (Y). It is a map with no height.
whenToUse: Reading the mouse position with `UserInputService:GetMouseLocation()`.
Reading a GUI object's `AbsolutePosition` or `AbsoluteSize` (in pixels).
Measuring the distance between two points on the screen.
Any 2D math, like a minimap or a top-down game.
kid.where: Vector2 is a built-in data type that works in Scripts and LocalScripts. Most screen and GUI uses happen in LocalScripts, because only the player's own device knows about its screen and mouse. Make one with `Vector2.new(x, y)`.

terms.vector: A group of numbers that can mean a spot or an arrow with a direction and a length. A Vector2 has 2 numbers.
terms.component: One of the numbers inside a vector: X or Y.
terms.pixel: One tiny dot on your screen. GUI positions like AbsolutePosition are measured in pixels.
terms.screen coordinates: On the screen, X grows to the RIGHT and Y grows DOWNWARD, starting at the top-left corner (0, 0).
terms.magnitude: The length of the arrow; for a difference of two points, it is the distance between them.
terms.unit vector: An arrow with length exactly 1. It keeps only the direction.
terms.dot product: One number showing how much two arrows point the same way: positive = same-ish, 0 = right angle, negative = opposite-ish.
terms.cross product (2D): For Vector2 it is a single number: positive if the second arrow is turned counter-clockwise from the first, negative if clockwise, 0 if they point along the same line.
terms.radians: The angle unit Roblox math uses. 180 degrees is pi (about 3.1416) radians. Use `math.deg` to convert to degrees.
terms.lerp / interpolate: Find a spot part-way between two vectors. 0.5 means halfway.
terms.epsilon: A tiny amount of difference you are willing to ignore, like 0.00001.
terms.NaN: Not a Number. A broken number, for example from making a zero-length arrow into a unit vector.
terms.UDim2: A different type used to SET GUI positions and sizes (with Scale and Offset). Vector2 is mostly what you READ back in pixels.

examples.title: Print where the mouse is
examples.code:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")

while true do
	local mouse = UserInputService:GetMouseLocation() -- a Vector2, in pixels
	print("Mouse is at X =", mouse.X, "Y =", mouse.Y)
	task.wait(1)
end
explain: `GetMouseLocation` gives a Vector2: X pixels from the left edge, Y pixels from the top edge.
This has to be a LocalScript, because only the player's own computer knows where its mouse is.

examples.title: Is the mouse near a button?
examples.place: LocalScript inside a TextButton in a ScreenGui in StarterGui
examples.code:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
local GuiService = game:GetService("GuiService")
local button = script.Parent

while true do
	-- GetMouseLocation counts the top bar, AbsolutePosition does not, so remove the top bar inset.
	local inset = GuiService:GetGuiInset()
	local mouse = UserInputService:GetMouseLocation() - inset

	-- Center of the button = top-left corner + half the size
	local center = button.AbsolutePosition + button.AbsoluteSize / 2
	local distance = (mouse - center).Magnitude

	if distance < 100 then
		button.Text = "Getting warmer!"
	else
		button.Text = "Come closer"
	end
	task.wait(0.1)
end
explain: `AbsolutePosition` is the button's top-left corner in pixels, and `AbsoluteSize` is its width and height.
Adding half the size to the corner finds the middle of the button.
Subtracting two Vector2s gives the arrow between them; `.Magnitude` is how many pixels apart they are.

gotchas: On the screen, Y goes DOWN, not up. (0, 0) is the top-left corner.
You cannot change one number in place: `v.X = 5` errors. Make a new Vector2.
To set a GUI's position or size you usually use UDim2, not Vector2. Vector2 is what you get back from AbsolutePosition and AbsoluteSize.
`.Unit` of (0, 0) gives NaN. Check `.Magnitude > 0` first.
`Vector2 * Vector2` multiplies matching numbers; it is not the dot product. Use `:Dot`.
Angles from `:Angle` are in radians. Use `math.deg` for degrees.

datatype/Vector2int16.d:
The Vector2int16 data type represents a vector in 2D space with a signed 16-bit integer for its components. It is similar to Vector2 in that it allows for the same arithmetic operations, but it lacks commonly used vector functions.

Vector2int16 should not be confused with:

  • Vector2, a more precise and complete implementation for 2D vectors.
  • Vector3int16, a similar implementation for 3D vectors.

For each component:

  • The lower bound is -215, or -32,768.
  • The upper bound is 215 − 1, or 32,767.

Converting to Vector2

To convert a Vector2int16 to a Vector2, construct a Vector2 by passing each component of the Vector2int16 to Vector2.new():

local vector2int16 = Vector2int16.new(1, 2)
local vector2 = Vector2.new(vector2int16.X, vector2int16.Y)
print(vector2)  --> 1, 2

Do not pass an entire Vector2int16 to Vector2.new(), as the constructor interprets a Vector2int16 as a 0 within its parameters without producing an error. This can lead to silent logic errors if you do something like:

local vector2int16 = Vector2int16.new(1, 2)
local vector2 = Vector2.new(vector2int16)
print(vector2)  --> 0, 0

Math Operations

The following math operations are valid for the Vector2int16 data type. For all operations, be mindful of the bounds associated with signed 16-bit integers, described earlier.

Operation Description
Datatype.Vector2int16 + Datatype.Vector2int16 Produces a Datatype.Vector2int16 whose components are the sum of the operands' respective components.
Datatype.Vector2int16 - Datatype.Vector2int16 Produces a Datatype.Vector2int16 whose components are the difference of the operands' respective components.
Datatype.Vector2int16 * Datatype.Vector2int16 Produces a Datatype.Vector2int16 whose components are the product of the operands' respective components.
Datatype.Vector2int16 / Datatype.Vector2int16 Produces a Datatype.Vector2int16 whose components are the quotient of the operands' respective components. The results of the division are rounded down.
Datatype.Vector2int16 * number Produces a Datatype.Vector2int16 whose components are the product of the respective Datatype.Vector2int16 components and the number (factor). This operation is commutative.
Datatype.Vector2int16 / number Produces a Datatype.Vector2int16 whose components are the quotient of the respective Datatype.Vector2int16 components and the number (divisor). The results of the division are rounded toward zero.
datatype/Vector2int16.s: Represents a Vector2 with signed 16-bit integers for components.

m.d: The x-coordinate of the Vector2int16, also accessible in its lower-case variant.
m.s: The x-coordinate of the `Datatype.Vector2int16`.

kid.simple: The X whole number.
kid.example: print(Vector2int16.new(4, 9).X) --> 4

m.d: The y-coordinate of the Vector2int16, also accessible in its lower-case variant.
m.s: The y-coordinate of the `Datatype.Vector2int16`.

kid.simple: The Y whole number.
kid.example: print(Vector2int16.new(4, 9).Y) --> 9

m.d:
Returns a new Vector2int16 given the x and y components. Non-integer components are rounded down.

The components must fall within the range [-215, 215). If outside this range, integer overflow may occur. For example, providing 32,768 (equal to 215) as a component overflows the 16-bit integer, and so the component is -32,768 (equal to -215) instead.
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.Vector2int16` from the given x and y components.

p.s: The x-component of the vector, rounded down to a signed 16-bit integer.
The y-component of the vector, rounded down to a signed 16-bit integer.

kid.simple: Makes a new Vector2int16 from two whole numbers. Decimal parts are rounded down. Each number must be from -32,768 to 32,767.
kid.example:
local v = Vector2int16.new(5, 8.6)
print(v.Y) --> 8
kid.gotcha: 32,768 is one too big and wraps to -32,768.

m.d: Produces a Vector2int16 whose components are the sum of the operands' respective components. Be mindful of the bounds associated with signed 16-bit integers, described earlier.
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.Vector2int16` whose components are the sum of the operands' respective components.

kid.simple: Adds matching numbers.
kid.example: print(Vector2int16.new(1, 2) + Vector2int16.new(10, 20)) --> 11, 22

m.d: Produces a Vector2int16 whose components are the difference of the operands' respective components. Be mindful of the bounds associated with signed 16-bit integers, described earlier.
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.Vector2int16` whose components are the difference of the operands' respective components.

kid.simple: Subtracts matching numbers.
kid.example: print(Vector2int16.new(11, 22) - Vector2int16.new(1, 2)) --> 10, 20

m.d: Produces a Vector2int16 whose components are the product of the operands' respective components. Be mindful of the bounds associated with signed 16-bit integers, described earlier.
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.Vector2int16` whose components are the product of the operands' respective components.

kid.simple: Multiplies matching numbers.
kid.example: print(Vector2int16.new(2, 3) * Vector2int16.new(5, 4)) --> 10, 12

m.d: Produces a Vector2int16 whose components are the quotient of the operands' respective components. The results of the division are rounded down. Be mindful of the bounds associated with signed 16-bit integers, described earlier.
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.Vector2int16` whose components are the quotient of the operands' respective components.

kid.simple: Divides matching numbers, keeping only whole-number answers.
kid.example: print(Vector2int16.new(10, 9) / Vector2int16.new(3, 2)) --> 3, 4

m.d: Produces a Vector2int16 whose components are the product of the respective Vector2int16 components and the number (factor). This operation is commutative. Be mindful of the bounds associated with signed 16-bit integers, described earlier.
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.Vector2int16` whose components are the product of the respective `Datatype.Vector2int16` components and the number (factor).

kid.simple: Multiplies both numbers by the same amount.
kid.example: print(Vector2int16.new(3, 5) * 2) --> 6, 10

m.d: Produces a Vector2int16 whose components are the quotient of the respective Vector2int16 components and the number (divisor). The results of the division are rounded toward zero. Be mindful of the bounds associated with signed 16-bit integers, described earlier.
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.Vector2int16` whose components are the quotient of the respective `Datatype.Vector2int16` components and the number (divisor).

kid.simple: Divides both numbers by the same amount; answers are rounded toward zero (decimals dropped).
kid.example: print(Vector2int16.new(9, 7) / 2) --> 4, 3

kid.simple: Vector2int16 is like a Vector2 (X, Y), but each number must be a WHOLE number between -32,768 and 32,767. It uses less memory but has no handy tools like Magnitude. You will rarely need it; Vector2 is the normal choice.
kid.analogy: Vector2int16 is like a checkerboard square label: you can say "column 3, row 5", but never "column 3.5".
whenToUse: Only when a Roblox API specifically asks for a Vector2int16.
Otherwise use Vector2.
kid.where: Built-in data type, works in Scripts and LocalScripts. Make one with `Vector2int16.new(x, y)`.

terms.integer: A whole number with no decimal part, like 3 or -40 (not 2.5).
terms.16-bit signed integer: A whole number stored in a small box of memory. It can only hold numbers from -32,768 to 32,767, and can be negative (that is what "signed" means).
terms.overflow: When a number is too big for its box and wraps around to the other end. Putting 32,768 into a 16-bit integer turns it into -32,768, like a car odometer rolling over.
terms.rounded down: Decimal parts are thrown away so you get a whole number, for example 3.9 becomes 3.
terms.component: One of the numbers inside the vector, like X or Y.

examples.title: Make one and convert it to a Vector2
examples.code:
local small = Vector2int16.new(4, 9)
print(small.X, small.Y) --> 4 9

-- Convert by passing each number separately
local normal = Vector2.new(small.X, small.Y)
print(normal.Magnitude) -- now you can use Vector2 tools
explain: `Vector2int16.new` stores two whole numbers.
To use Vector2 tools like Magnitude, copy X and Y into `Vector2.new`.

gotchas: Do not pass a whole Vector2int16 into `Vector2.new`; pass `.X` and `.Y` separately.
Decimals are dropped: `Vector2int16.new(2.9, 0).X` is 2.
Numbers past 32,767 wrap around to negative numbers (overflow).

datatype/Vector3.d:
The Vector3 data type represents a vector in 3D space, typically used as a point in 3D space or the dimensions of a rectangular prism. Vector3 supports basic component-based arithmetic operations (sum, difference, product, and quotient) and these operations can be applied on the left or right hand side to either another Vector3 or a number. It also features methods for common vector operations, such as Cross() and Dot().

Alternatively to Vector3, consider using the methods and properties of the vector library.

Some example usages of Vector3 are the Position, Rotation, and Size of parts, for example:

local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Position = part.Position + Vector3.new(5, 2, 10) -- Move part by (5, 2, 10)
print(part.Position) --> 5, 2, 10

Vector3 is also commonly used when constructing more complex 3D data types such as CFrame. Many of these data types' methods will use a Vector3 within their parameters, such as CFrame:PointToObjectSpace().
datatype/Vector3.s: Represents a 3D value with a direction and magnitude.

m.d:
A Vector3 with a magnitude of 0.

This API member is a constant, and must be accessed through the Vector3 global as opposed to an individual Vector3 object.

print(Vector3.zero) --> 0, 0, 0
m.s: A `Datatype.Vector3` with a magnitude of `0`.

kid.simple: A ready-made Vector3 of (0, 0, 0). Shorter than writing `Vector3.new(0, 0, 0)`. Good for "no movement" or "no speed".
kid.example: workspace.Part.AssemblyLinearVelocity = Vector3.zero -- stop the part

m.d:
A Vector3 with a value of 1 on every axis.

This API member is a constant, and must be accessed through the Vector3 global as opposed to an individual Vector3 object.

print(Vector3.one)  --> 1, 1, 1
m.s: A `Datatype.Vector3` with a value of `1` on every axis.

kid.simple: A ready-made Vector3 of (1, 1, 1). Handy for making a 1 by 1 by 1 size or scaling every number by the same amount.
kid.example: workspace.Part.Size = Vector3.one * 3 -- a 3 by 3 by 3 cube

m.d:
A Vector3 with a value of 1 on the X axis.

This API member is a constant, and must be accessed through the Vector3 global as opposed to an individual Vector3 object.

print(Vector3.xAxis)  --> 1, 0, 0
m.s: A `Datatype.Vector3` with a value of `1` on the **X** axis.

kid.simple: A ready-made Vector3 of (1, 0, 0): a 1-stud arrow pointing along +X.
kid.example:
local part = workspace.Part
part.Position += Vector3.xAxis * 4 -- slide 4 studs along +X

m.d:
A Vector3 with a value of 1 on the Y axis.

This API member is a constant, and must be accessed through the Vector3 global as opposed to an individual Vector3 object.

print(Vector3.yAxis)  --> 0, 1, 0
m.s: A `Datatype.Vector3` with a value of `1 `on the **Y** axis.

kid.simple: A ready-made Vector3 of (0, 1, 0): a 1-stud arrow pointing straight up.
kid.example:
local part = workspace.Part
part.Position += Vector3.yAxis * 10 -- lift 10 studs

m.d:
A Vector3 with a value of 1 on the Z axis.

This API member is a constant, and must be accessed through the Vector3 global as opposed to an individual Vector3 object.

print(Vector3.zAxis)  --> 0, 0, 1
m.s: A `Datatype.Vector3` with a value of `1` on the **Z** axis.

kid.simple: A ready-made Vector3 of (0, 0, 1): a 1-stud arrow pointing along +Z.
kid.example: print(Vector3.zAxis * 2) --> 0, 0, 2

m.d: The X coordinate of the Vector3. In world space, this axis corresponds to the left-right (east-west) direction.
m.s: The **X** coordinate of the `Datatype.Vector3`.

kid.simple: The first number: left/right. You can read it but not change it. A lowercase `.x` also works.
kid.example:
local v = Vector3.new(3, 7, -2)
print(v.X) --> 3

m.d: The Y coordinate of the Vector3. In world space, this axis corresponds to the up-down (vertical) direction.
m.s: The **Y** coordinate of the `Datatype.Vector3`.

kid.simple: The second number: up/down (height).
kid.example:
local part = workspace.Part
print("The part is " .. part.Position.Y .. " studs high")

m.d: The Z coordinate of the Vector3. In world space, this axis corresponds to the north-south (forward-back) direction.
m.s: The **Z** coordinate of the `Datatype.Vector3`.

kid.simple: The third number: forward/back in the world.
kid.example:
local v = Vector3.new(3, 7, -2)
print(v.Z) --> -2

m.d:
The length (magnitude) of the Vector3, computed as math.sqrt(X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2). This is useful for comparing distances or determining how far a point is from the origin.

local v = Vector3.new(3, 4, 0)
print(v.Magnitude) --> 5
m.s: The length of the `Datatype.Vector3`.

kid.simple: The LENGTH of the arrow. When you subtract two positions, the Magnitude of the result is the distance between them in studs. It is worked out with the Pythagorean theorem: square root of (X*X + Y*Y + Z*Z).
kid.example:
print(Vector3.new(3, 4, 0).Magnitude) --> 5

local a = Vector3.new(0, 0, 0)
local b = Vector3.new(6, 0, 8)
print((b - a).Magnitude) --> 10  (they are 10 studs apart)

m.d:
A normalized copy of the Vector3 — one that has the same direction as the original but a magnitude of 1. This is useful when you need only the direction of a vector without its length, for example to get a movement direction regardless of speed.

If the vector has a magnitude of 0 (i.e. all components are zero), the resulting Unit vector will have NaN components. Check Magnitude before using Unit when the vector may be zero-length.

local v = Vector3.new(3, 4, 0)
print(v.Unit)      --> 0.6, 0.8, 0
print(v.Unit.Magnitude) --> 1
m.s: A normalized copy of the `Datatype.Vector3` - one that has the same direction as the original but a magnitude of `1`.

kid.simple: A copy of the arrow shrunk (or stretched) to length exactly 1, pointing the same way. Use it when you only care about DIRECTION, not distance.
kid.example:
local v = Vector3.new(3, 4, 0)
print(v.Unit)            --> 0.6, 0.8, 0
print(v.Unit.Magnitude)  --> 1
kid.gotcha: The zero vector has no direction, so `Vector3.zero.Unit` gives NaN values. Check `v.Magnitude > 0` first.

m.d: Returns a new vector from the absolute values of the original's components. For example, a vector of (-2, 4, -6) returns a vector of (2, 4, 6).
m.s: Returns a new vector from the absolute values of the original's components.

kid.simple: Makes every number positive (removes minus signs). (-2, 4, -6) becomes (2, 4, 6).
kid.example: print(Vector3.new(-2, 4, -6):Abs()) --> 2, 4, 6

m.d: Returns a new vector from the ceiling of the original's components. For example, a vector of (-2.6, 5.1, 8.8) returns a vector of (-2, 6, 9).
m.s: Returns a new vector from the ceiling of the original's components.

kid.simple: Rounds every number UP to the next whole number. (-2.6, 5.1, 8.8) becomes (-2, 6, 9).

m.d: Returns a new vector from the floor of the original's components. For example, a vector of (-2.6, 5.1, 8.8) returns a vector of (-3, 5, 8).
m.s: Returns a new vector from the floor of the original's components.

kid.simple: Rounds every number DOWN to a whole number. (-2.6, 5.1, 8.8) becomes (-3, 5, 8). Useful for snapping things to a grid.
kid.example:
local pos = Vector3.new(7.3, 2.9, -1.2)
print(pos:Floor()) --> 7, 2, -2

-- Snap to a 4-stud grid
local snapped = (pos / 4):Floor() * 4
print(snapped) --> 4, 0, -4

m.d: Returns a new vector from the sign (-1, 0, or 1) of the original's components. For example, a vector of (-2.6, 5.1, 0) returns a vector of (-1, 1, 0).
m.s: Returns a new vector from the sign (-1, 0, or 1) of the original's components.

kid.simple: Replaces every number with -1 if it is negative, 0 if it is zero, or 1 if it is positive. (-2.6, 5.1, 0) becomes (-1, 1, 0).

m.d:
Returns the cross product of this vector and other. The resulting vector is perpendicular to both input vectors and has a magnitude equal to the area of the parallelogram they span. The direction follows the right-hand rule: if you curl the fingers of your right hand from self toward other, your thumb points in the direction of the result.

The cross product is commonly used to find normals to surfaces, determine the axis of rotation between two directions, and test whether two vectors are parallel (cross product of parallel vectors is the zero vector).

local a = Vector3.new(1, 0, 0)
local b = Vector3.new(0, 1, 0)
print(a:Cross(b)) --> 0, 0, 1
print(b:Cross(a)) --> 0, 0, -1
m.s: Returns the cross product of the two vectors.

p.s: The other Vector3 to compute the cross product with.

kid.simple: Gives a new arrow that points at a right angle (90 degrees) to BOTH arrows, like a flagpole sticking straight up out of a flat floor made by the two arrows. Swapping the order flips the answer to point the other way. If the two arrows point the same (or exactly opposite) way, the answer is (0, 0, 0).
kid.example:
local right = Vector3.new(1, 0, 0)
local up = Vector3.new(0, 1, 0)
print(right:Cross(up)) --> 0, 0, 1
print(up:Cross(right)) --> 0, 0, -1  (order matters!)

m.d:
Returns the angle in radians between this vector and other. The input vectors do not need to be unit vectors. Without an axis argument, the returned angle is always in the range [0, math.pi] (unsigned).

If you provide an axis Vector3, the returned angle is signed: positive when the rotation from self to other follows the right-hand rule around axis, and negative otherwise. The signed result is in the range [-math.pi, math.pi]. The axis is used only to determine the sign; the plane of rotation is still defined by self and other.

local a = Vector3.new(1, 0, 0)
local b = Vector3.new(0, 1, 0)
print(a:Angle(b))                         --> 1.5707963... (pi/2)
print(a:Angle(b, Vector3.new(0, 0, 1)))   --> 1.5707963... (positive, CCW about +Z)
print(b:Angle(a, Vector3.new(0, 0, 1)))   --> -1.5707963... (negative, CW about +Z)
m.s: Returns the angle in radians between the two vectors. If you provide an axis, it determines the sign of the angle.

p.s: The Vector3 to measure the angle to.
An optional Vector3 used to determine the sign of the angle via the right-hand rule.

kid.simple: Tells you the angle between two arrows, in radians (0 to pi, which is 0 to 180 degrees). If you also give an `axis`, the answer gets a plus or minus sign to tell you which way around it turns.
kid.example:
local a = Vector3.new(1, 0, 0)
local b = Vector3.new(0, 1, 0)
print(math.deg(a:Angle(b)))                    --> 90
print(math.deg(b:Angle(a, Vector3.zAxis)))     --> -90 (turns the other way around Z)

m.d:
Returns the scalar dot product of this vector and other, computed as self.X * other.X + self.Y * other.Y + self.Z * other.Z.

The dot product is useful for determining the relationship between two directions: it equals the product of their magnitudes multiplied by the cosine of the angle between them. For unit vectors, a result of 1 means they point in the same direction, 0 means they are perpendicular, and -1 means they point in opposite directions.

local a = Vector3.new(1, 0, 0)
local b = Vector3.new(0, 1, 0)
print(a:Dot(b)) --> 0

local c = Vector3.new(1, 2, 3)
local d = Vector3.new(4, 5, 6)
print(c:Dot(d)) --> 32
m.s: Returns a scalar dot product of the two vectors.

p.s: The Vector3 to compute the dot product with.

kid.simple: Gives one number that tells how much two arrows point the same way. You multiply the matching numbers and add them up: a.X*b.X + a.Y*b.Y + a.Z*b.Z. With two 1-length arrows: 1 = exactly the same way, 0 = at a right angle, -1 = exactly opposite. Great for "is it in front of me?".
kid.example:
local forward = Vector3.new(0, 0, -1)
print(forward:Dot(Vector3.new(0, 0, -1))) --> 1   same way
print(forward:Dot(Vector3.new(1, 0, 0)))  --> 0   to the side
print(forward:Dot(Vector3.new(0, 0, 1)))  --> -1  opposite way

print(Vector3.new(1, 2, 3):Dot(Vector3.new(4, 5, 6))) --> 32  (1*4 + 2*5 + 3*6)
kid.gotcha: Use `.Unit` on both arrows first if you want the simple -1 to 1 answer; otherwise the lengths make the number bigger.

m.d:
Returns true if the two vectors are approximately equal within the tolerance defined by epsilon. The comparison is performed per-component using a hybrid epsilon that scales relative to the magnitude of each component, making it suitable for both small and large values. The default epsilon of 0.00001 (1e-5) works well for most cases.

local a = Vector3.new(1, 2, 3)
local b = Vector3.new(1.000001, 2, 3)
print(a:FuzzyEq(b))        --> true  (within default epsilon)
print(a:FuzzyEq(b, 1e-8))  --> false (tighter tolerance)
m.s: Returns `true` if the difference between the squared magnitude of the two vectors is within `epsilon`. `epsilon` is scaled relative to the magnitude, rather than an absolute epsilon.

p.s: The Vector3 to compare against.
The tolerance threshold for the comparison, scaled relative to the component magnitudes.

kid.simple: Checks if two Vector3s are ALMOST equal. Computers make tiny rounding errors, so `==` might say false for values that are basically the same. The optional `epsilon` sets how close counts (default 0.00001).
kid.example:
local a = Vector3.new(1, 2, 3)
local b = Vector3.new(1.000001, 2, 3)
print(a == b)               --> false
print(a:FuzzyEq(b))         --> true
print(a:FuzzyEq(b, 1e-8))   --> false (stricter)

m.d: Returns a Vector3 linearly interpolated between this Vector3 and the given goal Vector3 by the fraction alpha. Note that alpha is not limited to the range [0, 1].
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.Vector3` linearly interpolated between this `Datatype.Vector3` and the given goal by the given alpha.

p.s: The target Vector3 to interpolate toward.
The interpolation fraction, typically between 0 (returns self) and 1 (returns goal), but not clamped.

kid.simple: Finds a point part-way from this vector to `goal`. `alpha` 0 is the start, 1 is the goal, 0.5 is halfway. Great for smooth sliding.
kid.example:
local a = Vector3.new(0, 0, 0)
local b = Vector3.new(10, 20, 0)
print(a:Lerp(b, 0.5))  --> 5, 10, 0  (halfway)
print(a:Lerp(b, 0.1))  --> 1, 2, 0   (10 percent of the way)
kid.gotcha: `alpha` is not limited: 2 goes twice as far as the goal, and -1 goes backward past the start.

m.d:
Returns a Vector3 with each component as the highest among the respective components of both provided Vector3 objects.

local a = Vector3.new(1, 2, 1)
local b = Vector3.new(2, 1, 2)

print(a:Max(b))  --> Vector3.new(2, 2, 2)
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.Vector3` with each component as the highest among the respective components of both provided `Datatype.Vector3` objects.

p.s: The Vector3 to compare component-wise against.

kid.simple: Builds a new Vector3 by picking the BIGGER number from each pair. (1, 2, 1) and (2, 1, 2) give (2, 2, 2).
kid.example: print(Vector3.new(1, 2, 1):Max(Vector3.new(2, 1, 2))) --> 2, 2, 2

m.d:
Returns a Vector3 with each component as the lowest among the respective components of both provided Vector3 objects.

local a = Vector3.new(1, 2, 1)
local b = Vector3.new(2, 1, 2)

print(a:Min(b))  --> Vector3.new(1, 1, 1)
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.Vector3` with each component as the lowest among the respective components of both provided `Datatype.Vector3` objects.

p.s: The Vector3 to compare component-wise against.

kid.simple: Builds a new Vector3 by picking the SMALLER number from each pair. (1, 2, 1) and (2, 1, 2) give (1, 1, 1).

kid.simple: Makes a new Vector3 from three numbers: X (left/right), Y (up/down) and Z (forward/back). Any number you leave out is 0.

local spot = Vector3.new(0, 10, -5) -- 10 studs up, 5 studs toward -Z
local empty = Vector3.new()         -- 0, 0, 0

m.d:
Returns a unit Vector3 pointing in the direction of the given NormalId. For example, NormalId.Top returns (0, 1, 0) and NormalId.Front returns (0, 0, -1).

print(Vector3.FromNormalId(Enum.NormalId.Right)) --> 1, 0, 0
print(Vector3.FromNormalId(Enum.NormalId.Left))  --> -1, 0, 0

kid.simple: Turns a face name (an `Enum.NormalId` like Top or Front) into a 1-stud arrow pointing out of that face, as if the part were not turned. Top gives (0, 1, 0), Front gives (0, 0, -1).
kid.example:
print(Vector3.FromNormalId(Enum.NormalId.Top))   --> 0, 1, 0
print(Vector3.FromNormalId(Enum.NormalId.Right)) --> 1, 0, 0

Returns a unit Vector3 for the given Axis. The mapping is Axis.X to (1, 0, 0), Axis.Y to (0, 1, 0), and Axis.Z to (0, 0, 1).

print(Vector3.FromAxis(Enum.Axis.X)) --> 1, 0, 0
print(Vector3.FromAxis(Enum.Axis.Z)) --> 0, 0, 1
m.s: Returns a new `Datatype.Vector3` for the given axis.

p.s: The Axis specifying which coordinate axis to convert into a unit vector.

kid.simple: Turns an `Enum.Axis` (X, Y or Z) into a 1-stud arrow along that axis. X gives (1, 0, 0), Y gives (0, 1, 0), Z gives (0, 0, 1).
kid.example: print(Vector3.FromAxis(Enum.Axis.Y)) --> 0, 1, 0

m.d:
A Vector3 with a magnitude of 0.

This API member is a constant, and must be accessed through the Vector3 global as opposed to an individual Vector3 object.

print(Vector3.zero)  --> 0, 0, 0
m.s: A `Datatype.Vector3` with a magnitude of `0`.

A Vector3 with a value of 1 on every axis.

print(Vector3.one)  --> 1, 1, 1

part.Position += Vector3.xAxis * 4 -- slide 4 studs along +X

part.Position += Vector3.yAxis * 10 -- lift 10 studs

m.s: Produces a `Datatype.Vector3` by adding each component of the first vector to the corresponding component of the second.

kid.simple: Adds each number to its partner: X+X, Y+Y, Z+Z. Use it to move a position by an offset.
kid.example:
print(Vector3.new(1, 2, 3) + Vector3.new(4, 5, 6)) --> 5, 7, 9
-- A part at (0, 5, 0) moved by an offset of (2, 0, 0) ends up at (2, 5, 0)

m.s: Produces a `Datatype.Vector3` by subtracting each component of the second vector from the corresponding component of the first.

kid.simple: Subtracts each number from its partner. `target - start` gives the arrow from start to target; its Magnitude is the distance.
kid.example:
print(Vector3.new(5, 7, 9) - Vector3.new(1, 2, 3)) --> 4, 5, 6
local distance = (Vector3.new(6, 0, 8) - Vector3.new(0, 0, 0)).Magnitude --> 10

m.s: Produces a `Datatype.Vector3` by multiplying each component of the first vector by the corresponding component of the second.

kid.simple: Multiplies each number with its partner (X*X, Y*Y, Z*Z). Handy to scale each direction differently, or to zero-out one direction.
kid.example:
print(Vector3.new(1, 2, 3) * Vector3.new(2, 0, -1)) --> 2, 0, -3

-- Remove the up/down part of a direction (keep it flat on the ground)
local dir = Vector3.new(5, 3, 2)
print(dir * Vector3.new(1, 0, 1)) --> 5, 0, 2
kid.gotcha: This is NOT the dot or cross product.

m.d: Produces a Vector3 by dividing each component of the first vector by the corresponding component of the second.
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.Vector3` by dividing each component of the first vector by the corresponding component of the second.

kid.simple: Divides each number by its partner (X/X, Y/Y, Z/Z).
kid.example: print(Vector3.new(10, 20, 30) / Vector3.new(2, 4, 5)) --> 5, 5, 6

m.s: Produces a `Datatype.Vector3` by **floor dividing** each component of the first vector by the corresponding component of the second.

kid.simple: Floor division: divides each number by its partner, then rounds DOWN to a whole number.

m.d: Produces a Vector3 by multiplying each component of the provided vector by the number.
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.Vector3` by multiplying each component of the provided vector by the number.

kid.simple: Multiplies every number by the same amount. Makes an arrow longer or shorter without changing its direction. `number * Vector3` works too.
kid.example:
print(Vector3.new(1, 2, 3) * 2) --> 2, 4, 6
-- 10 studs in front of a part:
local part = workspace.Part
local ahead = part.Position + part.CFrame.LookVector * 10

m.d: Produces a Vector3 by dividing each component of the provided vector by the number.
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.Vector3` by dividing each component of the provided vector by the number.

kid.simple: Divides every number by the same amount. Dividing by 2 makes the arrow half as long. Dividing the sum of two positions by 2 finds the middle point.
kid.example:
print(Vector3.new(10, 4, 6) / 2) --> 5, 2, 3
local middle = (Vector3.new(0, 0, 0) + Vector3.new(10, 0, 0)) / 2 --> 5, 0, 0

m.d: Produces a Vector3 by floor dividing each component of the provided vector by the number.
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.Vector3` by **floor dividing** each component of the provided vector by the number.

kid.simple: Floor division by one number: divides each number, then rounds DOWN. Good for finding which grid square a position is in.
kid.example:
print(Vector3.new(7, 8, 9) // 2) --> 3, 4, 4
-- Which 4-stud grid cell is (13, 0, 5) in?
print(Vector3.new(13, 0, 5) // 4) --> 3, 0, 1

kid.simple: A Vector3 is three numbers grouped together: X, Y and Z. Roblox uses it for anything in 3D: where a part is (Position), how big it is (Size), and which way something is moving or pointing. You can think of it as either a SPOT in the world or an ARROW (a direction with a length). You can add, subtract and multiply Vector3s, and they come with handy tools for distance and direction.
kid.analogy: A Vector3 is like directions to buried treasure: "walk 3 steps east, climb 5 steps up, walk 2 steps north". Those three numbers can tell you WHERE the treasure is, or HOW to get from one place to another.
whenToUse: Setting or reading a part's Position or Size.
Finding the distance between two things: `(a - b).Magnitude`.
Getting a direction from one thing to another: `(target - start).Unit`.
Moving things: `part.Position + Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)` is 5 studs higher.
Checking if something is in front of or behind you with `Dot`.
Setting velocities and forces (how fast and which way things move).
kid.where: Vector3 is a built-in data type, so it works in both Scripts (server) and LocalScripts (client). No game:GetService needed. Make one with `Vector3.new(x, y, z)`.

terms.vector: A group of numbers that can mean a spot, or an arrow with a direction and a length. A Vector3 has 3 numbers: X, Y, Z.
terms.component: One of the numbers inside a vector. A Vector3 has an X component, a Y component and a Z component.
terms.X / Y / Z: The three directions in Roblox. X is left/right, Y is up/down (Y is height), Z is forward/back.
terms.stud: Roblox's unit of distance. A Vector3 of (0, 10, 0) is 10 studs up.
terms.magnitude: The length of the arrow. For a position difference, it is the distance. (3, 4, 0) has a magnitude of 5.
terms.unit vector: An arrow with length exactly 1. It keeps only the direction. Getting one is called normalizing.
terms.normalize: To shrink or stretch a vector so its length is 1, keeping its direction. That is what `.Unit` does.
terms.dot product: A single number that tells how much two arrows point the same way. Big positive: same way. 0: at a right angle. Negative: opposite ways.
terms.cross product: A new arrow that sticks out at a right angle (90 degrees) from two other arrows, like the axle sticking out of a wheel.
terms.perpendicular: At a right angle (90 degrees), like the corner of a square.
terms.right-hand rule: A trick to know which way the cross product points: curl the fingers of your right hand from the first arrow toward the second; your thumb points the answer's way.
terms.radians: The angle unit Roblox math uses. 180 degrees is pi (about 3.1416) radians. Convert with `math.deg` and `math.rad`.
terms.lerp / interpolate: Find a spot part-way between two vectors. 0.5 means halfway.
terms.epsilon: A tiny amount of difference you are willing to ignore, like 0.00001.
terms.NaN: Short for Not a Number. A broken number you get from things like 0 divided by 0. A NaN position makes parts vanish.
terms.floor / ceil: Floor rounds DOWN to a whole number (2.7 becomes 2). Ceil rounds UP (2.1 becomes 3).
terms.absolute value: The number without its minus sign. The absolute value of -4 is 4.
terms.constant: A ready-made value that never changes, like `Vector3.zero`.
terms.NormalId: An Enum naming the six faces of a part: Top, Bottom, Front, Back, Left, Right.

examples.title: Move a part up by 5 studs
examples.place: Script inside a Part in Workspace
examples.code:
local part = script.Parent
part.Anchored = true

-- Add 5 to Y (height). X and Z stay the same.
part.Position = part.Position + Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)
explain: `Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)` means: 0 sideways, 5 up, 0 forward/back.
Adding two Vector3s adds each number to its partner: if the part was at (2, 3, 4) it ends up at (2, 8, 4).

examples.title: How far is the player from a part?
examples.place: Script in ServerScriptService (needs a Part named Goal in Workspace)
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local goal = workspace:WaitForChild("Goal")

while true do
	for _, player in Players:GetPlayers() do
		local character = player.Character
		local root = character and character:FindFirstChild("HumanoidRootPart")
		if root then
			-- Subtract to get the arrow from the goal to the player, then measure its length.
			local distance = (root.Position - goal.Position).Magnitude
			if distance < 10 then
				print(player.Name .. " is close to the goal! (" .. math.floor(distance) .. " studs)")
			end
		end
	end
	task.wait(1)
end
explain: `root.Position - goal.Position` gives an arrow that goes from the goal to the player.
`.Magnitude` is the length of that arrow, which is the distance in studs.
Example: goal at (0, 0, 0), player at (6, 0, 8): the arrow is (6, 0, 8) and its length is 10.

examples.title: Shoot a part toward a target
examples.place: Script in ServerScriptService (needs Parts named Cannon and Target in Workspace)
examples.code:
local cannon = workspace:WaitForChild("Cannon")
local target = workspace:WaitForChild("Target")

local ball = Instance.new("Part")
ball.Shape = Enum.PartType.Ball
ball.Size = Vector3.new(2, 2, 2)
ball.Position = cannon.Position + Vector3.new(0, 3, 0)
ball.Parent = workspace

-- Direction from the ball to the target, as a 1-stud-long arrow
local direction = (target.Position - ball.Position).Unit
-- Make the ball move 80 studs per second that way
ball.AssemblyLinearVelocity = direction * 80
explain: `(target - start)` is the full arrow from start to target. Its length is the distance.
`.Unit` shrinks it to length 1 so it only means "which way".
Multiplying by 80 makes an arrow 80 long, so the ball flies at 80 studs per second toward the target, no matter how far away it is.

examples.title: Can the guard see you? (Dot product)
examples.place: Script in ServerScriptService (needs a Part named Guard in Workspace)
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local guard = workspace:WaitForChild("Guard")

while true do
	for _, player in Players:GetPlayers() do
		local character = player.Character
		local root = character and character:FindFirstChild("HumanoidRootPart")
		if root then
			local facing = guard.CFrame.LookVector                     -- which way the guard looks
			local toPlayer = (root.Position - guard.Position).Unit      -- which way the player is
			local dot = facing:Dot(toPlayer)
			-- 1 = straight ahead, 0 = exactly to the side, -1 = straight behind
			if dot > 0.5 then
				print("The guard sees " .. player.Name)
			end
		end
	end
	task.wait(0.5)
end
explain: Both arrows are unit vectors (length 1), so the dot product is between -1 and 1.
1 means they point the exact same way: the player is straight in front.
0 means a right angle: the player is directly to the side.
-1 means opposite: the player is straight behind.
`dot > 0.5` means the player is within about 60 degrees of straight ahead, like a cone of vision.

gotchas: You cannot change one number in place: `part.Position.Y = 10` errors. Build a new one: `part.Position = Vector3.new(part.Position.X, 10, part.Position.Z)`.
Do not call `.Unit` on a zero vector (0, 0, 0). It gives NaN and parts can disappear. Check `.Magnitude > 0` first.
Y is up in Roblox, not Z.
Angles from `Angle` are in radians. Use `math.deg` to see degrees.
`Vector3 * Vector3` multiplies each number with its partner; it is NOT the dot or cross product. Use `:Dot` and `:Cross` for those.
Comparing with `==` can fail because of tiny rounding errors. Use `:FuzzyEq` to check "almost equal".
Part.Orientation is a Vector3 of DEGREES, but CFrame functions want radians.

datatype/Vector3int16.d:
The Vector3int16 data type represents a vector in 3D space with a signed 16-bit integer for its components. It is similar to Vector3 in that it allows for the same arithmetic operations, but it lacks commonly used vector functions.

Vector3int16 should not be confused with:

  • Vector3, a more precise and complete implementation for 3D vectors.
  • Vector2int16, a similar implementation for 2D vectors.

For each component:

  • The lower bound is -215, or -32,768.
  • The upper bound is 215 − 1, or 32,767.

Converting to Vector3

To convert a Vector3int16 to a Vector3, construct a Vector3 by passing each component of the Vector3int16 to Vector3.new():

local vector3int16 = Vector3int16.new(1, 2, 3)
local vector3 = Vector3.new(vector3int16.X, vector3int16.Y, vector3int16.Z)
print(vector3)  --> 1, 2, 3

Do not pass an entire Vector3int16 to Vector3.new(), as the constructor interprets a Vector3int16 as a 0 within its parameters without producing an error. This can lead to silent logic errors if you do something like:

local vector3int16 = Vector3int16.new(1, 2, 3)
local vector3 = Vector3.new(vector3int16)
print(vector3)  --> 0, 0, 0

Math Operations

The following math operations are valid for the Vector3int16 data type. For all operations, be mindful of the bounds associated with signed 16-bit integers, described earlier.

Operation Description
Datatype.Vector3int16 + Datatype.Vector3int16 Produces a Datatype.Vector3int16 whose components are the sum of the operands' respective components.
Datatype.Vector3int16 - Datatype.Vector3int16 Produces a Datatype.Vector3int16 whose components are the difference of the operands' respective components.
Datatype.Vector3int16 * Datatype.Vector3int16 Produces a Datatype.Vector3int16 whose components are the product of the operands' respective components.
Datatype.Vector3int16 / Datatype.Vector3int16 Produces a Datatype.Vector3int16 whose components are the quotient of the operands' respective components. The results of the division are rounded down.
Datatype.Vector3int16 * number Produces a Datatype.Vector3int16 whose components are the product of the respective Datatype.Vector3int16 components and the number (factor). This operation is commutative.
Datatype.Vector3int16 / number Produces a Datatype.Vector3int16 whose components are the quotient of the respective Datatype.Vector3int16 components and the number (divisor). The results of the division are rounded toward zero.

kid.simple: Divides matching numbers. The answers are rounded down to whole numbers.
kid.example: print(Vector3int16.new(10, 9, 8) / Vector3int16.new(3, 2, 2)) --> 3, 4, 4

m.d: Produces a Vector3int16 whose components are the product of the respective Vector3int16 components and the number (factor). This operation is commutative. Be mindful of the bounds associated with signed 16-bit integers, described earlier.
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.Vector3int16` whose components are the product of the respective `Datatype.Vector3int16` components and the number (factor). This operation is commutative.

kid.simple: Multiplies every number by the same amount. `number * Vector3int16` works too.
kid.example: print(Vector3int16.new(1, 2, 3) * 4) --> 4, 8, 12

m.d: Produces a Vector3int16 whose components are the quotient of the respective Vector3int16 components and the number (divisor). The results of the division are rounded toward zero. Be mindful of the bounds associated with signed 16-bit integers, described earlier.
m.s: Produces a `Datatype.Vector3int16` whose components are the quotient of the respective `Datatype.Vector3int16` components and the number (divisor). The results of the division are rounded toward zero.

kid.simple: Divides every number by the same amount. The answers are rounded toward zero (decimals dropped).
kid.example: print(Vector3int16.new(10, 9, 7) / 2) --> 5, 4, 3

kid.simple: Vector3int16 is like a Vector3 (X, Y, Z), but each number must be a WHOLE number between -32,768 and 32,767. It saves memory, but it has no handy tools like Magnitude or Unit. Most games never need it; you will usually use Vector3 instead.
kid.analogy: If Vector3 is a ruler that can measure tiny fractions, Vector3int16 is a ruler that only has whole-number marks and stops at 32,767.
whenToUse: When a Roblox feature specifically asks for one, for example building a Region3int16 (a box of whole-number spots used by some Terrain tools).
Almost never otherwise; use Vector3 for positions, sizes and directions.
kid.where: Built-in data type, works in Scripts and LocalScripts. Make one with `Vector3int16.new(x, y, z)`.

terms.integer: A whole number with no decimal part, like 3 or -40 (not 2.5).
terms.16-bit signed integer: A whole number stored in a small box of memory. It can only hold numbers from -32,768 to 32,767, and can be negative (that is what "signed" means).
terms.overflow: When a number is too big for its box and wraps around to the other end. Putting 32,768 into a 16-bit integer turns it into -32,768, like a car odometer rolling over.
terms.rounded down: Decimal parts are thrown away so you get a whole number, for example 3.9 becomes 3.
terms.component: One of the numbers inside the vector, like X or Y.

examples.title: Make one and turn it into a normal Vector3
examples.code:
local small = Vector3int16.new(1, 2, 3)
print(small.X, small.Y, small.Z) --> 1 2 3

-- Convert by passing each number separately
local normal = Vector3.new(small.X, small.Y, small.Z)
print(normal) --> 1, 2, 3
explain: `Vector3int16.new` stores three whole numbers.
To use it with Vector3 tools, copy each number into `Vector3.new` one by one.

gotchas: Do NOT write `Vector3.new(myVector3int16)`. It silently gives (0, 0, 0) with no error. Pass `.X, .Y, .Z` separately.
Decimals are thrown away: `Vector3int16.new(2.9, 0, 0).X` is 2.
Numbers past 32,767 wrap around to big negative numbers (overflow). Keep values in range, including after math.
